CLAUDE.content:
Contexto del proyecto — SOLE Voltaje

Este archivo es la memoria compartida del proyecto para agentes de IA (Claude, Gemini, etc.).
Actualízalo cuando cambie la estructura, los flujos o las convenciones del repositorio.


¿Qué es SOLE Voltaje?
Jardín digital de conocimiento práctico para comunidades rurales y semiurbanas de Colombia y Latinoamérica con baja conectividad. Enseña a personas —muchas con baja escolaridad, en zonas remotas— cómo mejorar su conectividad, conseguir equipos, convocar a su comunidad y usar internet en grupo.

URL producción: voltaje.solecolombia.org
Rama producción: voltaje
Stack: Quartz 4 (static site generator) + GitHub Pages
Idiomas: es/ (principal), en/, pt/ (traducidos con Gemini)
Organización GitHub: sole-colombia


Estructura del repositorio
voltaje-dev/
├── content/                   ← Working directory principal
│   ├── es/solve/              ← Soluciones en español
│   ├── es/inspire/            ← Inspiraciones en español
│   ├── es/glossary/           ← Conceptos/glosario en español
│   ├── es/disconnected/       ← Contenido desconectado
│   ├── en/                    ← Traducciones inglés (generadas)
│   ├── pt/                    ← Traducciones portugués (generadas)
│   ├── assets/                ← Imágenes (.webp preferido)
│   ├── templates/             ← Plantillas de contenido
│   ├── CLAUDE.md              ← Este archivo (memoria compartida)
│   └── .gemini/               ← Configuración agentes Gemini
│       ├── GEMINI.md          ← Memoria para Gemini CLI
│       └── skills/            ← Skills invocables
│           └── voltaje-editor/SKILL.md  ← Cacharrera Editora v2.7
├── docs/
│   ├── editorial/             ← Guías editoriales y prompts
│   └── tecnico/               ← Documentación técnica
├── scripts/                   ← Scripts de automatización
├── quartz/                    ← Código del sitio Quartz
│   └── components/            ← Componentes TSX personalizados
├── solutions_status.tsv       ← Estado de producción de soluciones
├── inspire_status.tsv         ← Estado de producción de inspiraciones
├── concepts_status.tsv        ← Estado de producción de conceptos
├── disconnected_status.tsv    ← Estado de producción de desconectados
└── PLAN.md                    ← Plan de desarrollo activo


Tipos de contenido
1. Soluciones (es/solve/solv-*.md)
Paso a paso concreto para construir, instalar o arreglar algo.
Frontmatter obligatorio:
title: "¿Cómo hacer X?"
resumen: "Una oración que diga qué logra el lector. Max 15 palabras."
date: AAAA-MM-DD
tags:
  - "Electricidad"        # Electricidad | Señal | Dispositivos | Espacio | Personas
permite:
  - "Compartir"           # Conseguir | Mejorar | Compartir | Medir
dificultad: "Muy Fácil"   # Muy Fácil | Fácil | Medio | Complejo
costo: "Gratis"           # Gratis | < USD 25 | USD 25 - 50 | > USD 50 | Gasto mensual
ayudantes: "Sin ayudantes" # Sin ayudantes | 1 persona | 2-3 personas | Más de 3 personas
tarda: "Minutos"          # Minutos | Horas | Días | Semanas
autor: "SOLE Colombia"
draft: false
Estructura del cuerpo:

Saludo según perfil de voz (sin encabezado)
## ¿Qué es [título]?
## ¿Para qué sirve?
## Antes de empezar...
## ¿Qué necesitas?
## ¿Cómo hacerlo? — pasos con formato > ### Paso N → [Acción]
## Recomendaciones
## ¿Cómo saber si esta solución funciona?
## Otros internets posibles
## Soluciones relacionadas
## Referencias
## Historial de cambios

2. Inspiraciones (es/inspire/insp-*.md)
Preguntas grandes, historias y reflexiones sobre conectividad comunitaria.
Frontmatter obligatorio:
title: "¿Pregunta grande?"
resumen: "..."
date: AAAA-MM-DD
tags:
  - "historias-potentes"  # o "vamos-a-romper", "te-ha-pasado", etc.
autor: "SOLE Colombia"
draft: false
3. Conceptos/Glosario (es/glossary/conc-*.md)
Definiciones de términos técnicos adaptadas para audiencias no técnicas.
4. Desconectados (es/disconnected/disc-*.md)
Recursos para comunidades sin acceso a internet.

Reglas de Markdown / Quartz

Nunca H1 en el cuerpo. Quartz lo genera desde title.
Wikilinks con flecha: [[es/solve/solv-nombre|Texto visible →]]
Imágenes con alt text: ![Descripción de acción](assets/images/carpeta/archivo.webp)
Pasos siempre dentro de blockquote: > ### Paso N → [Acción]
Callouts como blockquotes: > *Consejo: ...* > *Atención: ...* > *Ánimo: ...* > *Vas bien: ...* > *Para pensar: ...*
No archivos extra en content/ (no .txt, .csv, .json — solo .md y assets)
No comentarios HTML con metadatos en .md
Separadores --- entre secciones ##


Agentes disponibles
Cacharrera Editora (voltaje-editor)

Versión activa: v2.7
Archivo: content/.gemini/skills/voltaje-editor/SKILL.md
Rol: Creación y revisión de soluciones, inspiraciones y notas
NO es agente de código — solo trabaja con contenido editorial
Invocar en Gemini: @voltaje-editor
Invocar en Claude: a través del skill voltaje-editor

Agente de Frontmatter

Archivo: docs/editorial/PROMPT_AGENTE_FRONTMATTER_SOLUCIONES.md
Rol: Auditoría y análisis de frontmatter, criterios de dificultad, nivel editorial

en/disconnected/index.title: Disconnected
en/disconnected/index.summary: Learn about the Internet without being connected to the Internet
en/disconnected/index.content:
How to connect “the disconnected”?

This is one of the Big questions that inspired the creation of the platform you are currently on: SOLE Voltaje ⚡⚡

But… how can the 2.6 billion people who don’t have Internet access connect to a connectivity platform without being connected? 🤔

This is the Big question that inspired the creation of the tool you are currently using: The Disconnected (El Desconectado).

In 2024, the SOLE Colombia team designed a tool so that anyone, anywhere in the world, regardless of prior knowledge, could understand—in a practical and fun way—how the Internet works without having the Internet.
The tool is a deck of cards that invites people to navigate Internet concepts and connectivity solutions in a dynamic and simple way. With The Disconnected, you can:

Learn key Internet concepts (e.g., what megabytes are, what types of mobile signals exist, what a server is, etc.).
Identify how good your signal is for accessing the Internet (a mini-diagnostic).
Learn about and evaluate the connectivity solution(s) that work best in specific contexts.

The interesting thing about this deck of cards is that, like everything in Voltaje, it is a tool built day by day in community. This means that we will keep adjusting it based on the lessons and contributions from the communities we work with and from people like you who decide to use it.
Here is a summary of how it works 👇🏽

About The Disconnected
This tool consists of three types of cards:

Tinkering cards (Cartas cacharreras)
Navigator cards (Cartas navegadoras)
Connection cards (Cartas conectivas)

There is no specific order, so you can start with any of the three types of cards. Here is what you can do with each type 👇🏽

Tinkering cards: How is your signal?


To understand how the internet works wherever you are in the world, you can start by “tinkering” (cacharrear) with the signal you have. But what signal do you have? How does it work? We have two cards that will help you answer these questions in practice: how to tinker with your mobile signal? or how to tinker with your WiFi signal?
From this first distinction, you can identify how the Internet signal reaches any device! Just flip over either of the two cards and follow the instructions to start navigating.


Navigator cards: What would you like more?


These cards will help you navigate the internet while learning about the importance of asking Big Questions. You will also learn about how the Internet travels, how fast it is, what signal you have, how to make the most of it, and much more. You can use these cards in a thousand ways. We’ll share one of many possible dynamics:


Randomly choose 2 cards and place the “What would you like more?” card in the middle.


Answer what you would like more; which do you prefer… To be the Internet traveling through a cable across the earth and oceans, or to travel at the speed of light? You can combine the cards however you wish.


Flip the card you chose and read what it says. Each card will bring you new concepts or ideas about the Internet. Some of them will give you specific instructions—follow them! All the cards are connected to each other. Go ahead and look for the next one, and the next, and the next. Navigate them!


If you are with friends, family, or people from a community, you can do several rounds where everyone answers and shares what they would like more, reading the information and solving the challenges there as a team. We invite you to try all the variations you can think of!





Connection cards: What works best for me to connect?


These cards present different connectivity solutions. You can open any card, follow the instructions, and identify whether that solution works for what you want to learn or solve. These cards are “connective” because they will lead you to find solutions to get connected to the Internet.
Depending on your connectivity situation or your learning interests, you will find three types of cards for this category:

What are the differences between these cards? Flip them over and find out for yourself!


Recipe book of solutions: How to connect to the Internet?


In the recipe book of solutions, you will find a summary of the solutions presented in the connection cards. Remember that you can consult the solutions in the recipe book or directly on the SOLE Voltaje platform if you need more detail to carry out the solution.


The Disconnected is inspired by diverse connectivity challenges
SOLE Voltaje, and The Disconnected in particular, were designed for people with diverse connectivity challenges. After a survey conducted in 2020 by SOLE Colombia, we discovered that half of the people we interact with do not have Internet for one or more of the following reasons:

There is no signal: In the places where they live, there is no mobile or cable coverage. In some places, especially in scattered rural areas, there are public schools with satellite connectivity provided by the government, but its quality and consistency are poor.
The signal is bad: In other spots, the signal is intermittent, which prevents video calls or streaming videos. Usually, this forces people to travel across the territory to find a better connection point.
They don’t have money to pay for it: Even if a signal is available, the service represents a very high cost for a personal or family budget.
They don’t know what the Internet is for: Although many people mention the previous reasons, their answers suggest that there is also a lack of knowledge about the potential of the internet, as priority is given to paying for other services like satellite television. In many communities, there is a belief that the Internet is limited to Facebook and WhatsApp, as these are the applications that are usually included for free in mobile plans.


Do you want to take The Disconnected to a real disconnected context?
If you live in a place with very low or zero Internet connection, or if you know or work with a community or group of people in these conditions, you can use The Disconnected to navigate the Internet without being connected.

Write to us at hola@solecolombia.org if you are interested in having the tool printed (the one you see in the photos) or in digital format (ready for you to make it yourself).

en/glossary/conc-2g-net.title: "2G Network"
en/glossary/conc-2g-net.summary: "The technology that allowed the leap from analog to digital."
en/glossary/conc-2g-net.content:
The 2G (Second Generation) network is the mobile technology that marked the transition from analog to digital, making encrypted voice calls and text messages (SMS) possible. It’s used for basic voice and text communication, while also supporting some limited data services like email and low-speed internet access. It was fundamental to the global expansion of mobile telephony and served as the foundation for later technologies, even though its data speed is quite slow.
What is the 2G network?

Digitalization of communications: 2G was the first generation to adopt digital technology for mobile communications, replacing previous analog systems.
GSM Technology: It is based on the Global System for Mobile Communications (GSM).
Main services: Its primary function is voice calling and sending/receiving text messages (SMS).

What is it used for?

Voice calls: It allowed for encrypted voice calls with better quality than the analog generation.
SMS messaging: It made sending and receiving text messages possible, which revolutionized the way we communicate.
Limited data services: With the introduction of services like GPRS (General Packet Radio Service) →, it opened the door to basic data services, allowing for very limited internet access and email.
Coverage: It’s important because it provides good coverage in rural or mountainous areas where more advanced networks haven’t reached yet.
IoT devices (Internet of Things): It is still used in some machine-to-machine (M2M) communication devices and GPS tracking hardware.

Its legacy and future

Foundation for the future: 2G laid the groundwork for more advanced technologies like 3G and 4G by proving the efficiency of digital systems.
Gradual sunsetting: Due to its low data speed compared to newer generations, most carriers are shutting down and replacing 2G networks to reallocate those frequencies to more efficient technologies like 4G and 5G.

en/glossary/conc-3g-4g-antennas.title: 3G/4G Antenna
en/glossary/conc-3g-4g-antennas.summary: A device to connect to 3G or 4G networks.
en/glossary/conc-3g-4g-antennas.content:
A 3/4G antenna, also known as an LTE antenna, is a gadget that helps you get online using 4G and 3G mobile networks. These antennas handle sending and receiving radio signals to hook up your smartphones, tablets, and modems to the cellular network, giving your connection speed and quality a nice boost.
The lowdown:

How it works: 3/4G antennas act like a bridge between your devices and the cell towers, making wireless communication possible.
Types of antennas: There are a few different kinds out there, like directional ones that focus on a specific spot for better range, and omnidirectional ones that cover a wider area.
Boosting your signal: Using a 3/4G antenna can really beef up your signal, especially if you’re in a dead zone or stuck indoors.
Aiming matters: Getting the orientation right is key to snagging the best signal—ideally, you want it pointed straight at the nearest cell tower.
Connecting to devices: 3/4G antennas hook up to your gear using coaxial cables → and SMA connectors, or adapters if you’re using MIFI routers →.
MIMO technology: Some 4G antennas use MIMO (Multiple Input Multiple Output) tech, which uses multiple antennas to bump up your connection speed and reliability.
Difference from WiFi: Unlike WiFi antennas → that run on 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands, 4G antennas use different frequency bands set by your carrier.
Rural use: Out in the sticks where the signal can be pretty spotty, outdoor antennas are a lifesaver for getting a decent internet connection.

en/glossary/conc-ai-helper.title: "Wise Assistant (Local AI)"
en/glossary/conc-ai-helper.summary: "A consultant program that lives on your server and helps you by processing your own information."
en/glossary/conc-ai-helper.content:
The Wise Assistant is a special Artificial Intelligence program that lives and works right inside your own computer or server →. Unlike other AIs, it doesn’t need the internet because everything it knows comes from the files and “digital books” you keep in its memory yourself.
In our tech kitchen:

It acts as an Expert Consultant.
It’s not the one doing the heavy lifting (that’s the job of the Processor or Chef →), but rather someone who analyzes the recipes and gives you tips.
Internal reading: The assistant doesn’t go out into the street looking for answers; it reads the manuals, guides, and documents you have in the pantry (Storage →). That’s why it’s safe and private: what happens in the kitchen, stays in the kitchen.


The importance of the Countertop (RAM)
Even though the assistant is very smart, it has one limitation: to be able to think and answer, it needs to spread all the information out on the Work Countertop (RAM Memory →).

If you have plenty of RAM (a big countertop), the assistant can read many pages at once and answer you quickly.
If you have very little RAM (a small countertop), the assistant has to keep opening and closing folders constantly, which makes it take a long time to give you an answer.


In short: The assistant is only as agile as the space you give it to work on the countertop and how many of the chef’s helpers are assisting it.


What is it for?

Analyzing your own data: You can ask it to summarize meeting minutes from the neighborhood or help you find a date in a long document.
Educational support: It helps students understand difficult concepts by explaining them in simple terms.
Translation and writing: It helps translate texts from one language to another or write formal letters for the community.

en/glossary/conc-antenna.title: "Antenna"
en/glossary/conc-antenna.summary: "A device that receives and transmits waves."
en/glossary/conc-antenna.content:
In a nutshell, an antenna is just a gadget designed to send and/or pick up electromagnetic waves.
About antennas


Transmission: Antennas beam electromagnetic waves out into space, making long-distance communication possible. Nasa


Reception: They can also catch those electromagnetic waves and turn them into electrical signals that a receiver can actually make sense of. Invisible pillars of wireless communication


Types of antennas: There’s a whole bunch of them out there, like satellite dishes, dipoles, and Yagi antennas →, each with its own quirks for different jobs. Types of antennas


Applications: Antennas are the backbone of radio, TV, mobile communications →, wireless networks →, and a ton of other tech that relies on electromagnetic waves. Vicente Miralles Segarra Telecommunications Museum




References

Nasa
Wikipedia

en/glossary/conc-bandwidth.title: "Bandwidth"
en/glossary/conc-bandwidth.summary: "It is the maximum amount of information that can travel through your network at the same time."
en/glossary/conc-bandwidth.content:
Bandwidth is the capacity of a network connection to transport data. It is usually measured in Megabits per second (Mbps).
In our tech kitchen:

It’s the Width of the Hallway leading to the kitchen.
If the hallway is narrow, only one person can pass at a time with their plate; if there are too many people, they get bunched up and everyone arrives at the table late.
If the hallway is wide, many people can come and go with plenty of food at the same time, nice and smooth.


Don’t confuse it with speed
A lot of folks think bandwidth is speed, but it’s actually capacity. A wide hallway doesn’t make you walk any faster, but it does let more people walk together without getting stuck. The more bandwidth your community has, the more neighbors can use the server at the same time without things getting sluggish.

Related concepts

WiFi Signal →
Local Network →
How to measure bandwidth? →

en/glossary/conc-canva.title: "Canva"
en/glossary/conc-canva.summary: "An online graphic design platform for everyone."
en/glossary/conc-canva.content:
Canva is a free online graphic design platform that lets anyone—whether you’re a pro or a total beginner—whip up all sorts of professional-looking designs.
It’s got a super simple, intuitive interface packed with a huge range of templates, images, fonts, and graphic elements to make creating presentations, social media posts, infographics, cards, resumes, and a whole lot more a breeze.

en/glossary/conc-client.title: "Client"
en/glossary/conc-client.content:
In computing, a client is a piece of hardware or software that accesses a service or resource provided by a server →.
The term can refer to either a physical device (like a computer or smartphone) or a software program (like a web browser) used to interact with a server. (Source: Brave)
More about “clients”


Client role: The client sends requests to the server to access data, services, or resources that the server provides. (Source: IONOS)


Client-server interaction: In a client-server architecture, the client initiates the communication and the server → responds to the client’s requests. (Source: IONOS)


Examples:

A web browser like Google Chrome or Mozilla Firefox is a client that requests web pages from a server. (Source: Brave)
An email program that connects to a server to send and receive messages is another example. (Source: Linube)
A mobile device accessing a cloud application is another example of a client. (Source: TechTarget)

Types of clients:

Thick clients: They have local storage capacity and can run applications independently. (Source: Slideshare)
Thin clients: They rely primarily on the server for application execution and data storage. (Source: Slideshare)

Why are they important?
Clients allow users to access a wide range of services and resources remotely, making it easy to interact with distributed systems and networks. (Source: Oracle)

en/glossary/conc-coaxial-cable.title: "Coaxial cable"
en/glossary/conc-coaxial-cable.content:
A coaxial cable is a type of cable used to carry high-frequency electrical signals.
It has two concentric conductors:

The central one, called the core: responsible for carrying information.
The outer one, which looks like a tube and is called the mesh, shield, or braid: it serves as a ground reference and current return path.

Between the two, there is an insulating dielectric layer, and the quality of the cable mainly depends on its characteristics.
The whole assembly is usually protected by an insulating jacket (also called the outer sheath).

💡 Parts of the RG-59 coaxial cable (for signals). See also: RG6 Cable →
A: plastic protective jacket (thermoplastic elastomer)
B: copper mesh (shielded conductor made of copper-clad aluminum braid)
C: insulator (foam dielectric)
D: central conductor or copper core (copper-clad steel).
References:
A coaxial cable consists of electronic signals that make up the information Wikipedia.gov

en/glossary/conc-command-prompt.title: "CMD Command Prompt"
en/glossary/conc-command-prompt.summary: "Chatting with the computer... but in its own language."
en/glossary/conc-command-prompt.content:
In the context of Windows, CMD, or Command Prompt, it is a command-line interface that lets you interact with the operating system → using text commands.
It’s a handy tool for running commands, managing files, troubleshooting issues, and automating tasks.
The Command Prompt (CMD) is:

A command interpreter: CMD takes commands typed by the user and translates them into actions that the operating system can understand and execute.
An alternative to the graphical interface: Although Windows has a GUI, CMD offers a faster and more efficient way to get certain things done, especially for power users or for automating processes.
A troubleshooting tool: CMD lets you run commands to diagnose and fix system issues, like network errors or configuration hiccups.
A foundation for scripts: CMD is the base for creating and running scripts, which makes it easy to automate repetitive and complex tasks.

In short, CMD is an essential tool for managing and administering Windows systems, offering a powerful and flexible way to interact with the operating system through text commands.

en/glossary/conc-cpu-processor.title: "Processor (CPU)"
en/glossary/conc-cpu-processor.summary: "It is the computer's brain in charge of executing all instructions."
en/glossary/conc-cpu-processor.content:
slug: conc-cpu
The Processor or CPU (Central Processing Unit) is the component that crunches the numbers and makes the decisions in your rig.
In our tech kitchen:

The Processor is The Chef.
It’s the one who grabs the ingredients from the counter (RAM Memory →), reads the recipe (the program), and whips up the final result.
The chef’s speed (measured in Gigahertz or GHz) determines how fast information is processed or how quickly they can get things cooked.


Why does it matter?
A chef can have “multiple arms” (called Cores). If it has 4 cores, it’s like having 4 chefs working at the same time on different dishes. This is what lets your computer handle several tasks at once without freezing up.

Related concepts

RAM Memory →
Hardware →
Operating System →

en/glossary/conc-daemon.title: "Daemon (service or program)"
en/glossary/conc-daemon.content:
A service, resident program, or daemon is a special type of program that runs in the background, rather than being directly controlled by the user. These types of programs stick around in the system, meaning they can run persistently or restart themselves if you try to “kill” the process, depending on how the daemon is set up and the system’s policies. The name comes from the backronym Daemon (Disk And Execution Monitor).
Daemons usually have the following characteristics:

They don’t have a direct “interface” for the user, neither graphical nor textual.
They don’t use standard input/output to report errors or log their activity; instead, they use system files in specific areas (/var/log/ in most modern UNIX systems) or rely on other specialized logging daemons like syslogd.

For example, a machine hosting a web server → will use an HTTP daemon to provide the service so that visitors to said website can access it. Another example is “chronological” daemons like cron, which handle scheduled tasks like system maintenance in the background.

en/glossary/conc-dhcp-protocol.title: "DHCP Protocol"
en/glossary/conc-dhcp-protocol.summary: "The system that automatically assigns an IP address to each device that connects."
en/glossary/conc-dhcp-protocol.content:
DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) is the service in charge of assigning IP addresses automatically.
In our tech kitchen:

DHCP is The Host.
When someone arrives at the kitchen (connects to the WiFi), the Host greets them and says: “Welcome, today you’ll be identified as number 15 (IP 192.168.1.15)“.
Thanks to the Host, you don’t have to configure anything manually on your phone; they make sure everyone has a name and a seat at the table.


Why is it useful?
DHCP allows devices to request and receive an IP address from a DHCP server, simplifying network management and avoiding IP address conflicts. (Sources: Akamai and Arsys)
Imagine 20 people show up to a community meeting with their phones. Without a Host (DHCP), you’d have to go one by one assigning numbers so they don’t clash. DHCP does it in milliseconds.

Related concepts

IP Address →
Local Network →

en/glossary/conc-dns.title: "DNS (Domain Name System)"
en/glossary/conc-dns.summary: "It is the system that translates easy-to-remember names into IP addresses."
en/glossary/conc-dns.content:
DNS is like a massive address book that links a domain name (like google.com) to a numerical address (IP →). (Sources: Cloudflare and Wikipedia)
In our tech kitchen:

DNS is like Nicknames.
Instead of telling the delivery guy to go to “House 192.168.1.15,” we just tell him to head over to “David’s” or the “Community Kitchen.”
The nickname system is way easier for us humans to remember, but the system knows exactly which numerical address belongs to each nickname.


How does it work?
When you type a domain name into your browser, it sends a request to a DNS server. The server looks up the corresponding IP address and sends it back to your browser so it can connect to the web server hosting the site.
On your Pocket Server →, we set up a local nickname like solevoltaje.local. That way, any neighbor who connects to your WiFi just has to type that name into their browser to get into the “Community Kitchen,” without having to memorize any tricky numbers.

Related concepts

IP Address →
Nginx Web Server →
Local Network →

en/glossary/conc-dnsmasq.title: "Lightweight DNS forwarder and DHCP server"
en/glossary/conc-dnsmasq.content:
Dnsmasq is a piece of software that provides Domain Name System (DNS) caching, a Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP →) server, router advertisement, and network boot features for small computer networks, all built as free software.
Dnsmasq is pretty light on system resources, runs on Linux, BSD, Android, and macOS, and comes bundled with most Linux distributions.
As a result, “it’s found in many home routers → and various gadgets for the Internet of Things,” and it’s even included in Android.
If you want to dig into the details, you can check out Wikipedia.

en/glossary/conc-docker-container.title: "Docker Containers"
en/glossary/conc-docker-container.summary: "A portable, pre-equipped kitchen that works the same anywhere."
en/glossary/conc-docker-container.content:
slug: docker
Docker is a technology that lets you “package” an application along with everything it needs to run (like languages, databases, and settings) inside a box called a Container.
In our kitchen analogy:

Docker is a pre-equipped portable kitchen.
Imagine you want to set up a restaurant in another neighborhood. Instead of hauling bricks, pots, and hiring a plumber, you just bring a container that already has the stove installed, the pots in their place, and the recipes ready to go. You just plug it in and—boom—you’re ready to cook!
This ensures that if an application (like a digital library) works on my computer, it will work exactly the same on your Raspberry Pi or the school server.


What’s it for?
For community projects, Docker is a godsend because it lets you share complex systems (like a file server or a local AI) “plug-and-play” style. You just hand over the “container,” and the other person doesn’t have to wrestle with tricky installations; everything fires up on the first try.

Related concepts

Server →
Pocket Server →

en/glossary/conc-domain-name.title: "Domain name"
en/glossary/conc-domain-name.summary: "Like a home address, but for a website on the Internet."
en/glossary/conc-domain-name.content:
A domain name is a unique, easy-to-remember address used to access a website or an internet service.
Think of it like a website’s mailing address, but instead of numbers, it uses text. For example, “solecolombia.org” is a domain name. It lets users get to websites and services without having to memorize complicated IP addresses →. (Source: Google Help)
In more technical terms, a domain name is a way to translate a numerical IP address (like 192.0.2.1) into a string of text that’s easy to remember and type, like “example.com.” This translation process is handled by the Domain Name System (DNS) →, which acts like a directory that matches domain names to their corresponding IP addresses.
Here are a few key points about domain names:

Ease of use: Domain names make it much easier for people to find and visit websites, since they’re way simpler to remember and type than IP addresses.
Online identity: A domain name is essentially the identity of a website or service on the internet. It’s what users will type into their browser to visit your site.
Ownership and registration: Domain names are registered through authorized registrars and are paid for annually to keep them under your name.
Components of a domain: A domain name typically consists of two main parts: the name (e.g., “solecolombia”) and the extension or top-level domain (e.g., “.org”).

A domain name is an essential tool for navigating the internet, allowing users to access websites and services easily and efficiently, while also serving as a website’s identity on the web.

en/glossary/conc-edge-connection.title: "EDGE Connection"
en/glossary/conc-edge-connection.content:
The EDGE connection, in the context of mobile phone technology, refers either to “Enhanced Data rates for GSM Evolution” (EDGE)—a 2G network that acts as a bridge to 3G to provide basic internet—or to the concept of “Edge Computing,” a method of processing data near its source to speed up high-speed applications and services on connected devices, such as the Internet of Things (IoT).
It is an evolution of GPRS → that boosts data transfer speeds on 2G mobile networks →, serving as a stepping stone toward 3G networks.
It allows for a faster data connection than standard 2G, which was handy for basic tasks like video calls, messaging, and web browsing before 3G networks came along. The “E” symbol on a phone means you’re hooked up to this network.

en/glossary/conc-ethernet.title: "Ethernet connection/cable"
en/glossary/conc-ethernet.content:
An Ethernet connection is a technology that lets you hook up electronic devices to a local area network (LAN) → or a wide area network (WAN) using a cable. Its main job is moving data between devices, whether you’re sharing files or just getting online.
In a nutshell:

Wired connection: Ethernet uses cables—usually RJ45s—to get devices talking to each other. There are different types of Ethernet cables, sorted by their transfer speeds and network frequency. Ethernet gives you faster speeds and a much more stable connection than wireless options like Wi-Fi →, plus it’s safer and easier on the wallet.
Connects devices: You can use Ethernet to link up all sorts of gear, including computers, routers, gaming consoles, smart TVs, and more. It’s the go-to tech for connecting devices in the same space, like your home or office.
Transmits data: Through these cables, devices can send and receive data packets, making it easy to communicate and swap info.
Versus Wi-Fi: While Wi-Fi is definitely more convenient, Ethernet is the way to go if you want the best experience in terms of speed, stability, and security.

Bottom line: Ethernet is a fundamental piece of tech for wired data networks, providing a reliable and efficient way to get your devices connected and sharing info.

en/glossary/conc-firewall.title: "Firewall"
en/glossary/conc-firewall.summary: "It is a security system that controls who enters and leaves your network."
en/glossary/conc-firewall.content:
A Firewall is a security tool that monitors network traffic and decides whether to allow or block information based on a set of defined rules.
In our tech kitchen:

The Firewall is The Doorman.
He’s standing at the kitchen door, keeping an eye on every ingredient and every person trying to get in.
If someone tries to sneak in something rotten (a virus) or barge in uninvited (an attack), the doorman shuts the door on them to protect the chef and the diners.


Why does it matter?
In a community network, the Firewall ensures that outsiders can’t access neighbors’ private information or mess with how the Pocket Server → runs. It’s like having a smart lock on your kitchen door.

Related concepts

Server →
Local Network →
SSH Protocol →

en/glossary/conc-firmware.title: "Firmware"
en/glossary/conc-firmware.summary: "It is the basic software that comes embedded in the chips of your devices."
en/glossary/conc-firmware.content:
slug: firmware
Firmware is a type of computer program that provides low-level control for a device’s specific hardware. It sits “right in the middle” between the hardware and the software.
In our tech kitchen:

Firmware is The Stove’s Instruction Manual.
It’s the factory-set instructions that tell the stove how to ignite when you turn the knob, or tell the router how its lights should blink.


Why does it matter?
Sometimes, devices need a “firmware update.” It’s like the manufacturer sending over a new page for the stove’s manual so it uses less gas or runs more safely. Keeping it up to date helps your pocket server stay nice and stable.

Related concepts

Hardware →
Operating System →

en/glossary/conc-flashdrive-usb.title: "USB Flash Drive"
en/glossary/conc-flashdrive-usb.summary: "It's like a small portable trunk to take your information anywhere."
en/glossary/conc-flashdrive-usb.content:
title: USB Flash Drive
slug: usb-flash-drive
path: /glossary/usb-flash-drive
The USB Flash Drive (also known as a “thumb drive,” “pen drive,” or “stick”) is a small storage device that plugs into a computer via a USB port →.
In our kitchen analogy:

The USB drive is like a lunchbox or a small container.
It’s perfect for carrying a portion of food (your files) from one kitchen (computer) to another, without having to lug the whole pantry (Hard Drive →) along with you.


A bit of history
USB drives popped up in the late 90s and basically kicked floppy disks and CDs to the curb. Back then, just to save a single song or a document, you needed a clunky, noisy square disk that would break if you even looked at it wrong.
The USB drive changed the game because it’s small, tough, and doesn’t need batteries or extra cables. Its capacity has grown like crazy: nowadays, a drive the size of a finger can hold thousands of books or hundreds of movies.

What’s it good for?

Carrying files: Documents, photos, or music.
Backing up info: Keeping a spare copy of your stuff outside of your computer.
Installing software: It’s often used to install an Operating System → (like Windows or Linux) on a new machine.


A quick heads-up…

Heads up: USB drives are super handy but easy to lose. Never keep sensitive info (like passwords) on them without protection. They’re also one of the easiest ways for viruses to hop from one computer to another; make sure to scan them regularly.


Related concepts

USB Connection →
Storage (Hard Drive and SSD) →
SD Memory →

en/glossary/conc-gprs.title: "GPRS (General Packet Radio Service)"
en/glossary/conc-gprs.content:
GPRS was a key technology that introduced the concept of packet-switched data transfer to mobile networks, laying the groundwork for the mobile data services we take for granted today. It remains quite handy for applications where high-speed data transfer isn’t really a must.

General Packet Radio Service: This means information is broken down into small “packets” of data, which are sent independently across the network.
GPRS is a data communication protocol that runs on top of second-generation (2G) mobile networks →, acting as an upgrade to GSM technology.
Instead of using a dedicated, continuous channel for data (like GSM), GPRS allocates network resources only when data is actually being sent, which makes it way more efficient.

What’s it good for?

Internet Access and Mobile Data: It let users hop onto the internet from their mobile devices, even if the speeds were a bit modest.
Multimedia Messaging (MMS) and Email: It made sending and receiving messages more complex than simple SMS a breeze.
Location Services: It was used to provide location-based services through the mobile network.
Security Alarms: GPRS is still relevant in alarm systems today, as it allows for the secure transmission of alarm signals without needing to rely on a landline.

en/glossary/conc-hardware.title: "Hardware"
en/glossary/conc-hardware.summary: "It is the physical part of your equipment, everything you can touch."
en/glossary/conc-hardware.content:
Hardware refers to all the physical components of a computer system. It’s the metal, plastic, and circuitry that give the machine its body.
In our tech kitchen:

Hardware is the utensils and the furniture.
The pot (the computer), the burners (the processor), the countertop (the RAM), and the shelves (the hard drive).
Without hardware, the software (Operating System →) wouldn’t have anywhere to “cook” anything.


Why does taking care of it matter?
Just like a pot stops working right if it gets burnt or bent, if your hardware gets knocked around, wet, or overheated, the system will fail even if the recipes (the software) are perfect. Keeping your hardware clean and cool is the secret sauce to making your pocket-sized server last for years.

Related concepts

Software (Operating System) →
Processor (CPU) →
RAM Memory →

en/glossary/conc-hostapd-daemon.title: "Hostapd Daemon"
en/glossary/conc-hostapd-daemon.summary: "An Internet access point from your computer."
en/glossary/conc-hostapd-daemon.content:
A Hostapd (host access point daemon) is a user-space daemon that lets a network interface card (NIC) pull double duty as a wireless access point (AP) and an authentication server.
Basically, it turns your computer into a router Wi-Fi →, letting other gadgets hop onto the internet through it.
In more detail:

Access Point (AP): Hostapd sets up a wireless network that other devices can connect to, just like a regular router.
Authentication Server: It handles the heavy lifting of verifying users trying to join the network, making sure only the devices you’ve given the green light can get in.
IEEE 802.11: Hostapd runs on the IEEE 802.11 protocol—the gold standard for wireless networking—which covers everything from managing access points to authentication (WPA/WPA2) and keeping your network secure.
Implementations: There are a few versions of hostapd out there, like the one from Jouni Malinen (the go-to choice), OpenBSD, and Devicescape.
Linux and FreeBSD: Hostapd plays nice with Linux (Host AP, madwifi, and mac80211-based drivers) and FreeBSD (net80211).
Common Use: You’ll mostly see it used on things like Raspberry Pi to whip up Wi-Fi hotspots or in wireless security testing setups.

en/glossary/conc-hspa-technology.title: "HSPA Technology (High-Speed Packet Access)"
en/glossary/conc-hspa-technology.content:
HSPA stands for “High-Speed Packet Access” and is an enhancement technology for 3G mobile networks that boosts the speed and efficiency of data transfers, both for downloading (HSDPA) and uploading (HSUPA).
It’s basically there to let mobile devices hop onto the internet at speeds way faster than basic 3G networks, making it a breeze to use data-heavy services on smartphones → and tablets, especially in spots where 4G or 5G aren’t quite reaching yet.
What is HSPA?

HSPA is a third-generation (3G) technology that gives a nice upgrade to UMTS and WCDMA networks by packing in HSDPA for downloads and HSUPA for uploads.
HSDPA (High-Speed Downlink Packet Access): Cranks up your download speeds, so you can browse the web faster and grab those big files without waiting forever.
HSUPA (High-Speed Uplink Packet Access): Gives your upload speeds a kick, making it much easier to post photos, videos, and other hefty files to the web.

What is HSPA good for?

Faster data speeds: HSPA offers way punchier data speeds compared to the original 3G networks, giving you an experience that feels a lot like a DSL connection.
Better network efficiency: It uses clever tricks like advanced modulation and makes better use of the spectrum to move data around more efficiently.
Access to data services: It lets your mobile devices tap into high-speed services like web browsing, video streaming, and app downloads, keeping everything running smooth.
Support for multiple services at once: With 3G and HSPA, your phone can handle voice calls and data services at the same time without breaking a sweat.
Staying connected in dead zones: Even though 4G and 5G are the big players now, HSPA is still a workhorse and is super important for keeping you connected in rural areas or when the 4G network is feeling a bit sluggish or crowded.

en/glossary/conc-imei-code.title: "IMEI Code"
en/glossary/conc-imei-code.summary: "The identification document for your cell phone."
en/glossary/conc-imei-code.content:
The IMEI is a unique 15-digit code that identifies every mobile phone worldwide. It stands for “International Mobile Equipment Identity” and acts like a digital ID card for your phone, letting carriers tell one device apart from another on their networks. (Source: BBVA)

Unique ID: The IMEI is a one-of-a-kind serial number for every phone, making it easy to distinguish from any other device. (Source: Enacom)
Network info: Carriers use it to identify your device whenever it connects to the network, which allows them to track, lock, or unlock your phone. (Source:BBVA)
Security and control: The IMEI is used to report stolen or lost phones so they can be blocked, preventing them from being used with other SIM cards. (Source:BBC)
How to find it? You can find your phone’s IMEI by dialing *#06# on your keypad, checking your device settings, looking at the original box, or checking under the battery. (Source:T-Mobile)
Usefulness: Beyond security, the IMEI is handy for getting info about your device, like the model, brand, and country of origin.


  
  

It’s not the same as a SIM: Unlike the SIM card →, which you can swap between phones, the IMEI is a unique identifier for the device itself.

en/glossary/conc-information-system.title: "Information System (IS)"
en/glossary/conc-information-system.summary: "Physical and logical elements that allow us to exchange information."
en/glossary/conc-information-system.content:
We define a computer system as the set of physical and logical elements responsible for receiving, storing, and processing data to then deliver it as results. The framework of a computer system encompasses everything that contains a tangible part (hardware →) and a logical part (software →).
Nowadays, computer systems play a key role in human organization, as they turn out to be a powerful tool for exchanging information and building computer networks that overcome the barrier of distance.
Components of a computer system
The elements that make up the basic structure of every computer system are:

Hardware: covers all the physical parts of the system, that is, everything you can touch. In the case of a computer, these elements of the computer system would be: the screen, the keyboard, or the mouse.
Software: refers to the logical part of any computer system, the intangible side. It is the set of programs including data, instructions, applications, etc., that allow the user to communicate with the hardware to perform various tasks.
IT personnel: anyone who uses the system in some way, including software creators, programmers, or general users.

Characteristics of a computer system
Some characteristics that define a computer system are:

Computer systems are designed to process, store, obtain, and receive information.
They provide a user-friendly interface for people to use and manage.
They facilitate process automation, since the programming of a computer system is aimed at performing tasks autonomously.
Their primary goal is to offer new and better living conditions to human beings.

Classification of computer systems
Computer systems can be classified according to their:

Processing volume: depending on their capacity to process and manage data.
Usage: that is, the use given to the computer system, whether it is to fulfill tasks with limited criteria or to handle a larger number of variables.
Function: depending on whether it is designed to fulfill specific purposes within a series of jobs. It could be programmed to provide suggestions for decision-making or to make a decision on its own based on collected data.
Grouping: depending on whether they are isolated systems or part of networks of equipment interconnected in private, local, wide-area networks, and so on.

Once we understand what computer systems are, we move on to name some practical applications, that is, what a computer system is used for in the real world. (Source: Universidad Isabel I)

en/glossary/conc-interface.title: Interface
en/glossary/conc-interface.summary: A point of contact or connection between two systems.
en/glossary/conc-interface.content:
Generally speaking, an interface is a point of contact or connection between two systems, components, or entities that allows for interaction and the exchange of information between them.
It can be physical, like the connection between a keyboard and a computer, or logical, like the way a program talks to the operating system →.
Types of interfaces:

User Interface (UI): This is how a user interacts with a system, whether it’s a program, a webpage, or a device. It includes the visual and functional elements that let the user take action and navigate through the system. (Source: Wikipedia)
Application Programming Interface (API): This defines how different software programs or components can talk to each other, allowing them to use functions and data from other programs. (Source: Microsoft)
Network Interface: This is the connection point between devices on a network, like a network interface card (NIC) that hooks a computer up to a network. (Source: Microsoft)
Brain-Computer Interface (BCI): This is cutting-edge tech that allows for direct communication between the brain and an external device, like a prosthetic. (Source: Wikipedia)

In short, an interface makes it easy for different parts to interact and swap info, whether they’re physical, logical, or conceptual.
Wireless interfaces
A wireless interface is a mechanism that lets electronic devices talk to each other without needing physical cables, using radio waves or other wireless tech. It lets you connect to computer networks, like Wi-Fi, or communicate between nearby devices, like with Bluetooth.
In more detail:

Cable-free communication: Unlike wired interfaces, which need physical connections like Ethernet or USB cables, wireless interfaces use radio waves or other tech to beam data back and forth. (Source: Mastervolt)
Common types: The most common examples of wireless interfaces include Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11), Bluetooth, and NFC. (Source: Fibermall)
How it works: These interfaces are usually built into wireless network interface cards (WNICs) or adapters, which plug into devices and let them chat with other devices or networks via radio waves. (Source: Quora)
Applications: Wireless interfaces are essential for keeping mobile devices like laptops, smartphones, and tablets connected, and for setting up wireless local area networks (WLAN or Wi-Fi). (Source: Cisco)
Security: Wireless interfaces usually come with security features, like WPA3, to keep the info being sent safe and sound. (Source: Fibermall)
Operating modes: Some wireless network cards can act as access points (APs) for other devices to connect to, or as clients that hop onto a network through an access point. (Source: Vyos)

en/glossary/conc-ip-address.title: IP Address
en/glossary/conc-ip-address.summary: It is the unique number that identifies each device within a network.
en/glossary/conc-ip-address.content:
An IP Address (Internet Protocol) is a string of numbers that identifies a device (computer, phone, printer) on a network.
In our tech kitchen:

The IP is the House Address.
For data to get where it needs to go, every piece of equipment needs a unique address. For example, on your local network, addresses usually start with 192.168.1....
Without this address, the Delivery Guy (Nginx) → wouldn’t know which screen to drop the info off at.


Local IP vs. Public IP

Local IP: This is your device’s address inside your house or neighborhood. It’s like the room number inside a hotel.
Public IP: This is your network’s address to the outside world (the big internet). It’s like the hotel’s main street address in the city.


Related concepts

DNS (Network Nicknames) →
DHCP Protocol →
Nginx Web Server →

en/glossary/conc-javascript-language.title: "JavaScript Language"
en/glossary/conc-javascript-language.summary: "The dynamic waiter that makes everything move and shine on your screen."
en/glossary/conc-javascript-language.content:
JavaScript (JS) is the language that brings life to what you see on your browser or phone.
In our tech kitchen:

JavaScript is the dynamic waiter.
While HTML sets the table and CSS picks the color of the tablecloth, JavaScript is the one that makes the menu change when you swipe, the one that lets you know your order is ready, or the one that lets you chat with others without reloading the page.
Unlike PHP or Python, which usually work “inside” the kitchen (the server), JavaScript usually works “out front” with the customer (on your phone).


Why is it important?
Without JavaScript, the internet would be a series of static pages like old newspapers. Thanks to JS, we can have applications on the local server that feel fast and modern, allowing the community to interact seamlessly.

Related concepts

PHP Language →
Python Language →

en/glossary/conc-latency.title: "Latency"
en/glossary/conc-latency.summary: "Time it takes for a data packet to travel across the network."
en/glossary/conc-latency.content:
Latency is the exact amount of time it takes for a data packet to be transmitted across a network.
It’s the time that elapses from the moment your browser makes a request for information until the requested response arrives.
The lower the latency, the better your internet connection will be.
To calculate latency, two parameters are used: the ping →, a unit of measurement expressed in milliseconds (ms), and lag, which refers to excessive delay.
You can measure both parameters with a speed test.
What is ping?
Ping is the unit of measurement used to gauge latency. Before we go any further, do you know what latency actually is? In simple terms, latency is the time it takes for a data packet to travel across the network. In other words, it’s the exact time that passes from when your device sends a request to the server until you receive a response back.
On the other hand, ping is the metric used to measure that latency, expressed in milliseconds (or the abbreviation ms). This means that the lower the ping, the better. Ideally, you want your ping to be under 100 ms; anything from 65 ms is solid, and you shouldn’t have any trouble with video calls. If you’re a gamer, the sweet spot is around 20 ms so you don’t deal with too much delay or lag.
What is lag?
Lag refers to the excessive delay that can occur in real-time telecommunications. Its causes can be linked to high network latency or a lack of sufficient processing power on the service or client side you’re communicating with. It could be your computer or your internet connection.
Lag shows up differently depending on the format. For example, in videos, the image quality usually drops; your music might sound glitchy or distorted; and the classic scenario in online gaming: the delay between you hitting a button and your character actually performing the action.

en/glossary/conc-linux-system.title: "Linux System"
en/glossary/conc-linux-system.summary: "A free and powerful operating system, ideal for creating community servers."
en/glossary/conc-linux-system.content:
Linux is an open-source operating system, which means its original “recipe” is public and anyone can see it, copy it, or improve it.
In our tech kitchen:

Linux is a Modular and Open Kitchen.
Unlike other kitchens where you can’t change a thing, in Linux you can move the countertops, change the wall color, and even invent new ways of cooking.
It’s famous for being rock-solid and secure: once you fire up a Linux stove, it can run for years without ever needing to be turned off.


Why do we use it at Voltaje?
We use Linux because it doesn’t charge us a dime to use it, it respects our privacy, and it runs like a charm on old gear that other systems would just call “junk.” It’s the solid ground we build our Pocket Internet → on.

Related concepts

Operating System →
Giving an old computer a second life →
Terminal →

en/glossary/conc-local-network.title: "LAN (Local Area Network)"
en/glossary/conc-local-network.summary: "Computer networks that are not necessarily connected to the Internet."
en/glossary/conc-local-network.content:
A local area network, or LAN, is a group of devices (like computers, phones, printers, etc.) connected to each other within a limited geographic area, such as a home, an office, or a building.
These networks let your devices share resources like files, printers, and an internet connection. (Source: Cloudflare)
Key features of a LAN:

Limited coverage: LANs are designed for small geographic areas. (Source: NinjaOne)
Connecting nearby devices: Devices link up via cables → or wireless connections → within a defined physical space. (Source: Share.google)
Resource sharing: Devices on a LAN can access and share files, printers, and other gear. (Source: Servicios UNS)
Shared internet connection: A LAN can split a single internet connection among several devices. (Source: Cloudflare)
Control and security: LANs allow for centralized management of security and access to shared resources. (Source: AWS)
Speed: LANs usually offer faster data transfer speeds than larger networks. (Source: Coltecno)

Examples of LANs:

A home network connecting computers, smartphones, and other gadgets in a house.
An office network connecting employees’ computers and printers.
A school network connecting students’ and teachers’ computers.

(Source: OliviaWireless)
In short, a LAN is a computer network that lets devices communicate and swap resources within a local area. (Source: Share.google)

en/glossary/conc-lte-4g-connection.title: 4G or LTE connection
en/glossary/conc-lte-4g-connection.summary: A mobile communication standard for high-speed browsing.
en/glossary/conc-lte-4g-connection.content:
LTE, which stands for Long Term Evolution, is a global wireless communication standard that provides fourth-generation (4G) mobile network technology, offering much faster data transfer speeds and reduced latency → compared to the previous generation (3G). Its main job is to give you high-speed internet access on your mobile devices, making things like video streaming, quick downloads, and IoT (Internet of Things) applications run like a charm.
What’s LTE good for?


Web browsing and streaming: Lets you load websites, videos, and music way faster and smoother.


High-quality calls: Voice over LTE (VoLTE) technology lets you make voice calls over the LTE data network, which makes the sound quality crisp and gets your calls connected in a snap.


Better mobile communication: Makes sending instant messages and hopping on video calls way more efficient.


Expanding IoT applications: LTE is the backbone for connecting a whole bunch of gadgets, like smartwatches, sensors, and automation systems, to the internet.


Telecommuting and remote work: Allows you to jump into video conferences and access cloud platforms with better stability and speed, so you can get your work done from just about anywhere.


Standardization and evolution:
LTE is a long-term standard that still serves as the foundation for 5G mobile networks and will keep evolving with variants like LTE-Advanced (LTE-A) to deliver even faster speeds and better performance.

en/glossary/conc-mifi-modem.title: MiFi Modem
en/glossary/conc-mifi-modem.summary: A portable device for creating a WiFi network using mobile data.
en/glossary/conc-mifi-modem.content:
A MiFi modem, also known as a portable WiFi router, is a gadget that lets you set up a local WiFi network using a mobile data connection, like 4G or 5G, so a bunch of devices can hop online wirelessly. Basically, it’s a portable hotspot you can just toss in your bag and take anywhere. (Source: Verizon)
The MiFi provides high-speed broadband connectivity that can be shared by up to ten users at once. You can use it with all sorts of WiFi-enabled gear, like: desktops, laptops, tablets, mobile phones, cameras, game consoles, and MP3 players. In many cases—like with an Apple iPad—it can save you from needing a separate data plan for the device itself, so you don’t have to pay for an extra service.
Plus, some of these gadgets can even double as a USB flash drive since they have built-in storage, and you can often expand that space with memory cards.
When you’re ready to use it, your devices just connect to the MiFi network like any other WiFi. The speeds you get will depend on your service plan and the type of network (like 3G or 4G) it’s hooked into. (Source: Wikipedia)

en/glossary/conc-network-agents.title: "Network Agents"
en/glossary/conc-network-agents.summary: "Auxiliary programs that help computers communicate automatically."
en/glossary/conc-network-agents.content:
Network Agents are small programs or services (like hostapd or dnsmasq) that handle automated tasks to keep the network running smoothly.
In our tech kitchen:

They are The Prep Cooks.
While the head chef is busy cooking, these helpers take care of things like: announcing that the kitchen is open, handing out tickets at the door, or making sure the tables are clean and connected.


Which agents do we use?
On your Pocket Server →, we use agents like hostapd to create the WiFi and dnsmasq so that everyone gets an IP address automatically. Without them, the network admin would have to do all the heavy lifting by hand.

Related concepts

DHCP Protocol →
WiFi Signal →
How to build your Pocket Server? →

en/glossary/conc-nginx.title: "Nginx Web Server (The Dispatcher)"
en/glossary/conc-nginx.summary: "The one in charge of taking orders and delivering information to whoever requests it."
en/glossary/conc-nginx.content:
Nginx (pronounced “en-gine-ex”) is a piece of software called a “Web Server.” Its main job is to take requests from browsers (like Chrome or Firefox) and respond by serving up the files they’re asking for.
In our tech kitchen:

Nginx is the Delivery Guy.
When someone types an address into their phone, the Delivery Guy runs to the kitchen, grabs the prepared dish (the webpage or file), and zips it over to your screen.
He’s lightning-fast and can handle hundreds of orders at the same time without breaking a sweat.


Nicknames and Addresses
Since real addresses are long, clunky numbers that are a pain to remember (called IPs), we use the DNS → system to give the delivery guy some nicknames.
Instead of telling the neighbors to look for the delivery guy at “Street 192.168.1.15,” we tell them: “Look for solevoltaje.local.” It’s a friendly name that’s easy for everyone to memorize, just like how we use nicknames for delivery apps or for our buddies around the neighborhood.

Related Concepts

Server →
DNS (Network Nicknames) →
How to install Nginx? →

en/glossary/conc-operating-system.title: "Operating System"
en/glossary/conc-operating-system.summary: "It is the set of rules and the structure that makes your computer functional."
en/glossary/conc-operating-system.content:
An Operating System (OS) is the main program that manages all the hardware and software on a computer or phone.
In our tech kitchen:

The Operating System is the Kitchen Layout and Rules.
It defines where the countertops go (RAM), how to access the pantry (Hard Drive), and who has permission to use the knives (security).
It’s in charge of making sure the cook (processor) doesn’t get overwhelmed and knows which order to handle first.


Different kitchen styles
Every operating system has its own way of organizing things:

Windows: It’s like a pre-fab, super popular kitchen. Everything comes in its place and it’s easy for most folks to use, but sometimes it’s a bit heavy and tricky to customize.
macOS (Apple): It’s a designer kitchen—very sleek and smooth—but it only works in the houses (devices) they build themselves.
Linux: It’s a kitchen you can build and tweak exactly how you like it. It’s the foundation for almost all the Servers → in the world.


Related concepts

Hardware →

en/glossary/conc-paquetes-internet.title: "Internet packets"
en/glossary/conc-paquetes-internet.summary: "The micro-files into which all information traveling over the internet is divided, from a WhatsApp message to a video."
en/glossary/conc-paquetes-internet.content:
When you send a WhatsApp message, watch a YouTube video, or open a webpage, your device doesn’t send or receive that information all at once like a solid block. It breaks it down into tiny little pieces called packets, sends them one by one (or several at a time), and once they reach their destination, it puts them back together in order.

Why are they called “packets”?
Think of it like sending a really long letter by mail, but instead of sending it in one giant envelope, you cut it into a hundred pages and send each page in a separate envelope. Each envelope has written on it: “Page number 34 of 100, going to address X, coming from address Y.” Upon arrival, the recipient puts all the pages in order and reads the full letter.
That’s exactly what your router does with data: it breaks it into packets, sends them across the network, and the receiving device reassembles them.

What’s inside each packet?
Every packet has two parts:

Header: The control information — where it’s coming from, where it’s going, what packet number it is in the sequence, and how to verify that it arrived intact.
Payload: The actual content — those bytes of the video, the message, or the image.


What happens if a packet gets lost?
On the internet, packets don’t always all make it. Sometimes one gets lost along the way because the network was congested or the signal dropped for a split second. The communication protocol (usually TCP) detects that the packet is missing and automatically asks for it to be resent. That’s why sometimes a download “stutters” for a moment and then continues — it was waiting for a lost packet.

How is packet loss measured?
Packet loss is expressed as a percentage. If out of 100 packets sent, only 97 arrive, there is 3% loss.

























LossPerceived effect0–1%No noticeable issue1–5%Small stutters in video or voice5–10%Frequent cutouts in video callsMore than 10%Very unstable connection, hard to use
In a radio link →, the CCQ metric indicates exactly how well the packets are arriving: a CCQ of 90% or higher means almost all of them are arriving correctly.

Everything travels in packets
It doesn’t matter if it’s an HD video, a text message, a voice call, or a photo — everything gets turned into packets before traveling across the network. The difference is just how many packets there are: a high-definition video can have millions; a text message, only a few.

Related concepts

Radio Link →
Router →
WiFi Signal →

en/glossary/conc-php-language.title: "PHP Language"
en/glossary/conc-php-language.summary: "It is the specialized assistant for reading and executing your server's recipes."
en/glossary/conc-php-language.content:
PHP is a programming language designed specifically for creating websites and applications that run on a Server →.
In our community kitchen:

PHP is a specialized kitchen assistant.
While HTML is like a printed menu (which doesn’t change), PHP is the assistant who knows that if a customer orders “Sancocho,” they need to go to the pantry, grab the ingredients, and whip it up on the spot.
Thanks to PHP, the server can show different things to each person (for example, displaying your username or your personal files).


Why is it important?
PHP is the engine behind very famous tools like WordPress, Wikipedia (MediaWiki), or Facebook. In a local community network, installing PHP allows your server to stop being just a simple list of files and turn into an interactive platform where people can post their own stories or manage their documents.

Related concepts

How to create your own Pocket Server? →
Server →
JavaScript Language →

en/glossary/conc-ping-program.title: "Ping program"
en/glossary/conc-ping-program.summary: "A tool to measure the connection speed between two devices."
en/glossary/conc-ping-program.content:
The ping program is a network diagnostic tool used to check connectivity and latency between two devices.
Essentially, ping sends a data packet to a target device and measures how long it takes to get a response back. This time, measured in milliseconds, is known as latency → or ping, and it’s used to gauge how good your connection really is.
How does it work?

The ping command sends an ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) packet to the target device.
The target device, if it’s online, replies with an ICMP echo packet.
The ping tool measures the time it takes for the response to arrive and displays it as “round-trip time” (RTT) in milliseconds.
Plus, ping can tell you if there’s any packet loss, which just means some of those packets didn’t make it to their destination.

What’s it used for?

Checking connectivity: Making sure a device is actually connected and responding on the network.
Measuring latency: Figuring out the quality of your connection, which is super important for online gaming and video calls.
Troubleshooting network issues: Pinpointing connectivity problems, packet loss, or high latency.

In short, ping is an essential tool for diagnosing and checking the quality of the network connection between two devices.

en/glossary/conc-python-language.title: "Python Language"
en/glossary/conc-python-language.summary: "The versatile chef that knows how to prepare everything from a simple recipe to artificial intelligence."
en/glossary/conc-python-language.content:
Python is one of the most popular programming languages in the world because it’s super easy to read and can handle just about anything you throw at it.
In our tech kitchen:

Python is the Head Chef.
It’s famous because its recipes read almost like plain English.
It knows how to do it all: from automatically organizing your shopping list to training a “wise assistant” (Artificial Intelligence →).
It’s the go-to language for building AI Agents that can live right inside your pocket server.


What’s it good for?
In a community setting, Python is the perfect tool for automating tasks, analyzing weather or crop data, or running language models that help summarize important info without needing to be connected to the internet.

Related concepts

PHP Language →
JavaScript Language →
Local AI Possibilities →

en/glossary/conc-radio-enlace.title: "Radio Link"
en/glossary/conc-radio-enlace.summary: "A wireless internet bridge that connects two distant points with directional antennas."
en/glossary/conc-radio-enlace.content:
A radio link (also called a microwave link or point-to-point link) is a system that transmits information between two distant locations using directed radio waves, acting like an invisible beam of light traveling from one antenna to another.

How does it work?
Imagine two people shouting at each other in an open field. If you cup your hands around your mouth to direct your voice, your sound travels much further than if you just yell in every direction. The antennas in a radio link do exactly that: they focus all the signal energy in one direction to reach much greater distances.
A radio link requires two antennas pointing directly at each other, with the path between them free of obstacles (trees, buildings, hills). This is what we call line of sight.

Difference from regular WiFi






























Home WiFiRadio LinkCoverage20–50 meters1–50 kilometersDirectionAll directionsOnly between two pointsUseConnecting phones and computers at homeConnecting two networks or distant communitiesAntennaSmall, omnidirectionalLarge, directional

Types of radio links

Point-to-Point (PtP): One antenna on hill A and another on hill B. It’s the most common and the most powerful.
Point-to-Multipoint (PtMP): A central antenna that distributes a signal to several “client” antennas in different locations. It works like the sun shining on several communities at once.


Most common frequencies
In Colombia, the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands are license-free (no permit needed). These are the same frequencies used by WiFi, but directional antennas turn them into long-range tools:

2.4 GHz: Reaches up to 5–8 km. Better at penetrating rain and light vegetation. More budget-friendly.
5 GHz: Reaches up to 3–25 km. Higher speed. Requires a clearer path. (Depends on the size and power of the antenna).


What is it used for in rural communities?

Bringing internet from a point where there is a signal to a village that doesn’t have one.
Connecting one organization’s office to another several kilometers away.
Setting up a community network where the cost of the service is shared among several families.


Key terms

RSSI: Indicates how strong the signal is when it arrives. Measured in dBm. The sweet spot: between -45 and -65 dBm.
CCQ: Measures the connection quality as a percentage. Anything above 90% is solid.
Fresnel Zone: The “bubble” of space that must be clear around the radio beam so the signal doesn’t degrade.
PoE (Power over Ethernet): A system that powers the antenna electrically through the same network cable.
dBi: A unit that indicates the gain (focusing power) of an antenna. The higher the dBi, the further it reaches.
