Router →
4G Antenna →
Yagi Antenna →

en/glossary/conc-ram-memory.title: "RAM Memory"
en/glossary/conc-ram-memory.summary: "It is your computer's immediate workspace, like a kitchen countertop."
en/glossary/conc-ram-memory.content:
RAM (Random Access Memory) is the place where your computer keeps the information it’s using right this second.
To make it easy to understand, imagine your computer is a kitchen:

The RAM is your countertop.
The bigger the countertop, the more ingredients (programs) you can have out and ready to chop without them falling on the floor or getting cluttered.
The processor is the chef, grabbing whatever they need from the counter.


How does it work?
When you open a program (like your browser or a document), the computer pulls it out of the “pantry” (the hard drive) and puts it on the “counter” (the RAM).
The catch is that RAM is a kitchen assistant with a short-term memory: it’s incredibly fast at handing you things, but as soon as you turn off the stove (the computer), it wipes the counter clean and forgets everything that was there. That’s why, if you don’t “save” your work to the hard drive, it’s gone.

Why does it matter?
If you have plenty of RAM, you can have several pots on the stove and chop different ingredients all at once. If you have very little, the chef has to keep putting things back in the pantry and pulling them out again every time they’re needed, which makes the whole lunch (your work) take a lot longer.

Related concepts

Storage (Hard Drive and SSD) →
Operating System →
Swap Memory →

en/glossary/conc-raspberry-pi.title: "Raspberry Pi"
en/glossary/conc-raspberry-pi.summary: "A small, low-cost computer ideal for learning and creating projects."
en/glossary/conc-raspberry-pi.content:
What is it?
A Raspberry Pi is a credit-card-sized computer that you can set up however you need.
Out of the box, it doesn’t come with a keyboard, mouse, or monitor, but you can hook those and other peripherals up to it without any hassle.
Its “hard drive” is a MicroSD card →, where you install a version of Linux → optimized for these kinds of devices. This gives you a super portable computer that sips electricity and lets you do pretty much everything you’d normally do on a desktop.
How to power your Raspberry Pi?
To power up a Raspberry Pi, you need to plug it into a power source.
The most common way is using a USB to microUSB or USB-C cable (depending on the model) plugged into a USB power adapter. Just make sure the adapter provides the right voltage and current for your specific Raspberry Pi model.
Steps:

Identify the power port: Older models, like the Raspberry Pi 3 and earlier, use a microUSB port, while newer ones like the Raspberry Pi 4 and 5 use USB-C.
Connect the power adapter: Plug the USB power adapter into the wall outlet and then connect the corresponding USB cable to the Raspberry Pi’s port.
Check the power: If everything is hooked up right, the Raspberry Pi should fire up. Some models have indicator lights to help you confirm it’s getting power.

Keep in mind:

Voltage and current: The Raspberry Pi needs a 5V power source. The required current can vary by model, but generally, 2.5A to 3A is recommended for models like the Raspberry Pi 4. (Source: Bret).
Phone chargers: While some phone chargers might work, it’s best to use a power adapter specifically designed for the Raspberry Pi to ensure top-notch performance and avoid power issues.
USB hubs: If you need to plug in a bunch of USB devices, think about using an externally powered USB hub to avoid power supply headaches.
Batteries: If you need to run your Raspberry Pi off a battery, make sure to use a DC/DC converter to step the battery voltage up to 5V.
Raspberry Pi Pico: The Raspberry Pi Pico can be powered by an external battery connected via a microUSB to USB cable.

en/glossary/conc-rg6-cable.title: "RG6 Cable"
en/glossary/conc-rg6-cable.summary: "A type of coaxial cable used for television and internet signals."
en/glossary/conc-rg6-cable.content:
An RG6 cable is a type of coaxial cable → used mainly for transmitting cable TV, satellite, and internet signals, as well as for some high-definition video applications.
It’s well-known for its ability to handle higher frequencies and cut down on signal loss, making it a go-to choice for both indoor and outdoor setups.
Key features:

Center conductor: Generally, an RG6 cable has a copper center conductor, sometimes copper-clad steel.
Dielectric insulation: An insulating material that separates the center conductor from the shielding mesh.
Shielding: RG6 cable features a shielding layer to protect the signal from electromagnetic interference (EMI) and noise. It can be single, double (foil and braid), or quad-shielded.
Impedance: Typically 75 ohms, which is the standard impedance for most video and television applications.
Applications: It’s used to hook up antennas, cable boxes, satellite dishes, and to carry internet and TV signals.
Advantages: It offers better signal quality and less signal loss than other coaxial cables like the RG59, especially for high-frequency and long-distance runs.

In short, the RG6 cable is a versatile, high-performance coaxial cable that’s perfect for getting video and data signals where they need to go, across all sorts of distances.

en/glossary/conc-router.title: "Router"
en/glossary/conc-router.summary: "The device responsible for directing information traffic on your network."
en/glossary/conc-router.content:
slug: router
path: /glossary/router
A Router is a device that connects different networks and decides which path data should take to reach its destination.
In our tech kitchen:

The Router is The Expediter.
Its job is to take the dishes coming out of the kitchen and know exactly which table (phone or computer) they need to go to, without them getting cold or getting lost along the way.
If two people order sancocho at the same time, the expediter makes sure each one gets theirs correctly.


How does it help the community?
The router allows many neighbors to connect to the same Local Network → at the same time. By acting as the “Expediter,” it manages traffic so that everyone has a smooth experience, sharing the Bandwidth → fairly.

Related concepts

Local Network →
WiFi Signal →
DHCP Protocol →

en/glossary/conc-sdmemory.title: SD Memory
en/glossary/conc-sdmemory.summary: A small card for storing photos, videos, and files on devices.
en/glossary/conc-sdmemory.content:
A MicroSD card is a tiny, portable storage device.
Sometimes they’re just called SD cards, though it’s more accurate to name them by their size: SD (the big ones), MiniSD (the medium ones), and MicroSD (the smallest ones).
It’s important to keep an eye on the memory class, as that tells you the read and write speed. Generally, it’s a good idea to go with class 10 cards to make sure you’ve got decent speed and that your devices don’t run into any hiccups when accessing your saved data.

en/glossary/conc-server.title: "Server"
en/glossary/conc-server.summary: "A powerful computer that provides services and data to other devices."
en/glossary/conc-server.content:
A server is a type of computer or computing system designed to provide services, resources, or information to other devices or users over a network →.
It acts as a middleman that processes requests and sends them off to other machines or individual users. These services can include file storage, database management, website hosting, and more.
At its core, a server is just a beefy computer built to handle massive amounts of data and knock out complex tasks efficiently for multiple users all at once.
Some common examples of servers include:

Web servers: Store and serve up web pages.
Mail servers: Handle sending and receiving email messages.
Database servers: Store and manage large sets of data.
File servers: Allow for shared storage and access to files.
Application servers: Run applications for various users.

Depending on their purpose, we can classify them as:

Test servers: A test server, also known as a staging or pre-production server, is a standalone environment used to test and validate apps or websites before they go live on a production server (the one end-users actually see). The main difference is the goal: the test server is for running things through the wringer, while the production server is for the real deal.
Production server: Its purpose is to serve apps and websites to end-users who interact with the application or site. It holds the actual user data and the live, running application. It’s open to the public or a specific group of users.

Servers are a fundamental part of the internet’s infrastructure and business networks, as they make communication and information exchange between different devices and users possible.

en/glossary/conc-simcard.title: SIM Card
en/glossary/conc-simcard.summary: The small smart card that connects your cell phone to the mobile network.
en/glossary/conc-simcard.content:
A SIM card, or Subscriber Identity Module, is a small, removable card that you pop into smartphones → and other gadgets to identify them on a cellular network and get them connected to services like calls, texts, and data.
It basically acts like a digital key that lets your device hook up to your carrier’s network and verifies that you’re the one using it.
What does a SIM card actually do?

Identification: The SIM stores your unique info, like your phone number and the details of your service plan.
Authentication: It lets your device securely connect to your carrier’s network.
Service Access: It enables you to make calls, send texts, and use mobile data.
Storage: It can also hold onto contacts, SMS messages, and other bits of user data.

How have SIM cards evolved since they first came out?

Original SIM: It was the size of a credit card.
MiniSIM: Smaller than the original.
MicroSIM: More compact than the MiniSIM, famously used in devices like the iPhone 4.
NanoSIM: The smallest one, used in most modern smartphones.
eSIM: A SIM built right into the device, letting you switch carriers without having to swap out a physical card.

en/glossary/conc-smartphone.title: "Smartphone"
en/glossary/conc-smartphone.summary: "A smartphone with internet connection and multiple applications."
en/glossary/conc-smartphone.content:
A mobile phone, also known as a cell phone, is a portable electronic device that lets you make and receive calls over a wireless connection, using a mobile communications network.
Beyond the basic calling and texting features, modern mobile phones—especially smartphones—come packed with a wide range of tools like internet access, apps, a camera, a media player, and much more.

Mobile communication: The main job of a mobile phone is to let you talk to people from a distance over a wireless network.
Portability: The real beauty of mobile phones is that you can carry them around and use them on the go, as long as you’re within the network’s coverage area.
Extra features: Smartphones, in particular, are like Swiss Army knives; they handle everything from web browsing and streaming music or video to snapping photos and running all sorts of apps.
Mobile networks: Mobile phones connect to mobile communication networks →, which use base stations to beam radio signals back and forth so devices can talk to each other.
Evolution: Mobile phones have come a long way from being simple gadgets just for calls to becoming full-blown multifunctional smartphones, all thanks to tech breakthroughs like shrinking down components, better networks, and the explosion of software and apps.

en/glossary/conc-ssh-protocol.title: SSH Protocol
en/glossary/conc-ssh-protocol.summary: A secure way to access and control your server from another computer.
en/glossary/conc-ssh-protocol.content:
SSH (Secure Shell) is a protocol that lets you access and manage a computer or server remotely through an encrypted, secure connection.
In our tech kitchen:

SSH is The Master Key.
It lets the kitchen manager slip in through the back door without having to be there in person.
Most importantly, this key travels inside a sealed envelope (encryption); nobody along the way can see what the manager is doing or swipe their password.


What’s it for?
On a Pocket Server →, we use SSH to install programs, organize folders, or fix glitches right from our own chair, using the Terminal →. It’s the go-to tool for tinkerers to get things done from afar.

Related concepts

Terminal →
Server →
Firewall →

en/glossary/conc-ssid-identifier.title: "SSID Identifier"
en/glossary/conc-ssid-identifier.summary: "The public name that identifies a WiFi wireless network."
en/glossary/conc-ssid-identifier.content:
The SSID, or Service Set Identifier, is the name that identifies a Wi-Fi network →.
It’s the name you see when you’re looking for available wireless networks on your device, like your phone or computer. It lets folks tell the difference between various Wi-Fi networks in a given area so they can hop onto the one they want. (Source: Lenovo)
To put it simply, the SSID is just the name of a Wi-Fi network, like “Juan’s House” or “Starbucks_Wi-Fi.” Devices use the SSID to find and connect to the right network. It’s worth keeping in mind that the SSID doesn’t provide security on its own; network security is handled by protocols like WPA2 or WPA3. (Source: Kaspersky)
In short, the SSID is the name that identifies a Wi-Fi network and makes it easy for users to connect to the network they’re looking for. (Source: Fortinet)

en/glossary/conc-storage-disk.title: "Storage (Hard Drive and SSD)"
en/glossary/conc-storage-disk.summary: "It is the place where you save all your information so that it is not lost when you turn off the computer."
en/glossary/conc-storage-disk.content:
Storage is the part of the computer in charge of keeping your files, photos, programs, and the operating system permanently.
If we stick with the kitchen analogy:

Storage is the pantry or a big warehouse outside the house.
That’s where you keep your bulk groceries (your files) so they stay put even when you’re done cooking.
When you need something to cook with, you grab it from the pantry and put it on the countertop (the RAM Memory →).


Types of storage
As technology moves forward, we’ve gone from slow but giant “pantries” to ultra-fast “refrigerators.”
HDD (Hard Disk Drive)
This is the traditional hard drive. It works with spinning platters and a needle that “reads” the information physically. It’s like a huge, cheap warehouse, but it’s slow. It’s still the best bet for storing massive amounts of files (like in Servers →) because you can get a lot of space for not much money.
SSD (Solid State Drive)
This is the solid-state drive. It doesn’t have any moving parts; it uses chips (like USB flash drives). It’s way faster than an HDD. Imagine the pantry is now right next to the countertop, making it super easy to grab what you need. Your computer boots up in seconds!
NVMe (Non-Volatile Memory Express)
This is the latest evolution of SSDs. They’re tiny and plug directly into the computer’s “brain.” It’s like having an automated system that puts the ingredients right into the cook’s hand instantly.

The real world and technology
Technology was designed by mimicking how we humans organize ourselves. Networks, for example, are like water pipes: information flows from one place to another. Servers are like community warehouses where we all store things (the cloud). Understanding these concepts helps us see that the digital world is just a translation of what we already know how to do in the kitchen or the workshop.

Related concepts

RAM Memory →
Server →
SD Memory →

en/glossary/conc-swap-memory.title: SWAP Memory
en/glossary/conc-swap-memory.summary: Disk space that helps when RAM memory is full.
en/glossary/conc-swap-memory.content:
SWAP memory, also known as swap space or virtual memory, is a section of the hard drive → that an operating system → uses as if it were RAM memory → when physical RAM is running low.
It acts as an extension of your RAM, letting the system shuffle less-used data from the RAM over to the hard drive to clear up space for more active processes. (Source: Aprendo Linux)
In simpler terms, swap memory is like a temporary storage spot on your hard drive that the OS leans on when it needs more memory than what’s physically available in the RAM. When a program gets hungry for more memory, the OS can move less-used data from the RAM to the swap space, freeing up the RAM so you can keep your programs running smoothly.
Why use it?

Avoid running out of memory: When your RAM is maxed out, the OS can use swap to keep your apps from freezing up or getting glitchy.
Run more programs: Swap memory lets you juggle more programs at once than you could with just your available RAM.
Hibernation: On some operating systems, swap memory is used to save the system’s state when you hibernate.

How does it work?

RAM exhaustion: When the RAM fills up, the OS identifies the data that hasn’t been used in a while.
Transfer to swap: This “dusty” data is moved from the RAM to the swap space on the hard drive.
RAM cleanup: The newly freed-up RAM can then be used for other processes that need it right now.
Accessing swap: When you need to get back to that data moved to the swap, the OS loads it back into the RAM, sometimes shuffling other less-used data back to the swap to make room.

Pros and cons:

Pros: It lets you run more programs and keeps things from crashing when your RAM is full.
Cons: Accessing swap memory (on the hard drive) is way slower than accessing RAM, which can really drag down your system’s performance if you rely on it too much.

Swap memory is a handy tool for managing memory in computer systems, especially if you’re working with limited RAM. Even though it’s useful, keep in mind that overusing swap can definitely put a damper on your system’s speed.

en/glossary/conc-system-folders.title: "Folders and Paths"
en/glossary/conc-system-folders.summary: "It is the organization and labeling system to find your files on the computer."
en/glossary/conc-system-folders.content:
Folders (or directories) and Paths are how the operating system organizes information so it doesn’t get lost.
In our tech kitchen:

It’s the System of Shelves and Jars.
A Path is the exact address of where you put something away. For example: Pantry > Top Shelf > Salt Jar.
On a computer, a path looks like this: /home/user/documents/photo.jpg.


How are they organized?
Every system has its own “organizing style”:

On Windows: Everything starts with a letter, usually the C: trunk. (e.g., C:\Users\David\Photos).
On Linux: There are no letters. Everything sprouts from a common root called / (slash). Think of it like a big tree where every branch is a folder. (Always picture it as a tree).
The server folder: By convention, the stuff the world can see on your server is usually kept in a folder called /var/www/. It’s like the kitchen counter!


Related concepts

Operating System →
Linux System →
Pocket Server →

en/glossary/conc-terminal.title: "Terminal or console"
en/glossary/conc-terminal.summary: "An application to give commands to the computer using text."
en/glossary/conc-terminal.content:
In computing, a terminal or console is a device you use to connect to a computer. In more technical terms, it’s a text-based user interface that lets you interact with an operating system → or an application.
Historically, it referred to a physical device with a keyboard and a monitor, but nowadays, it usually refers to a software application that emulates that function—basically, a program that lets us talk directly to our operating system without needing to mess around with graphical interfaces.
In more detail:

Terminal: It’s the interface that lets you run commands, control apps, and see results in a text-based environment. Nowadays, it most commonly refers to a program that emulates a physical terminal, allowing you to interact with the OS through commands.
Console: Traditionally, a console referred to a physical device, like a keyboard and monitor, plugged directly into the computer. These days, the term can also refer to the terminal interface used to manage and configure systems, and it’s also used to talk about management interfaces for cloud services.
Difference between console and terminal: Even though the terms are often used interchangeably, the console can refer to the physical hardware, while the terminal can refer to the software that emulates that device. In practice, both terms are used to describe the command-line interface that users interact with to give instructions to the system.

In short, both the terminal and the console are interfaces that allow for communication with the operating system, whether through a physical device (historically) or a software program (currently).

References

Terminal on Wikipedia

en/glossary/conc-umts.title: "UMTS (Universal Mobile Telecommunications System)"
en/glossary/conc-umts.summary: "A third-generation technology for mobile data transmission."
en/glossary/conc-umts.content:
UMTS (Universal Mobile Telecommunications System) is a third-generation (3G) mobile phone technology that provides high-speed internet access and multimedia services, succeeding GSM (2G) →.
Its main goal is to offer broadband wireless communications with faster upload and download speeds than previous networks, making web browsing, video calls, and using multimedia apps a whole lot smoother.
(Source: 1NCE)
What is UMTS used for?

Mobile broadband internet access: It lets you connect devices to the internet at speeds significantly faster than the previous generation (2G).
Multimedia services: It handles high-speed data transmission, which makes it easy to use bandwidth-heavy apps like video calling, downloading multimedia content, and seamless web browsing.
Better quality and capacity: It offers superior communication quality, similar to a landline network, and allows more users to connect to the network at the same time.
Evolution toward 4G/LTE: Even though it’s a 3G technology, successive upgrades like HSPA (High Speed Packet Access) and HSPA+ brought its capabilities closer to 4G (LTE) networks, extending the lifespan of the network infrastructure.
Compatibility with various devices: It supports a wider range of terminals and applications, including “Internet of Things” (IoT) devices that need to crunch a lot of data.

Key features of UMTS


CDMA technology: It uses W-CDMA (Wideband Code Division Multiple Access) technology to transmit data at high speeds across a wider radio frequency band.


Network components: It includes the Terrestrial Radio Access Network (UTRAN), the Core Network (CN), and the User Equipment (UE).


Improvements over GSM:
It offers speeds of up to 2 Mbps (initially), with later improvements via HSPA and HSPA+ reaching up to 42 Mbps or more, far surpassing the speeds of GSM networks.


Referencias | References

WirelessLogic
Avance Digital
Emnify
ScienceDirect

en/glossary/conc-usb-connection.title: "USB Connection"
en/glossary/conc-usb-connection.summary: "It is the universal language for connecting and powering your devices."
en/glossary/conc-usb-connection.content:
The USB (Universal Serial Bus) is the standard that lets almost any electronic device talk to another. It’s like a smart plug that doesn’t just pass power, but also information (photos, music, documents).
Following our kitchen analogy:

The USB port is like a wall outlet, but one that works for the blender, the radio, and even for charging your phone.
Back in the day, every appliance brand had its own weird plug; USB came along so everyone could use the same one.


The history of standards
At first, USB was a mess: there was USB-A (the big rectangular one), micro-USB (the one from old phones), and mini-USB. Each one had a different shape, and you never had the cable you actually needed.
Brands wanted you to buy their specific cables, which created tons of electronic waste (cables that are now good for nothing).

The power of the people and USB-C
USB-C is that small, rounded connector that you can plug in either way (it doesn’t have a “right side up” or “upside down”). What makes it special isn’t just its technology, but how it became the standard:

Citizen movements: Groups of people, consumer organizations, and movements like “Right to Repair” put pressure on governments.
Laws for the planet: In places like the European Union, laws were created to force all brands (even the most stubborn ones) to use a single universal charger: USB-C.
Result: Thanks to people coming together to demand less waste and more convenience, today we can use a single cable for our computer, phone, and headphones. A huge win for the collective over the market!


What is it used for?

Power: Charging your devices.
Data: Moving files between a USB Flash Drive → and your computer.
Connecting tools: Keyboards, mice, cameras, and even fans.


Related concepts

USB Flash Drive →
Storage (Hard Drive and SSD) →
Hardware →

en/glossary/conc-username.title: "Username"
en/glossary/conc-username.summary: "The unique name that identifies a person in a computer system."
en/glossary/conc-username.content:
A username is a unique string of characters that identifies a user within a computer system, such as a social network, website, or app.
It’s what you use to log in and get into your account, and it usually goes hand-in-hand with a password to verify it’s really you. (Source: Dashlane)
In a nutshell, a username:

Identifies you uniquely: It sets every user apart within the system, avoiding any mix-ups and making sure you get the right permissions.
Is used to log in: It’s how you introduce yourself to the system to access your account and all your stuff.
Can be public or private: In some systems, your username is out there for everyone to see, while in others, it stays strictly between you and the system.
Must be one-of-a-kind: No two users can have the same username; otherwise, the system wouldn’t know who’s who.
Can be alphanumeric: It’s usually a mix of letters and numbers, though some systems let you throw in special characters like underscores or dots.
Is not your password: Think of your password as the secret key that keeps your account safe, while your username is just your digital ID tag.

en/glossary/conc-whatsapp.title: "WhatsApp"
en/glossary/conc-whatsapp.summary: "A messaging application for sending texts, audio, and making calls."
en/glossary/conc-whatsapp.content:
WhatsApp is an instant messaging and calling app, owned by Meta, that lets users send messages, make voice and video calls, and share files over the internet.
It’s widely used for both personal communication and business.
It lets you send text, voice, and video messages, make voice and video calls, and share files like photos, documents, locations, and contacts.
While it’s mainly known for personal use to keep in touch with friends and family, there’s a business version called WhatsApp Business, which lets you interact with customers, manage sales, and provide customer support.
Heads up! WhatsApp is usually included in the data plans of most mobile carriers in Colombia, though it can still lead to extra charges for data and downloads not covered by your specific plan.
It’s available for different operating systems →, including Android and iOS, and it also has a web version.
The app ensures that personal chats, calls, and media content are protected with end-to-end encryption, which means only the sender and the receiver can access them.
The WhatsApp interface is simple and intuitive, making it easy to chat with others, especially with people who are already in your contact list.

en/glossary/conc-wifi.title: WiFi Signal
en/glossary/conc-wifi.summary: It is the wireless connection that allows information to travel through the air.
en/glossary/conc-wifi.content:
WiFi (or Wireless Fidelity) is a technology that lets you connect devices to a network without needing cables, using radio waves.
In our tech kitchen:

WiFi is The Kitchen Aroma.
When the server → has the info ready, it “wafts” it through the air just like the smell of a good stew.
Your phone or computer is like the “nose” that catches that scent and connects to grab the data.
If you wander too far or there are thick walls in the way, the aroma (the signal) gets weak until it fades away.


How to boost the aroma?
To make sure your WiFi reaches every corner of your place, it’s key to put your Router → in a high, clear spot—just like you’d place a steaming pot near an open window so the smell invites everyone in.

Related concepts

Router →
Local Network →
Bandwidth →

en/glossary/conc-yagi-antenna.title: "Yagi-type antenna"
en/glossary/conc-yagi-antenna.summary: "A directional antenna designed to pick up signals from long distances."
en/glossary/conc-yagi-antenna.content:
A Yagi antenna → is a type of directional antenna, well-known for its high gain and its knack for focusing a signal in one specific direction.
It’s made up of a main element called the boom (or active element) and several shorter pieces, known as directors and reflectors, all lined up along the boom.
How does it work?

Active element: This is the one that hooks directly into the transmitter or receiver; it’s where the main signal is either sent out or picked up.
Directors: These are shorter than the active element and sit in front of it, pointing toward where you want the signal to go. They help “steer” the signal, giving the antenna a nice boost in gain.
Reflector: This one is longer than the active element and sits behind it. It bounces the radio waves forward, helping to concentrate the signal in the right direction while cutting down on interference from behind, which really sharpens the antenna’s focus.

Key features:

Directivity: Yagi antennas are super directional, meaning they’re at their best when you’re aiming them at a specific target.
Gain: Gain is basically how well the antenna packs the signal into a tight beam. Yagi antennas have high gain, which makes them perfect for reaching out over long distances.
Size: The size of a Yagi antenna depends on the frequency it’s built for, but they’re generally a lot more compact than other directional options like satellite dishes.

Common uses:

TV and radio reception: You’ll often see these used to clear up TV or radio signals, especially if you’re out in an area where the signal is a bit spotty.
Wireless communications: They’re great for point-to-point or point-to-multipoint links where you need a solid, focused connection.
Ham radio: Radio enthusiasts love Yagi antennas for reaching long-distance contacts and jumping into radio contests.
Radar systems: In some military and radar setups, Yagi antennas are used to focus and aim radar beams.

Bottom line: the Yagi antenna is a handy piece of gear for boosting signal reception and transmission in all sorts of setups, thanks to its high directivity and gain.

en/inspire/insp-big-questions.title: "Everything begins with a Big Question"
en/inspire/insp-big-questions.summary: An experience to spark curiosity and learn in a group.
en/inspire/insp-big-questions.content:
Download this solution to use it offline
This is an experience designed to spark curiosity in anyone around the world, encouraging them to use the Internet in groups to learn.
If you like it, you can download SOLE Voltaje Desconectado (Disconnected Voltage) and take it to places with little or no connectivity. Enjoy!
So, how can I know something I don’t know?
We’re going to tell you a little story about how we learn.
[Taken from SOLE Colombia (2019) A conversation with Sugata Mitra]

  
  

Taken from SOLE Colombia (2019) A conversation with Sugata Mitra


Read the transcript
Historically, if you wanted to know something, the traditional way was to find someone who knew it and ask them. That isn’t very practical because you can’t always find the person in question or you can’t go see them, so it used to take a long time to learn things. All of this changed thanks to writing. People could write down what they knew, and if you wanted to know it, you would find it and read it.
But some people opposed writing. Surprisingly, the most famous of those who opposed writing was Socrates, the Greek philosopher. His objection was that you can read what someone has written, but you can’t ask them questions, and sometimes it isn’t easy to find what has been written either. That problem was solved with libraries, where the writings of many people are kept in one place, but even that had a problem because, first of all, you have to find the library and go to it. Second, if you are reading something and have a question, you have no one to ask.
This started to change thanks to the Internet. Now, you can find what anyone writes at any time, and while you are reading, if you have a question, you can (usually) find someone to ask. So, the two problems Socrates had—namely: 1) where do I find the writings, and 2) who do I ask if I have a doubt—seem to have been solved thanks to the Internet.
To this, we must add one last thing: if reading is done with many people together, everyone can ask each other. Therefore, a group of learners can build a very affordable learning space with little material available where they have a computer, the Internet, and can ask each other questions. In other words, it turns out to be very easy to create a learning environment by yourself, and that is what we call a Self-Organized Learning Environment, or SOLE.
The idea is very simple and powerful: it is possible for learners to create their own learning environment using the Internet!


So, if you wanted to know the answer to something you don’t know, how would you do it?
Think of any person, like you, young or old, anywhere in the world who wants to answer a question they’ve always had and never been able to solve: their possibilities for learning, from the oldest to the most recent, could be:
1. Ask someone who knows: Oral tradition
Look for someone around you who knows the answer to your Big Question. It could be a friend, your parents or grandparents, a teacher, or a neighbor.
If they don’t have the answer, ask them who might, and travel together with this question to ask that other person.
This is how most ancestral knowledge is passed down, even today.
2. Search in writings: Textual transmission
Where are there writings on the topic of that question? At home, at a neighbor’s house, at school, at the public library, or somewhere in the nearest town?
Go and look for them together. Like in the story of the libraries, knowledge can be passed down in writing, and librarians or teachers might know which books your answer could be in.
Imagine… This is how we have learned since writing was invented, and it has gradually become more equitable as public education has become universal. However, there are still many people who do not have access to it.
Did you find the answer?


Yes!
Great! And did any new questions come up? Go back to asking someone who knows, or go back to searching in writings that you have within reach.


No.
Then where else can we find it? I suppose if you are reading this, it might sound obvious that you can search on the Internet. Just keep in mind that, in 2024, half the people in the world DO NOT have access to the Internet.


3. Search on the Internet: Digital interconnection
Doing a search on the Internet is like having the biggest library in the world in your pocket. Google or any other search engine where you type your Big Question is like the librarian who searches through all the texts, videos, audios, and other content on the Internet and offers them to you so you can explore them.
However, I don’t know if you know this, but searching the Internet on your own is difficult. There are many answers to your Big Question; some are better than others, but there are also many wrong ones. There are even lies written by people or even machines, like those they call Artificial Intelligence (AI). Learning to judge that sea of information in order to learn is an art form. The same thing happens when you ask someone who knows or search through writings.
The best way to overcome this is to doubt, be curious, and ask new questions. This is what scientists and artists do; they don’t just settle for the first thing they learn. Although sometimes learning alone—being self-taught—is demanding, regardless of whether you have access to all the information.
4. Search on the Internet in a group: “SOLEar” (Doing a SOLE)
At SOLE Colombia, we have discovered that many people who don’t have access to good education can learn to learn almost anything by using the Internet in a group, because they can doubt, be curious, and ask new questions together. It’s like being self-taught, but in a group, which is not only easier, more fun, and more powerful than using the Internet alone, but it also proposes a new way of being together. We call this “SOLEar.”

WHAT IS A SOLE?
SOLE (Self-Organized Learning Environments) is a disruptive learning methodology that empowers communities to develop autonomy, collaboration, deep learning, and, most importantly, to solve real-life problems!
A SOLE session is simple. You need a space with people, a few computers with Internet access, and Big Questions. In a SOLE session, learners self-organize to find answers to questions using the Internet, without the need for a teacher.
WHAT IS THE CLOUD OF GRANDMOTHERS?
Along with SOLE is the concept of the “Grandmother.” Research has shown that limited intervention from an untrained facilitator can promote thriving learning processes. The role of a Grandmother consists of sparking curiosity, asking questions, listening carefully, and providing a warm environment. The Cloud of Grandmothers is a network of volunteers from all professions and social backgrounds who connect remotely with SOLEs to co-facilitate and offer participants the opportunity to experience worlds far removed from their own.
And what if you don’t have the Internet?
If you don’t have the Internet, you will always be able to learn more by using the first options, even with the difficulties Sugata Mitra mentions in the video.
However, at SOLE Colombia…
At SOLE Voltaje, we believe that using the Internet in a group to learn is a way to have new, healthy human relationships that will allow us not only to change the way we learn and dialogue but also the way we create the world we want together. Even more, it will change the shape of the Internet to be more inclusive, diverse, and equitable. But for this, it is important that everyone can access the Internet.

en/inspire/insp-build-memory-solelab.title: "How to build memory in a SOLE Lab?"
en/inspire/insp-build-memory-solelab.summary: Collects the history of the SOLE Lab from the perspective of each group.
en/inspire/insp-build-memory-solelab.content:
Purpose: To quickly gather the history of the Boca de Camarones SOLE Lab from the perspective of each group of collaborators (Boca de Camarones Community, SOLE Colombia, and the Internet Society Foundation).
Instructions
In groups, tell the life story of the SOLE Lab. On colored cards, draw:

1st card: The beginning—why did the idea or need arise?
Last card: What is the SOLE Lab today, and how does it feel to have it?
Intermediate cards: Milestones or key moments in the history of the SOLE Lab.



How do our SOLE Lab stories connect? On a canvas, we will organize the drawings, connecting the stories with yarn.


How does my life story connect with the history of the SOLE Lab?


Device Development

The experiences narrated below are the result of what each group shared regarding their time with the SOLE LAB. To avoid misrepresentation, we use ““ as a way to quote what the person actually said. In other parts of the text, we paraphrase the individuals while striving to remain faithful to what was expressed throughout the session.
We use the word milestone to refer to those events or happenings that are significant to the person telling the story.

Boca de Camarones Community
Elainer:
Milestone 1: “The SOLE LAB originated from when I worked at the Puntos Vive Digital.” Elainer was an ICT manager. Once that project ended for him, the idea of having a SOLE LAB emerged.
Milestone 2: He remembers holding a SOLE session on what internet connection is.
Milestone 3: When he heard the story of the SOLE LAB, he realized it could be the starting point for sharing with the community. An event he remembers with joy is the SOLE Festival.
Milestone 4: “For my work, I had to do a webinar. I remembered what I learned in SOLE and I was able to do it. The grandmother helped me lose my fear of screens.”
Milestone 5: Elainer mentions that it’s not just SOLE sessions that have happened in that space. The SOLE LAB has been used as a point of interest for tourists. Tourists rest and connect to the internet; plus, they are told the story of the space.
Caril:
Milestone 6: Caril tells us everything she learned about shrimp thanks to a SOLE. “Thanks to a great question, we learned about shrimp: what does a shrimp eat?”
Marcelo and Ana María:
Milestone 7: The two of them organized a SOLE with the children. They say it was very exciting for the community.

Marcelo works with the children in the community and has ideas that could generate economic sustainability, through video games or by offering the connection space to foreigners.
Marcelo remembers when the materials for the construction of the SOLE LAB started arriving and everything that process entailed. For his part, he remembers how rewarding it was to help with the construction and see it finished.
Ana María takes care of the space, the garden, and the SOLE LAB. Ana María mentions that they have managed and held bingos and other activities of interest to the community.

Internet Society Foundation
Gustavo
Milestone 1: “Everyone should have access to the internet.” For this reason, ISOC scholarships exist, where they are interested in the internet being used in a communal and open way. That is why the SOLE LAB is a space of great interest to him and to the mission of his work.
Milestone 2: For Gustavo, the SOLE LAB is a way to connect the internet and people.
Milestone 3: For him, the SOLE LAB should have a flag showing that it is a space to democratize knowledge.
Milestone 4: “We think differently, but our stories connect.”
SOLE COLOMBIA
Milestone 1 [2015]: Sanjay wondered what a library of the future with internet, mediated by the SOLE methodology, would look like.
Milestone 2 [2017]: They met Elainer and learned about the Puntos Vive Digital, where he worked.
Milestone 3 [2018]: The first version of the SOLE LAB was held in La Sevillana.
Milestone 4 [2021]: The first SOLE LAB was funded through the Internet Society call for proposals.
Milestone 5 [2022]: Sanjay and Belén travel to Boca de Camarones and begin managing the design and construction of the first SOLE LAB.
Milestone 6 [2023]: “Now the first SOLE LAB in Boca de Camarones is a reality. It exists and it works, and we want it to be sustainable for the community.”
Findings and Learnings

All the stories of the SOLE LAB connect people, histories, and affections. It is interesting how the tastes and passions of the people in the community and in SOLE are empowered.
Creating a SOLE LAB implies the synergy and meeting of several common wills.
The stories go beyond the SOLE LAB; in other words, this space becomes a pretext for living and coexisting in new ways.
Having been part of the project generates pride and dignity.

title: “Guía rápida para arreglar tus vainas”
slug: guia-arreglar-vainas
¡Manos a la obra! Guía para arreglar tus vainas
¿Se te dañó algo en la casa y no sabes ni por dónde empezar? ¡Tranquilo, que eso nos pasa a todos! Aquí te traigo unos consejos prácticos para que no te varés y saqués adelante esos arreglos sin tanto complique.
Lo básico que necesitás tener a la mano
No necesitás ser un experto ni tener un taller profesional. Con estas herramientas básicas, ya tenés medio camino ganado:

Destornilladores: De estrella y de pala (los infaltables).
Alicate: Para cuando algo se pone rebelde.
Cinta aislante: La vieja confiable para cualquier “ñapa”.
Martillo: Por si toca aplicar un poquito de fuerza bruta.


“El que no tiene herramientas, no tiene excusas. ¡A veces con un poquito de ingenio se arregla hasta lo que parece perdido!”

Pasos para no hacer un desastre

Analizá el problema: No te pongás a desarmar todo a lo loco. Mirá bien qué es lo que está fallando.
Buscá ayuda: Si no sabés, no te las tirés de genio. Echale un ojo a algún tutorial en YouTube o preguntale a alguien que sepa.
Orden ante todo: Si vas a desarmar algo, poné los tornillos en un vasito o en un lugar donde no se pierdan. ¡Nada peor que terminar el arreglo y que te sobren piezas!

¿Cuándo es mejor llamar a un profesional?
Hay veces que uno quiere hacerse el “toderos”, pero hay que saber cuándo soltar. Si el arreglo tiene que ver con:

Electricidad de alto voltaje: ¡Ni se te ocurra! Eso es peligroso.
Gas: Eso es mejor dejárselo a los que saben, no queremos sustos.
Algo muy costoso: Si es un equipo delicado, mejor no le metás mano si no estás seguro, no sea que terminés dañando más la vaina.

Si querés aprender más sobre mantenimiento, revisá nuestra sección de Tips para el hogar.
¡Ánimo, que con paciencia todo se arregla!

title: “Guía rápida para arreglar tus cosas”
slug: guia-rapida-arreglos
¡Manos a la obra! Guía para no dejar morir tus aparatos
¿Se te dañó algo en casa y no sabes ni por dónde empezar? ¡Tranquilo! Aquí te traigo unos consejos prácticos para que no te toque salir corriendo a comprar todo nuevo. A veces, con un poquito de maña y paciencia, uno mismo puede sacar adelante el arreglo.
Lo primero: ¡No te desesperes!
Antes de desarmar medio mundo, respira. Muchas veces el problema es más sencillo de lo que parece.

Revisa lo básico: ¿Está bien conectado? ¿Tiene pilas? ¿Se soltó algún cablecito?
Busca el manual: Ese papelito que uno siempre guarda y nunca lee, ahí está la clave.
El “toque mágico”: A veces, un buen reinicio o una limpieza con aire comprimido hacen milagros.

Herramientas que no te pueden faltar
No necesitas un taller profesional, con esto vas sobrado:

Destornilladores: De estrella y de pala, de varios tamaños.
Alicates: Para apretar o soltar lo que esté rebelde.
Cinta aislante: La vieja confiable para cualquier cable pelado.
Multímetro: Si te quieres poner un poco más técnico y medir voltajes.


“El que no sabe es como el que no ve”, decía mi abuelo. ¡Así que no tengas miedo de aprender!

¿Cuándo es mejor llamar a un experto?
Ojo, tampoco te las des de genio si ves que la cosa es seria. Si ves humo, hueles a quemado o el aparato tiene que ver con gas o alta tensión, ¡suelta eso y llama a alguien que sepa! No queremos que el remedio salga más caro que la enfermedad.
Recursos útiles

Comunidad de reparadores
iFixit - La biblia de los arreglos.


Recuerda: ¡La idea es aprender y ahorrar unos pesitos!

en/inspire/insp-fish-game.title: "Resources for one, resources for all"
en/inspire/insp-fish-game.summary: We learned to play to reflect on the use of common goods.
en/inspire/insp-fish-game.content:
Did you know you can use games to build community agreements? 💭
In the Fish Game, we learn through a simple but powerful experience: the more we fish for ourselves, the fewer fish are left for everyone else. But when we work together, we make sure there’s enough for everyone.
This game is a metaphor for real life. The fish aren’t just fish. 🌱 They represent the resources we share: the internet, land, food, even the air we breathe!
Think of it this way: imagine sharing an internet plan with your neighbors. If we all use it mindfully, we can make it go further and benefit the whole community. But if we only look out for our own interests, the resource runs out fast and hurts everyone. Are you ready to make agreements with your community?

¿Se te dañó algo en casa? ¡Tranquilo! Antes de que corras a comprar uno nuevo, dale una oportunidad a la reparación. Aquí te enseño cómo meterle mano a esos cacharros sin morir en el intento.
Lo básico que debes tener a la mano
No necesitas un taller profesional, con esto te defiendes como un berraco:

Destornilladores: De estrella y de pala (los infaltables).
Cinta aislante: La vieja confiable para cualquier cable pelado.
Alicates: Para cuando las cosas se ponen difíciles.
Un poquito de paciencia: Esto es lo más importante, ¡no te me desesperes!

Pasos para no hacer un desastre

Desconecta todo: ¡Ojo! No queremos que te lleves un susto con la corriente.
Mira bien qué pasó: A veces es solo un cable suelto o algo que se trabó.

Si ya intentaste de todo y nada, quizás es hora de buscar un técnico de confianza. Recuerda que a veces es mejor pagar por un buen arreglo que comprar algo que se va a dañar a los dos días.

en/inspire/insp-granny-cloud.title: "How to change the world from your home? Meet the Granny Cloud"
en/inspire/insp-granny-cloud.summary: Discover how to support learning from a loving perspective.
en/inspire/insp-granny-cloud.content:
Download this Inspiration to use offline
What is The Granny Cloud?
The Granny Cloud is a concept born alongside the SOLE idea. It captures the spirit of those who support learning with a loving gaze—those who encourage us to learn in a subtle way, offering warm encouragement, asking the right questions, and marveling at our discoveries.
They are people who have fun learning, are curious, and enjoy interacting with learners. Sugata Mitra called this perspective “the Granny gaze.” Suneeta Kulkarni, his research partner, formed The Granny Cloud, and at SOLE Colombia, we’ve picked up the torch and their legacy to form La Nube de Abuelitas (The Granny Cloud) in Spanish.
Who makes it up?
We are volunteers—men and women—from all over the world. We have Grannies in Spain, Portugal, Denmark, Mexico, Colombia, the United States, Peru, Chile, Vietnam… there are Grannies everywhere!
There is a Granny Cloud Coordinator who manages the sessions, sends out invites, and communicates the schedules and the people who will be attending each session that requests a Granny.
Every year, coinciding with the start of our projects, new Grannies join us. They discover their motivation, and we train them in the methodology so they can “SOLE” and enjoy this incredibly rewarding role.
How can you become a Granny?
All you need to be a Granny is the desire to connect with communities learning through the SOLE Methodology. Need some tools? You can download the Granny Manual and find stories about Grannies on the SOLE Colombia website. You can also request to join The Granny Cloud via this form, and we’ll get in touch to tell you all about it.
Keep an eye on our social media and other platforms (take a look at our website) to find out when the next “costurero” (gathering) is called and what the schedules for the upcoming SOLEs are—don’t miss out!

en/inspire/insp-granny-no-connection.title: "Grandma's Cloud: what happens when there is no connection"
en/inspire/insp-granny-no-connection.summary: Communication and presence do not need many embellishments.
en/inspire/insp-granny-no-connection.content:
Download this Inspiration to use offline
There’s a question I get asked a lot when I talk about what a Granny does in a SOLE: what happens if there’s no connection? The answer is easy to say, but not so easy to grasp. I always say: you just figure it out! And people look at me wondering, “but if it’s a video call and there’s no connection, what’s the point of being a SOLE Granny?”
What really happens is that you realize communication and presence don’t need a lot of bells and whistles to happen.
Obviously, if the SOLE has a super good connection, everything is very organic. People chat, we hear everyone, we can interact easily, we talk and do incredible searches… it feels easy, pleasant, and by the end, your heart feels full and happy.
When those conditions aren’t met and the connection is rough, the image is pixelated, the sound is choppy, we can’t even hear the Big Question, or even the video call chat doesn’t seem to work in real-time. Frustration takes over, we don’t understand what’s going on, we feel like hanging up and getting on with our day because this makes no sense at all… This feeling is multiplied if it’s one of our first connections, if we’ve just started in the Granny Cloud.
At the same time, on the other side, there’s a community that can’t hear us either, they see us blurry, there are many of them, the computer screen where the Granny is is small, the sound coming out of the speaker is very low. Maybe it’s hot or it’s after lunch. In the Tuning Visits, for example, it’s the first time the communities are doing a SOLE and they don’t really understand what’s happening, how they’re going to find answers on the Internet, how to use the computer, what they’re supposed to do at each moment, or who that person is trying to talk to them from who knows where.
From experience, I tell you: the power of the Internet is like the power of water… it seeps through anywhere! It seeps through everywhere! And that’s when a message, somehow, from the other side of the world tells you “I’m with you, that question you’re asking is great, I’m searching and I found (…) congratulations on that research, I’ll see you for the next SOLE!” and that’s when the room fills with joy and lets us all know that we came here to learn, that we are TOGETHER. And that TOGETHER takes on a much bigger and more powerful meaning.
From here, we thank all those who didn’t give up, those who sent a question or an answer via WhatsApp, those who voted later on, all those who followed the game, minute by minute… THANK YOU to everyone!

en/inspire/insp-granny-questions.title: "Questions and answers about the experience of being a Granny"
en/inspire/insp-granny-questions.summary: We answer the most common questions about being a Granny.
en/inspire/insp-granny-questions.content:
Download this Inspiration to use offline
What is the minimum time commitment for the sessions?
‍Consistency is the key to learning. We know that life and responsibilities change, and that some Grannies won’t be able to continue indefinitely. If you can’t commit long-term or on a regular basis, just let us know what you can manage: it could be an occasional session, or just touching base with the coordination team or other Grannies to help us brainstorm ways to tackle upcoming challenges.
How does seeing the “privilege” gap between your environment and theirs affect us?
Feel free to share your reality and your world with others: we all grow, get inspired, and explore new possibilities when we connect with the realities of others.
This experience touches us all equally. You, too, will discover and learn from other worlds. You, too, will be enriched by this experience. Let this experience and these people into your life!
What happens to the children or adults when the experience with the Granny ends?
It’s a question many have asked, and it’s a valid concern. Even if some experiences are shorter than expected, the impact on the children and the people involved stays with them. Read our SOLE stories to see what people say about the Granny Cloud in the areas where we’ve supported SOLE sessions, and let yourself be touched by the magic.
What should I do if I’m contacted by the media to talk about or film my interaction as part of the Granny Cloud?
If we are interacting with children, we must protect their best interests and avoid exposing them inappropriately. Before speaking to the media or taking photos or videos of the participants, please contact the SOLE Colombia team.
How is the Granny Cloud funded?
As we’ve mentioned, the Grannies are volunteers, and thanks to this, many children, youth, and adults have been able to connect and share experiences. We want to keep it that way, though perhaps at some point, we can explore new ways to sustain the relationship with the Grannies.
And if I can’t be a Granny, can I help in any other way?
There are always opportunities to join this global movement to transform the future of learning. At SOLE Colombia, we are open to exploring the best way for you to get involved. You can check out the SOLE Colombia Community roles and find where you feel most comfortable—let us know what interests you or if you have any ideas!
If you still have unanswered questions, write to us at hola@solecolombia.org; we’re just a message away.

en/inspire/insp-how-internet-travels.title: "Have you wondered how the Internet, electricity, or mobile signal reaches you?"
en/inspire/insp-how-internet-travels.summary: Discover the journey of information from the source to your home.
en/inspire/insp-how-internet-travels.content:
Every day we check messages on our phones, flip on a light, or take a phone call.
It all seems like everyday stuff, but 150 years ago, it was pure magic when cities like Bogotá—in Colombia—witnessed the miracle of electric light for the first time.
[How the light came to Bogotá](www.senalmemoria.co/piezas/luz-llego-bogota#:~:text=Bogotá fue la primera ciudad,inconvenientes de ahí en adelante)
Or take Myanmar, for example—over in Asia—where they didn’t get to experience the internet until 2012.

en/inspire/insp-how-internet-works.title: "How does the Internet work?"
en/inspire/insp-how-internet-works.summary: Discover how information travels across the network.
en/inspire/insp-how-internet-works.content:
Download this Inspiration to use it offline
Think about when you go to a restaurant and order a cup of coffee. You, as the client, ask or consult the waiter, who goes to the kitchen, comes back a while later, and serves you the ready-made cup of coffee, just like a good server. You don’t really know how they made it, but you know it’s a cup of coffee when you taste it. The Internet works in a similar way. Let’s take a look.

  
  SOLE Colombia, 2024.

When you connect to the internet and have a question, what you’re doing is consulting it from a cell phone or computer, communicating with many computers belonging to other people or companies that store exactly what you’re looking for.
The information you want to consult could be a webpage, a video, a photo, a video call, a file, or a message. These are some of the formats for digital files that get sent over the internet.
The cell phone, computer, or tablet you use to connect to the internet is called the client.
The computer where the information you are consulting is stored is called the server.
How does information travel across the Internet?
For the information sent by a server to reach your home, neighborhood, rural area, or community, the client you’re using connects to the Internet. Let’s take your cell phone, for example, somewhere in Colombia, and imagine the answer is on a server in Europe. This is the grand adventure your question takes.

  
  How does your question travel across the Internet? SOLE Colombia, 2024.

Your cell phone connects via electromagnetic or wireless waves to one or more cell towers. Your question travels in the form of zeros “0” and ones “1” to one of those towers and goes down through a cable that runs underground to a central cable hub. Then, it’s redirected to a seaport where that cable connects to a submarine cable. This cable runs under the ocean to the other continent, then comes out of the water to another cable point that carries your question to the place where the server holding your answer is located. The server receives your question and responds with the information it has stored—also in zeros “0” and ones “1”—and it’s sent back along that same route to your phone. And all of that happens in a matter of milliseconds! It’s incredible, don’t you think?
Diver installing a submarine cable

  
  Taken from Erbauer 2. Klasse Christopher Farmer, aus Taylorsville.

Internal structure of a submarine cable

  
  Taken from: youtu.be/k1SMnnddpvI

Global map of submarine Internet cables

  
  Global map of submarine Internet cables. Data by Greg Mahlknecht, map by OpenStreetMap contributors (CC BY-SA 2.0).

Keep in mind that submarine cables allow us to transmit data so that telecommunication services can exist. The reason information travels so fast is that these cables are made of fiber optics—in other words, glass. This means that the information, the zeros “0” and “1,” is sent in the form of light, and light is the fastest thing in the entire universe.
Isn’t it wild what we humans have come up with?

en/inspire/insp-imagine-collective-futur.title: "How to imagine futures in community?"
en/inspire/insp-imagine-collective-futur.summary: A methodology for dreaming collective futures.
en/inspire/insp-imagine-collective-futur.content:
Instructions:

Pair up, with each pair consisting of 1 person from the SOLE Team and 1 person from Boca de Camarones:


Elainer + Mateo
Ana María + Liz
Marcelo + Nico
Caril + Sanjay


Each pair gets 3 cards, along with post-its and markers. They need to answer the following questions and follow the instructions to fill out the cards:

Card 1 - Blue: In a future where…
Guiding question: What hasn’t happened yet that you wish had happened?
Card 2 – Fuchsia: I decide/We decide
Instruction: People fill out this card based on the situation.
Card 3 – Green: To
Guiding question: How do we do what we do when we live and work well together?
Example:

Activity Development
Results Card 3 – Green: Desirable futures


To replicate leadership and preserve culture
To fix the Internet as a community
To get people to spark their curiosity and solve things using the Internet
To manage to make the SOLE Lab a source of income
To make the kids smile and have their smiles rub off on the adults
To bring the community together
To organize, look after, and use the space

Card 2 – Fuchsia: Decisions


I decide/We decide to host different types of activities at the SOLE Lab so we’re interested in showing up, like video games, a gym, and crafts.
I decide/We decide to provide snacks and use the Internet.
I decide/We decide that the kids should be able to enjoy the space.
I decide/We decide to hold community activities to raise funds.

Card 1 - Blue: Problems or difficulties


In a future where we have financial trouble keeping the space going
In a future where adults don’t support the kids in their learning
In a future where we can’t get people to see it as a community space
In a future where it’s hard to get to know the adults
In a future where we have trouble connecting to the Internet
In a future where older adults aren’t interested in the space
In a future where the heat and mosquitoes make it hard to be comfortable in the SOLE Lab
In a future where we have to go into town to run errands and use the Internet
In a future where people feel shy about being in the SOLE Lab
In a future where we feel tired of keeping the SOLE Lab running

title: “Guía rápida para arreglar tus cosas”
slug: guia-rapida-arreglos
¡Manos a la obra! Guía para no dejar morir tus aparatos
¿Se te dañó algo en casa y no sabes ni por dónde empezar? ¡Tranquilo, que eso nos pasa a todos! Aquí te traigo unos consejos prácticos para que dejes de sufrir y te pongas en modo “yo mismo lo arreglo”.
Lo primero es lo primero: ¡No te compliques!
Antes de desarmar medio mundo, revisa lo básico. A veces el problema es más sencillo de lo que parece:

¿Está conectado? Parece chiste, pero es la fija. Revisa el cable.
¿Hay energía? Mira si el taco de la luz se bajó o si el enchufe está muerto.
¿Tiene pilas? Si usa baterías, cámbialas por unas nuevas, no por las que sacaste del control remoto.

Herramientas que no te pueden faltar
No necesitas un taller profesional, con esto ya tienes para defenderte en la mayoría de los casos:

Destornilladores: Un kit básico de estrella y pala.
Alicates: Para apretar, doblar o sacar lo que se quedó atascado.
Cinta aislante: La vieja confiable para cualquier cable pelado.
Multímetro: Si quieres ponerte un poco más técnico y ver si hay corriente.


“El que no mete la mano, no aprende. ¡Anímate a destapar eso!”

¿Qué hacer si la cosa se pone difícil?

en/inspire/insp-internet-in-a-box.title: "We connect to the Internet with a box"

en/inspire/insp-internet-in-a-box.content:

en/inspire/insp-internet-in-group.title: "When was the last time you used the Internet in a group?"
en/inspire/insp-internet-in-group.summary: Discover how sharing the Internet can create communities.
en/inspire/insp-internet-in-group.content:
Download this Inspiration to use offline
So, let’s go back to the beginning: when was the last time you used the Internet as a group? Maybe that memory—sharing a search, a screen, a question—is the start of another possible Internet. The Future Library is just that: proof that other Internets are possible, and that we’re already building them.

Reload Your SOLE Lab, El Tambo, Cauca.
That’s what we’re building with The Future Library: an ecosystem where access isn’t the end goal, but the starting point. A space where the network doesn’t just connect devices, but also stories, doubts, and hunches—a space to connect and ask questions without fear.
In the SOLE Labs, we’ve seen how something shifts when a community gathers around a screen. Girls, young people, and elders asking questions together. The Internet stops being a stream of information we consume in isolation and becomes a shared territory. In a group, questions emerge that wouldn’t come up when we’re alone. Memories mingle, curiosity is sparked, and collective projects are born. Using the Internet as a group is, in itself, a radical act because it challenges the speed, the noise, and the instruction to accept things without questioning.

Plug in your SOLE Lab in Dominguillo, Cauca.
The Internet has become a personal space for consumption; “being connected” doesn’t really mean being connected to others or connecting with others. And that’s what changes when we use the Internet as a group.

SOLE Festival in Boca de Camarones, La Guajira.
Today, nearly three billion people around the world remain disconnected. And that digital exclusion cuts across bodies, languages, and landscapes. It’s not just a technical problem: it’s a silent way of saying who counts and who doesn’t. But that’s not all; those of us who do have Internet access usually use it not to connect, but to isolate ourselves further from those around us. We use it to order food, to keep up with other people’s lives, to buy things, to read about what interests us. We rarely use it to cook with others, to meet up with others, to exchange knowledge, to create together.
Maybe you don’t remember. Because most of the time, we connect alone: in front of a cell phone, a laptop, or a tablet. The Internet experience has become intimate, individual, and often passive. We accept answers that appear without us asking, we navigate through algorithms that predict what we want before we even say it. But something is lost when we use the Internet in solitude: the possibility of looking each other in the eye while we search, of asking questions out loud, of inventing together.
When was the last time you used the Internet as a group?
While millions remain without Internet, those of us who have access use it each on our own. What if the future of the Internet was using it as a group?

en/inspire/insp-internet-signal-transmis.title: "How does a message travel from your cell phone to your friends'?"
en/inspire/insp-internet-signal-transmis.summary: Discover how the Internet signal is transmitted.
en/inspire/insp-internet-signal-transmis.content:
Download this Inspiration to use offline
Internet signals are transmitted through physical infrastructure like fiber optic and copper cables, as well as radio waves (Wi-Fi) and, to a lesser extent, via satellite or mobile networks (4G/5G). Data is converted into electrical or light pulses (bits) that travel through these mediums to their destination, using routers and other gear to send and receive the info.
Guided Media (wired):

Fiber optic: Transmits data as light pulses through thin glass strands.
Copper (Coaxial and twisted pair cable): Uses metal wires to carry electrical signals, like in ADSL connections.
Submarine cables: Most global internet traffic travels through fiber optic cables laid under the ocean.

Wireless Media (no wires):

Wi-Fi: Uses radio waves to connect devices (like your phone or computer) to a router.
Mobile networks (3G, 4G, 5G): Signals are transmitted through antennas and cell towers to provide internet access on mobile devices.
Satellite: Sends and receives signals to and from a satellite in orbit.

How does the process work?


Conversion to bits: When you send data (like an email), your computer turns it into pulses of electricity or light (bits).


Transmission: These bits travel through the physical infrastructure (cables, air, or space) to network equipment.


Routing: Routers and other network gear steer these bits along the most efficient path to their destination.


Reception: On the receiving device, the bits are converted back into the original information you can see or use.


(Source: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medio_de_transmisi%C3%B3n)

en/inspire/insp-internet-usage-measure.title: "How much do the data that travel over the Internet weigh?"

Gigabytes (GB) are the amount of data you can use to browse, chat, listen to music, watch videos, and more. When you’re offered an internet plan in GB, you’re being offered the amount of internet data you can consume.
1 GB = 1000 MB (megabytes)
Do you know how much you can actually do with a Gig?

You can watch a 30-minute HD (high definition) video
You can listen to 200 songs
You can have 4 hours of video calls
You can visit 600 web pages
You can send 350,000 text messages

en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-caceres.title: "How did the Internet improve in Cáceres, Antioquia?"
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-caceres.summary: Five community leaders improve Internet access in their community.
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-caceres.content:
In the community of Altos del Tigre, in the municipality of Cáceres, five community leaders are making the near-impossible a reality: improving Internet access in their neighborhood.
Yadiris Vaquero, Luz Cenith Acevedo, Kenia Yepes, Blanca Ofir Moreno, and David Ojeda, SOLE Ambassadors for their community, have been working for a long time to ensure that having Internet stops being a hidden treasure in their territory. Because, let’s be honest, in Cáceres—just like in many places around Colombia—a connection has always been a luxury.
This year, however, something changed. Starting with the Tuning Visit back in May, the Ambassadors and other community members took the opportunity to learn together how this whole Internet thing works and why, specifically in Cáceres, getting a signal was such a tall order. The answer? Basically, because there aren’t any cell towers for miles around, and the telecommunications infrastructure is minimal.
But that didn’t discourage them. On the contrary, they rolled up their sleeves and got to work. They assessed the situation, looked for solutions, and with the program’s support, they managed to find the perfect fit: a Jangala device. This small but mighty gadget makes it possible to connect communities in hard-to-reach areas, and for the people of Cáceres, it was like opening a door to a whole new world.

  
  

Tuning Visits in Altos del Tigre, Antioquia, (2024).

  
  

Tuning Visits in Altos del Tigre, Antioquia, (2024).
So, thanks to the Jangala and the hard work of the SOLE Ambassadors—and everyone in the community who chipped in to get this solution installed—Cáceres now has Internet at a community access point.

  
  

Tuning Visits in Altos del Tigre, Antioquia, (2024).

  
  

Tuning Visits in Altos del Tigre, Antioquia, (2024).
And for many, this achievement means much more than just “having a connection”: it’s an opportunity to learn, to stay informed, and to keep up with the world. Kids, young people, and adults can now access information, participate in SOLE sessions, and, as they put it, “solve those big questions that used to seem like something from another planet.”
Listen to what one of the local tinkerers has to say—he was the one who jumped in to help set up the Jangala antenna with the whole SOLE crew:

  
  

Arnulfo, Tuning Visits in Altos del Tigre, Antioquia, (2024).
The work of Yadiris, Luz Cenith, Kenia, Blanca Ofir, and David Ojeda has marked a turning point in Cáceres. Today, thanks to their dedication and the Jangala, the community not only has Internet but is transforming how they use it—discovering, sharing, and creating endless possibilities for their community.

en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-chalan.title: "How did the Internet improve in Chalán, Montes de María?"
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-chalan.summary: The story of how connectivity improved in Chalán.
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-chalan.content:
Chalán is a municipality in the department of Sucre, Colombia. In this region, rural communities like Monte Bello, Rancho Rojo, and Alemania are using the Internet in a unique way: they connect as a group to answer big questions, do homework, watch movies, or simply share their stories with the world.
Since 2023, Yulieth Farasica has been a SOLE Ambassador who has sparked a major change in her community, leading collaborative learning sessions. Furthermore, this year she helped us install, teach, and promote the shared use of the Internet in her village, Alemania. Now, neighboring villages can also connect to the network, improving communication and access to information.
Listen to Yulieth as she tells her story about the lessons learned from connecting the community:

  
  

This is how Alemania has become a meeting point for Monte Bello, Rancho Rojo, and other nearby communities. Now, people travel there to use this connection, which has been installed and set up through everyone’s hard work.

  
  

There are now six ambassadors trained in the SOLE methodology who have learned how the Internet works and how to use their Jangala to share it with others!
Yulieth, Astrid, Yuranis, Johana, Celia, Maryuris, and Yolanda are changing the world. Thanks to their work, more children, young people, adults, and seniors in Chalán have access to the Internet today. From neighboring villages like Monte Bello and Rancho Rojo, people come to the Alemania village to connect and be part of this network, which they themselves have created and sustained.

en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-coloso.title: "How did the Internet improve in Colosó, Montes de María?"
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-coloso.summary: The story of how connectivity improved in Colosó.
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-coloso.content:
La Estación and the La Esmeralda Indigenous Council are just a 15-minute motorcycle ride apart. Both are neighboring communities in the Colombian municipality of Colosó, in the department of Sucre. Until recently, neither of these communities had a public space to access the Internet as a group. However, since 2023, they’ve been diving in and using the connectivity solutions we installed together in their territory to boost Self-Organized Learning.
There’s no one better than Mónica Vega, one of the star Ambassadors from La Estación, to share the story of how these communities are transforming their access to information, connection, and education. Are you ready to hear her out? Don’t forget to turn up the volume!

  
  

Mónica Vega, during Tuning Visits, Montes de María, (2024).
Did you hear her? It’s incredible how their community has used Jangala and the Internet connection to strengthen the bonds between their members. But Mónica’s story doesn’t end there. This year, she took the initiative to visit her neighboring community, La Esmeralda, to motivate more people to tinker and get hands-on with the technology.
Even though Jangala wasn’t the right fit for that specific community, Mónica and Gabriel—being the absolute pros at tinkering that they are—rolled up their sleeves and didn’t let anything stop them. Together, we explored other connectivity options, and finally, with Mónica’s help, we installed an omnidirectional antenna and a router. Now, the Ambassadors of La Esmeralda are empowering their neighbors to use the Internet together.

  
  

Gabriel, during Tuning Visits, Montes de María, (2024).
Furthermore, the community has created its own website to tell the whole world about their products, traditions, services, territory, history, and customs. Community Internet is now in their hands!
