en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-domingui.title: "How did the Internet improve in Dominguillo, Cauca?"
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-domingui.summary: The story of how connectivity improved in Dominguillo.
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-domingui.content:
In 2023, the community of Dominguillo began experiencing an unexpected transformation, thanks to a new opportunity for connection. It all started when a device called Jangala arrived at the local public school library, courtesy of USAID’s Hilando Vidas y Esperanza (Weaving Lives and Hope) program, implemented by the IOM. For the first time, this equipment provided stable Internet access, which quickly became an invaluable resource for everyone.
Here is Luis Miguel Mina—or Lucho, as we all know him—presenting the Jangala, or “Jang,” as they decided to call it. He is one of the SOLE Ambassadors we trained in 2023:

Franki, Lucho, and Mateo at the Inspiration Workshops in Dominguillo, Cauca (2023).
Inspiration Workshops, Dominguillo, Cauca (2023).
The device was installed in the library to facilitate SOLE (Self-Organized Learning Environments) sessions, a methodology that invites participants to learn autonomously and collaboratively through Big Questions. With these tools up and running, the people of Dominguillo didn’t just explore topics of interest; they started answering questions about their own culture and traditions, bringing the community together through shared knowledge and rediscovering their roots via the Internet.
Listen to Luis Miguel Mina and Nancy Campo talk about this experience:

  
  

Luis Miguel Mina and Nancy Campo
SOLE Ambassadors at the Dominguillo SOLE Festivals, Santander de Quilichao (2023).
However, as time went on, the community could no longer use the school library for their SOLE sessions. By then, the impact of this connection had been so profound that the residents of Dominguillo didn’t want to give it up. Convinced of the importance of having a community space for learning and connectivity, they sought support to create their own connection hub: the Dominguillo SOLE Lab.
And… guess what? Together, we worked on developing the SOLE Lab, a public space where chairs, tables, and computers were installed, and Internet access was restored. With the SOLE Lab, the people of Dominguillo regained the chance to connect with the world, continue their SOLE sessions, and explore new ways of learning.

Dominguillo SOLE Lab, Cauca (2024).

Learning and community work at the SOLE Lab, Dominguillo (2024).

Children and youth participating in SOLE sessions, Dominguillo (2024).

Connectivity and global communication from Dominguillo, Cauca (2024).
Thanks to this effort, Dominguillo didn’t just improve its Internet connection; it strengthened the bonds of the community. Now, the SOLE Lab is a meeting point where residents continue to learn and share their knowledge.

  
  

Video of the “Plug In Your SOLE Lab” event in Dominguillo, Cauca (2024).

en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-nepomuce.title: "How did the Internet improve in San Juan Nepomuceno, Montes de María?"
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-nepomuce.summary: The story of how connectivity improved in San Juan Nepomuceno.
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-nepomuce.content:
The following snippets are a collection of testimonials, images, and scenes showing how group Internet use in the municipality of San Juan Nepomuceno is transforming network access for neighboring communities, such as San José del Peñón and La Haya.
First Stop




SOLE Festivals, Montes de María, (2024).
To get to San José del Peñón, you have to cross seven rivers, keep your fingers crossed that the rain doesn’t play a nasty trick on you, and marvel at the majestic beauty of this territory. It’s no coincidence that, upon arrival, a large sign proudly welcomes you: “San José del Peñón, magical, fertile, and powerful land.”
The geography of San José del Peñón, with its mountains and dense vegetation, prevents signals from nearby antennas from reaching the village. Installing a community connectivity solution was a challenge that required the effort of the entire community. With collective support and hard work, we managed to install our Rural KIT against all odds: a Yagi antenna and a router that now make it possible for the community to gather periodically to do SOLE.

  
  

Gabriel, Tuning Visits, Montes de María, (2024).

  
  

Tuning Visits, Montes de María, (2024).
Rafael Antonio García, a natural-born tinkerer in his community, tells us in his own words what the process of installing the antenna was like: Turn up the volume to hear his story!

  
  

Rafael Antonio at Tuning Visits, Montes de María, (2024).
You don’t have to be an expert or have experience building networks, antennas, or cables to tinker around. Like Don Rafael Antonio, you too can get inspired to collaborate with others to create a common good.
Currently, the community of San José del Peñón has continued to hold SOLE sessions on their own, using Group Internet to research Big Questions like: Why does water make things wet? Why don’t humans use 100% of our brains? Why is there fresh water and salt water? Why are babies born without teeth?

SOLE led by Ambassadors at SOLE Festivals, Montes de María (2024).

SOLE led by Ambassadors at SOLE Festivals, Montes de María (2024).

SOLE led by Ambassadors at SOLE Festivals, Montes de María (2024).
That’s not all; the San José del Peñón community also created their own website, where they can upload their products and services, share their traditions, games, and everything they want to show the world about their community. Take a look!
SOLE: San José del Peñón

Second Stop:
Since 2023, we have built a super close relationship with the community of La Haya. This year, one of the SOLE Ambassadors from there joined us as a SOLE Explorer to help us bring a connectivity solution she was already familiar with to San José del Peñón. Mariana Fernández was our indispensable support in training new ambassadors in her municipality and successfully installing the connectivity solution in this new SOLE community.
Turn up the volume to hear in her own words what this experience was like, and how using the internet as a group has transformed her territory:

  
  

Mariana Fernández, Tuning Visits, Montes de María, (2024).
Thanks to community collaboration and the implementation of solutions like the Rural KIT, today San José del Peñón and La Haya have community Internet access, facilitating both learning and cultural exchange in the Montes de María.

en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-nuevomex.title: "How did the Internet improve in Nuevo México, Santander de Quilichao?"
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-nuevomex.summary: The story of how connectivity improved in Nuevo México.
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-nuevomex.content:
Care, a desire for change, and reconciliation? You can feel it in the Nuevo México rural district, home to the Nasa Kiwe Tekh Kxsaw community located in Santander de Quilichao.

Community research on connectivity, Nuevo México, Santander de Quilichao (2024).

Community analysis process regarding Internet access, Nuevo México, Santander de Quilichao (2024).
Using the SOLE methodology, the community asked themselves: what happens to our bodies when we get a hug? It was mostly women using the internet and computers as a group. Laughing, chatting, and researching online, they explored things they had never talked about before, or things they had always just assumed. Sharing their feelings and creating new knowledge. Together.

Hands-on tinkering and learning at the SOLE Lab, Nuevo México, Santander de Quilichao (2024).
How the internet works was the topic tackled in a workshop format: submarine cables that carry the internet signal along the ocean floor to the community, how to use it together, and what we can do with that great network that connects us on a global scale.
We installed a Jangala and an omnidirectional antenna in a space where the community regularly meets to make decisions.

Implementation of the Jangala device for community connectivity, Nuevo México, Santander de Quilichao (2024).
Currently, the Nasa Kiwe Tekh Kxsaw community continues to ask themselves Big Questions using the internet and technology as a group. Let them tell you about it themselves 👇🏽

en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-piendamo.title: "How did the Internet improve in Piendamó, Cauca?"
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-piendamo.summary: The story of how connectivity improved in Piendamó.
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-piendamo.content:
The Hilando Vidas y Esperanza (Weaving Lives and Hope) program by USAID and IOM brought SOLE Colombia to El Agrado. Together, we’ve been working to bridge the digital divide, bringing Internet access to isolated communities and giving that connection a real purpose: using the Internet together to learn in a self-organized and autonomous way. Since 2023, Piendamó, Cauca, has been the star of this story of change.
Alexander García, the “Tech Whiz” Building Bridges
It was in El Agrado that we met Alexander García, a young community leader with a curious and committed spirit. From the start, Alexander was enthusiastic about technology and, especially, the Internet. With SOLE’s support, we installed a connectivity solution and a few computers in the community hall, which soon became the hub for learning and gathering for his neighbors.

Collective explanation about connectivity and the Internet, Piendamó, Cauca (2023).

Practical demonstration of Internet use during the SOLE Festivals, Piendamó (2023).

Children and youth exploring the Internet during SOLE activities, Piendamó (2023).

The Journey to the Misak Pisicatau Reservation
Alexander’s curiosity about how routers, antennas, and networks actually work quickly turned him into an expert. In a matter of months, he went from someone who didn’t care much about tech to a real “tech whiz” (or cacharrero). This newly acquired skill has turned him into a bridge between his community and neighboring ones, as he shares what he knows with everyone else.
In 2024, Alexander joined us on a new mission: to bring the Internet to a neighboring indigenous community in the Misak Pisicatau Reservation. Upon arrival, we ran speed and signal tests, and it was Alexander who quickly figured out that no antenna could get a stable connection in that mountainous terrain.

  
  

SOLE Tuning Visits, Piendamó, (2024)
The good news is that the Reservation already had a stable satellite Internet connection, so we just had to install a router to make it more precise. Listen to him talk about the moment we installed that router—he really knows his stuff!

  
  

Tuning Visits, Piendamó, (2024).
With his technical skills and passion for teaching, Alexander was the first to motivate the residents of the reservation to explore the possibilities of the Internet and join the SOLE movement. With his help, we installed computers in the community hall, and Alexander encouraged them to keep using Self-Organized Learning in their community. Thanks to his push, the Misak Pisicatau community has now created its own website, a space where they share their traditions, culture, and knowledge with the world.

Misak Piscitau Reservation, Piendamó, Cauca (2024).

Misak Piscitau Reservation, Piendamó, Cauca (2024).

Misak Piscitau Reservation, Piendamó, Cauca (2024).
This is just one of many stories that show the power of connectivity to open doors and connect worlds. We invite you to learn more about the activities this community has carried out and the projects they have created on their website.
SOLE: Resguardo Piscitau

en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-tambo.title: "How did the Internet improve in El Tambo, Cauca?"
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-tambo.summary: The story of how connectivity improved in El Tambo.
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-tambo.content:
Have you ever imagined a place where an entire community can get online, learn, and create together? In El Tambo, Cauca, that dream was a shared necessity.
In this community, rural internet access is very limited, and in the urban area, access is mostly private. A public space with internet became essential so that everyone could get connected, work on their collective projects, and strengthen their territory.
In 2023, thanks to our partners at ADAPT Peace Building, we met the community of El Tambo and their community circles: the youth circle, the water circle, and the women’s circle. These groups had been working for over a year on peacebuilding and strengthening the social fabric. From that first meeting, a deep connection was formed. The circles quickly took ownership of the SOLE methodology and saw group internet access as a tool to achieve a collective dream: a community space with an internet connection. That’s how the spark for the SOLE Lab was lit in this community.

SOLE Lab, El Tambo, Cauca (2024).

SOLE Lab, El Tambo, Cauca (2024).

SOLE Lab, El Tambo, Cauca (2024).

SOLE Lab, El Tambo, Cauca (2024).
Throughout 2024, the Ambassadors of El Tambo trained in the SOLE methodology and, together with RUTA 4 Taller, collective effort and the hands of the community brought their own SOLE Lab to life: the Second Library of the Future in Colombia!
This is how one of the neighbors of the SOLE Lab in the Barrio Obrero describes it:

  
  

Plug into your SOLE Lab in El Tambo, Cauca, (2024).

  
  

Plug into your SOLE Lab in El Tambo, Cauca, (2024).
The SOLE Lab isn’t your average library. It’s a meeting point where kids, youth, and adults explore, create, dream, and learn together. With community internet access and collaborative spaces, the SOLE Lab invites the community to turn ideas into action, make collective decisions, enjoy self-organized group learning, and—why not—even watch movies.

  
  
Plug into your SOLE Lab in El Tambo, Cauca, (2024).
Thanks to the SOLE Lab, internet connectivity in El Tambo has improved significantly. Today, anyone can drop by and enjoy a more stable and faster connection, allowing students, families, and neighbors to connect, research, and create new ways of using the internet together.
Now the El Tambo community can communicate and build ties with other SOLE Lab communities and people all over the world. With every connection, bridges of collaboration are built that strengthen the sense of belonging and collective learning; every participant in the Library of the Future is part of a global network of learning and transformation.

  
  

Plug into your SOLE Lab in El Tambo, Cauca, (2024).
Check out some of the activities the community has sparked in this space:

Community participation at the SOLE Lab in El Tambo, Cauca (2024).
Today, the SOLE Lab awaits us with open doors to keep building the future of the internet together!

en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-valdivia.title: "How did the Internet improve in Valdivia, Antioquia?"
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-valdivia.summary: The story of how connectivity improved in Valdivia.
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-valdivia.content:
KM15 is the geographic point on the road leading to the township of Puerto Valdivia from the municipal seat. It is also the name of the community settled in this spot. Life in Km15—kilometer 15, as it sounds in Spanish—unfolds right along the road that connects it to the rest of the world… or doesn’t. Its geographic situation is a metaphor for its digital situation: while in many places the Internet is an everyday thing, here it feels far away.
Community Internet access was a dream for its inhabitants. Most relied on expensive data plans on their cell phones or satellite Internet, options that aren’t always affordable and that limit their possibilities.

  
  

Following exposure to new ways of using the Internet through the Hilando Vidas y Esperanza (Weaving Lives and Hope) program—run by USAID and implemented by IOM and SOLE Colombia—the women of KM15, who had already experienced the power of using the Internet as a group, became the driving force for change.
Their commitment to learning led them to tinker and get their hands dirty to transform that reality. Accompanied by SOLE Colombia, and guided by their enthusiasm and dedication, we managed to install a Jangala device in the community hall: a space that, in the blink of an eye, became the connection hub for Km15.

  
  


  
  

Tuning-in Visits, KM 15 in Valdivia, Antioquia, (2024).
The donation of several computers completed the toolkit that these Ambassadors can now use to lead SOLE sessions in their community, bringing their neighbors closer to learning, technology, and a world full of possibilities.
Today, the community hall is not just a meeting place, but also a place to share Internet and manage resources as a community.

Tuning-in Visits, KM 15 in Valdivia, Antioquia (2024).

Tuning-in Visits, KM 15 in Valdivia, Antioquia, (2024).
The story doesn’t end there. The Ambassadors now understand how the Internet works, why it’s important to manage it, and the difference in data consumption between watching a movie or sending a message, both in terms of usage and their own finances. Now, they are experts at using computers and the Internet as a group.

  
  

Tuning-in Visits, KM 15 in Valdivia, Antioquia, (2024).

  
  

The women are taking ownership of Internet use in Valdivia. And you, have you ever wondered why you pay what you pay for your cell phone plan or home Internet?

2023/11/04
Figure 1. Photograph showing the connections participants made regarding their life experiences in relation to technology.


Purpose: To recognize each other as part of the SOLE Lab project through our life stories in relation to technology.
Device instructions


Tell your life story through what technology has allowed you to do. To do this, select 3 milestones or relevant moments and draw them in a vignette.


How do our stories connect? We will use yarn to connect everyone’s stories.


Device development

The experiences narrated below are the result of what each participant said about their life experiences in relation to technology. To avoid misrepresentation, we use ““ as a way to quote what the person actually said. In other parts of the text, the person is paraphrased, trying to remain faithful to what was expressed throughout the session.
We use the word milestone to refer to those important events or happenings that are relevant to the person telling them.
The order of the names appearing in this systematization is the order in which people connected the stories. For example: Óscar started by telling his three milestones. Subsequently, Lizeth from SOLE Colombia followed, because she connected what she had drawn with one or several of Óscar’s milestones.
There were moments in the session where the speaker connected with the stories of several participants who had already spoken.

Óscar [Boca de Camarones]:

Milestone 1: “My first TV was the first one in the community.”
Milestone 2: “When I gave presentations at school, others did it with a Video Beam and I did it manually; this made me feel inferior. However, the teachers valued my posters much more because of how creative they were.”
Milestone 3: “I didn’t touch a computer until I was eleven (11) years old. I locked that computer up and was very afraid of technology.”

Lizeth [SOLE Colombia]:

Milestone 1: Her father bought a cell phone that became the community’s phone.
Milestone 2: The video game machine at her parents’ store allowed her to have more popularity and friends.
Milestone 3: “I filled up on floppy disks of my favorite series and learned many songs.”

Elainer [Boca de Camarones]:

Milestone 1: His first contact with computers was while studying.
Milestone 2: He worked at a Punto Vive Digital and was able to help many people.
Milestone 3: “I found SOLE Colombia and lived the experience of setting up a SOLE LAB in my community.”

Marcelo [Boca de Camarones]:

Milestone 1: He helped at the Punto Vive Digital where he worked with his brother. He says that in his childhood he knew nothing about technology, as he hadn’t had contact with those “gadgets.”
Milestone 2: He recognizes the moment when the SOLE LAB materials arrived.
Milestone 3: His first cell phone. “My first cell phone broke.”

Sebastián [audiovisual production]:

Milestone 1: “They gave me my first tape recorder. ‘Let the music play!’” he said.
Milestone 2: “They gave me my first guitar. ‘Let’s make some noise!’” he said.
Milestone 3: He talked about his first computer and how exciting it was to know everything he could do with it.

Gustavo [Internet Society Foundation]:

Milestone 1: Since he was little, he liked making magazines. When he was a kid, he started writing a blog. “This was my first job at a digital newspaper.”
Milestone 2: “My first cell phone allowed me to see the world without being afraid of the information I could find.”
Milestone 3: “Video calls allow me to connect with my sister and my nephews.”

Ana María [Boca de Camarones]:

Milestone 1: “Through the internet, I connect with my friends in Aracataca.”
Milestone 2: “From age 9 to 11, I had my first MP3 player.” She says she has always liked listening to music. “I would take over the remote for our first DVD player and wouldn’t lend it to my brothers.”
Milestone 3: I met Marcelo (her partner) through social media. “He lived in Santa Marta and we couldn’t see each other,” she said.

Mateo [SOLE Colombia]:

Milestone 1: He remembers his first heartbreak email. “I was writing to someone I liked, but who didn’t pay attention to me.”
Milestone 2: “My aunt gave me my first analog camera. It had a roll with 20 photos.”
Milestone 3: “My first computer broke. It was frustrating for my parents, who had gone into debt for it.”

Nicolas [SOLE Colombia]:

Milestone 1: He was calling a radio station asking for tickets to a Soda Stereo concert. “The station answered me, but the dog took the internet cable and the call to the station was cut off.”
Milestone 2: He remembers his first video game and Game Boy.
Milestone 3: His father taught him how to ride a bike.

Caril [Boca de Camarones]:

Milestone 1: “I learned to use a calculator at age 9. I didn’t know how to use it, I was scared, but I learned.”
Milestone 2: She learned to use a laptop. “The internet has been a great tool for learning how to use technology,” she said.
Milestone 3: “Thanks to SOLE, I’ve gotten into the world of networks and technology. I want to keep learning.”

SanJay [SOLE Colombia]:

Milestone 1: “I bought a sampler to make music.” It gave him a lot of happiness because he felt he could make his own music.
Milestone 2: “At 16, I won a scholarship to study in Hong Kong and I bought a laptop and the movie Matrix on CD. The movie was divided into two parts; my brother scratched CD 2 trying to put it into the DVD player, but it got damaged and we couldn’t keep watching the movie.” He says it was frustrating, although now it makes him laugh.
Milestone 3: “I started making my own music.”

Paola [audiovisual production]:

Milestone 1: “They gave me my first camera. It was red. I’m nearsighted, but I learned how to use it. I’ve collected many cameras throughout my life because I like keeping the memory of moments.”
Milestone 2: “I remember my first cell phone looked like a brick.”
Milestone 3: “The internet arrived at the house. This gave me the possibility to connect with my friends in Uruguay.”

Findings and takeaways

In the session, participants connected their stories emotionally and intuitively. There was no sense of moral or material superiority between the stories.
Having to connect with another person’s story keeps everyone in a constant state of listening.
It is interesting how stories about the first technological device appear—whether it’s a TV, a cell phone, a printer, etc.—and how these devices allow new relationships with other people to be generated.
It is interesting how life stories in relation to technology say a lot about who we are and what we have stopped being today. Many stories connect with people’s passions, tastes, or character traits.
The milestones are related to happy, pleasant stories, but also to those that generate shame, pain, or nostalgia.
The importance of these devices lies not in the story itself, but in the way people connect their stories to one another.

title: “Guía rápida para arreglar tus vainas”
slug: guia-arreglar-vainas
¡Manos a la obra! Guía para arreglar tus vainas
¿Se te dañó algo en la casa y no sabes ni por dónde empezar? ¡Tranquilo, que eso nos pasa a todos! Aquí te traigo unos consejos prácticos para que no te varés y saqués adelante esos arreglos sin tanto complique.
Lo básico que necesitás tener a la mano
No necesitás ser un experto ni tener un taller profesional. Con un par de herramientas bien puestas, hacés maravillas:

Destornilladores: De estrella y de pala, ¡infaltables!
Alicates: Para cuando algo se pone rebelde.
Cinta aislante: La vieja confiable para cualquier cablecito suelto.
Un buen martillo: Por si toca aplicar un poquito de fuerza bruta (con cariño, eso sí).


“El que no sabe es como el que no ve”, así que no le tengás miedo a meterle mano a las cosas. ¡Lo peor que puede pasar es que toque llamar a alguien que sí sepa!

Pasos para no perderse

Analizá el problema: Mirá bien qué es lo que está fallando. A veces es solo un tornillo flojo o un cable mal puesto.
Buscá ayuda: Si no tenés ni idea, pegale una buscada en YouTube o consultá algún Manual de usuario.
Desconectá todo: ¡Ojo con la corriente! No queremos sustos innecesarios.
Hacé el arreglo: Con calma y sin afanes. Si algo no encaja, no lo forzés.

¿Cuándo es mejor pedir ayuda profesional?
Hay veces que uno tiene que saber cuándo tirar la toalla. Si el arreglo implica:

Temas eléctricos complejos: Si ves chispas o huele a quemado, ¡mejor llamá a un electricista!
Plomería pesada: No querás terminar inundando la cocina por ahorrarte unos pesos.
Equipos muy costosos: Si todavía tiene garantía, ¡no le metás mano! Llevá eso al Servicio Técnico de una vez.


¿Tenés algún truco bajo la manga? ¡Compartilo en los comentarios y ayudanos a todos a ser más “cacharreros”!

title: “Guía rápida para arreglar tus vainas”
slug: guia-arreglar-vainas
¡Manos a la obra! Guía para arreglar tus vainas
¿Se te dañó algo en casa y no sabes ni por dónde empezar? ¡Tranquilo, que eso nos pasa a todos! Aquí te traigo unos consejos prácticos para que dejes de sufrir y te pongas en modo “yo mismo lo arreglo”.
Lo básico que debes tener a mano
No necesitas ser un experto, pero sí tener un “kit de supervivencia” básico. Si tienes esto, ya tienes medio camino ganado:

Destornilladores: De estrella y de pala (los infaltables).
Cinta aislante: La vieja confiable para cualquier cable rebelde.
Alicates: Para cuando las cosas se ponen difíciles.
Un buen pegante: De esos que pegan hasta el alma.


“El que no tiene herramientas, no tiene soluciones.” — Dicho popular de mi abuelo.

Pasos para no hacer un desastre

Observa bien: Antes de meterle mano, mira cómo está armado. Si puedes, toma una foto para que después no te sobren piezas.
Desconecta todo: Si es algo eléctrico, ¡por favor, quita la corriente! No queremos sustos innecesarios.
Ten paciencia: Si ves que la vaina se pone difícil, respira. A veces es mejor dejarlo un rato y volver con la mente fresca.

¿Cuándo pedir ayuda?
Si ves que el asunto es muy complejo o que te puedes hacer daño, mejor llama a alguien que sepa. No hay nada de malo en admitir que uno no puede con todo. Puedes revisar nuestra sección de Servicios Técnicos si la cosa se puso color de hormiga.

¿Tienes algún truco bajo la manga? ¡Compártelo en los comentarios!

title: “Guía rápida para arreglar tus cosas”
slug: guia-rapida-arreglar-cosas
¡No lo botes todavía! Guía para revivir tus cacharros
¿Se te dañó algo en casa? ¡Tranquilo! Antes de que corras a comprar uno nuevo, dale una oportunidad a la reparación. Aquí te enseño cómo meterle mano a esos cacharros sin morir en el intento.
Lo básico que debes tener a la mano
No necesitas un taller profesional, con esto te defiendes como un berraco:

Destornilladores: De estrella y de pala (los infaltables).
Cinta aislante: La vieja confiable para cualquier cable pelado.
Alicates: Para cuando las cosas se ponen difíciles.
Un poquito de paciencia: Esto es lo más importante, ¡no te me desesperes!


“El que no mete mano, no aprende.” — Dicho popular de mi abuelo.

Pasos para no hacer un desastre

Desconecta todo: ¡Por favor! No queremos que te lleves un susto eléctrico.
Observa bien: Mira por dónde se abre. A veces los tornillos están escondidos bajo etiquetas o gomitas.
Toma fotos: Si vas a desarmar algo complejo, sácale fotos a cada paso. Así sabrás dónde iba cada pieza cuando te toque armar.
Limpia: A veces el problema es solo mugre acumulada. Un poquito de alcohol isopropílico hace milagros.

¿Cuándo pedir ayuda?
Si ves que el aparato tiene Circuitos Integrados quemados o si huele a quemado, mejor déjalo quieto. No queremos que causes un corto o te hagas daño. En esos casos, es mejor buscar a alguien que sepa de Electrónica básica.

¿Tienes algún truco bajo la manga? ¡Compártelo en los comentarios! Recuerda que reparar es un acto de rebeldía contra el consumismo. ¡Manos a la obra!

¿Se te dañó algo en casa? Antes de que corras a comprar uno nuevo, dale una oportunidad a la reparación. A veces es solo cuestión de maña y un poquito de paciencia. Aquí te enseño cómo meterle mano a tus cosas sin morir en el intento.
Lo básico que debes tener a la mano
No necesitas un taller profesional, con esto te defiendes como un berraco:

Destornilladores: De estrella y de pala (los infaltables).
Cinta aislante: La vieja confiable para cualquier cable pelado.
Alicates: Para cuando las cosas se ponen difíciles.
Un trapito: Porque siempre hay algo que limpiar o secar.

Observa bien: A veces el problema es más bobo de lo que parece. ¿Está bien conectado? ¿Tiene pilas?

Hay que ser realistas, mi hermano. Si ves que el arreglo es más caro que el aparato nuevo, o si de plano no tienes ni idea de por dónde empezar y te da miedo que te pase corriente, mejor busca a alguien que sepa. No queremos accidentes.

en/inspire/insp-sociotech-cacharreras.title: "Socio-technical trajectory · Cacharreras Community"
en/inspire/insp-sociotech-cacharreras.summary: Logbook of the development of SOLE Voltaje.
en/inspire/insp-sociotech-cacharreras.content:
We set out to create this divergent space you are currently exploring, called SOLE Voltaje: The Connectivity Solutions Guide. In this logbook, you will find the account of the development of a multitude of experiments we designed and executed to improve the user experience and interaction with our community of cacharreras (tinkerers). Below, you will find a logbook organized into macro-events and micro-events, where the story of what happened unfolds through the analytical lens of “socio-technical trajectories.”

Macro-events: These are phases we designed for the development and implementation of SOLE Voltaje. They can be seen in the following diagram:



Micro-events: These are the specific, significant occurrences that take place within each of the trajectories.
Socio-technical trajectory: A socio-technical trajectory is a process of co-construction involving products, production and organizational processes, institutions, user-producer relationships, learning processes, problem-solution relationships, processes of constructing the functionality/non-functionality of a technology, rationalities, policies, and specific strategies. To learn more about socio-technical analysis, you can visit our conceptory.

Stating three major controversies of interest in this trajectory, we have:

Understanding the controversy related to creating and nurturing a community of cacharreras. There are several experiments and concrete actions that managed to spark interest and action in specific users, but which ultimately could not be sustained. It seems that, given the possibilities and limitations of SOLE-Voltaje to date, considering the “Cacharrera” as a subjectivity that is maintained over time is very costly. It makes more sense to think of it as punctual activations that occur through deployments in events, workshops, or by chance, which do not necessarily permeate over time; rather, this user enters into a “tinkerer” logic in very limited times and spaces.
The evolution of user testing showed a broader understanding of the concept, allowing it to be configured in itself as a deployment of Voltaje where observation and analysis are central. That is, it seems the most appropriate way to deploy Voltaje is through user testing, because the very novelty of this guide means our understanding of appropriation is still very short-lived and particularized. If we do not continue in that exercise of praxis and reflection, it will be very difficult to achieve its appropriation.
Two rhetorical and material lines were built that we have not yet synchronized: on one hand, SOLElab as the Library of the Future, and on the other, Voltaje: The Solutions Guide. Due to the ways we approached execution and the inherent complexity of both processes, we only managed to articulate very concrete points of connection that did not achieve proper integration. Although this is how it remained as of the completion of this trajectory, it is not very clear whether the integration of the two lines is the most appropriate way to allow for the understanding of the appropriation of one virtual space versus the other physical space.

en/inspire/insp-sole-unal.title: "What does water mean to you and your community?"
en/inspire/insp-sole-unal.summary: SOLE conducted by students from the National University.
en/inspire/insp-sole-unal.content:
SOLE conducted by students of the Water and Energy Observatory IV from the School of Industrial Design at the National University. April 25, 2025.

Add your answers here. Careful! Don’t delete anyone else’s work. You can add photos, videos, links…
Group 1
Authors:

Juan Hansmeier
Daniel González
Angie Ospina
Andrea Castañeda

Answer: By adapting the “self-photography” tool, we proposed “self-drawing” focused on children; where, through questions and drawings, we arrived at the required answer.

Draw your day-to-day life.
The facilitator asks different questions that, in this context, guide the child to answer “what does water mean to you?” without being literal and asking that specific question.
A drawing is obtained with the answer to the big question.

Group 2
Authors:
Sebastián Caraballo
Angie Varón
Cynthia Obando
Deidy Rosero
Answer:

Group 3
Authors:
Angie Caroprese
Sergio Castro
Maikol Bello
Alejandro Mateus
Answer: Mind Map as a tool.
Data discrimination based on the following concepts:


Life and health (main source for drinking and cooking)


Culture and spirituality (Cultural identity and celebrations)


Sustenance and economy (fishing and food)


Relationship with nature (Traditional knowledge and environmental awareness)


Education and future (community water care projects)



Group 4
Authors:
David Linares
Luis Ortiz
Antonio Diaz
Gabriela Leaño
Herib Campos
What does water mean to you and your community?
We are going to work with two tools: participatory mapping and ethnographic video.
Participatory mapping:
Participatory mapping will work to visualize and understand the social and emotional dynamics, as well as the care taken regarding the meaning of water for the community. It is a tool for working with the community through talking circles.
1. Community activation and trust

Meeting with community leaders and key community members.
Explain the purpose and ask for permission to document with ethics and consent.

”Support tool: Talking circle + Audiovisual consent form.”
Proposed games and dynamics:
1. The voice of the river (creative presentation dynamic)
Objective: break the ice, introduce ourselves, connect with water.
How to play:


Each person introduces themselves by saying their name and completing this sentence:

“If I were water, I would be…” (a waterfall, a calm river, a storm, a happy little puddle, etc.)



Variation: have them do it by imitating the sound or movement of the water they chose.
2. Emotional map of water (on the floor)
Objective: identify emotional bonds.
How to play:

A large circle is drawn on the floor (with tape or branches) representing the territory.
The facilitator asks questions like:

“Where did you feel joy with water?”
“Where were you afraid of water?”
“Where did you learn something important about water?”


People walk and position themselves within the map according to their answer. They can share if they wish.


Material: dry leaves, tape, chalk, stones to mark zones.

2. Ask, feel, and draw (Participatory mapping)
Activity:


In groups, a large poster board is handed out with a silhouette of the territory (it can be free-form, not necessarily geographic).


The question is asked:
What does water mean to you?
Where is water present in your daily life?
Where does the water flow? Where does it stop? Where is it missing?


Draw and write:

Rivers, streams, wells, sacred sites, areas of scarcity, memories, uses, threats.
You can also use symbols, words, or emotional colors.


Materials: poster boards, markers, crayons, stickers, printed icons, colored paper.

Ethnographic video
The ethnographic video will help us identify and record the underlying dynamics of behavior and meaning regarding water from an external perspective.
During the mapping:

Film the conversations while they draw.
Interview key people with open-ended questions (children, elders/knowledge keepers, fishermen, women leaders):

What memories do you have of water?
What rituals or stories exist about water?
What has changed in the water of the territory?



Additionally:

Record landscapes, bodies of water, ambient sounds, daily activities (washing, navigating, collecting).


Recommendation: use close-up shots of hands drawing, faces while speaking, the lines as they grow. That adds a lot of visual and emotional value.

en/inspire/insp-speed-access-info.title: "Has it ever happened to you that a video loads faster on someone else's phone?"
en/inspire/insp-speed-access-info.summary: Understand how information can be accessed quickly on the Internet.
en/inspire/insp-speed-access-info.content:
We say the Internet is fast if we can quickly access the information we’re looking for.
Download megabytes (MB) are a measure of how quickly internet data is transmitted. The more MB you have, the faster your internet is.
If you have:

More than 5 MB: that’s a good speed for watching videos, listening to music, and doing all sorts of things online.
Between 1 MB and 5 MB: you can handle a stable video call.
Less than 1 MB: you can browse the web and send text messages.

The more devices you have connected to the internet, the fewer download MB you’ll have available. This happens because the speed gets split up among all the connected devices.

The photo-textual breakdown
Being a child, boy, girl, non-binary, being other

When I remember my childhood, I see myself taking toys apart to understand how they worked; sometimes I put them back together and they worked, and other times they didn’t. I can’t forget a battery-operated police car that would pop out two uniformed officers—gringo style, with a gun in hand—from each door as it moved. This was one of those that, fortunately, I could never put back together.
Part of my childhood was permeated by the presence of toys. Just as that police car existed, I remember taking my soccer ball everywhere. Even when I had the chance to see the ocean, I packed my futsal ball in my airplane luggage, and thankfully, it didn’t burst. My toys are with me.
Without knowing the world behind it, the naive instinct of a child who only knows what their parents provide allowed me to disassemble structures, just for the sake of being curious. I didn’t see interest behind the artifacts; I only saw smaller worlds that I wanted to understand, that I wanted to open.
What can bring more enjoyment than a toy? Sometimes, just a smooth stone, thrown with the right technique, can bring free moments of joy and memory when we approach a lake.
Being an adult is taking charge of your inner child. Just as I used to paint, play, and study, my identity increasingly returns to its multiple and rhizomatic childhood. Being a cacharrero (tinkerer) is sometimes an identity, but now, thanks to Mate, I see it’s also a noun. Sometimes we are tinkerers, and we figure things out; other times we don’t. What is it that moves you to tinker?

Having your bag of toys

My bag of toys for the workday. 1. The bag with pockets. 2. The headphones to listen better. 3. The headphone case to protect them. 4. The hard drive to back up information. 5. Pens, cutter, and eraser. 6. The phone charger. 7. The toothbrush and toothpaste. 8. The USB drive so I don’t have to work in the cloud and can keep the information close to me. 9. The Game Boy Advance. 10. Pokémon Sapphire.
The Carrier Bag Theory of Fiction
Ursula K. Le Guin
1986


Now the full essay:
pdf essay
Retrieved from: mirror.anarhija.net/es.theanarchistlibrary.org/mirror/u/uk/ursula-k-le-guin-la-teoria-de-la-bolsa-de-transporte-de-la-ficcion.pdf
The tinkering kit, the collection of toys and potions

Taking a part of the text “Hacer Disidencia Una Política De Nosotros Mismos” (Making Dissent a Politics of Ourselves) by Eric Sadin, I appeal to witchcraft (the past), and witches like the powerful Isabelle Stengers, and to science fiction (the future) with psychonauts like Aldous Huxley. I invite you tomorrow to create potions together. Just as we used to do the Sabbath, this last Saturday, as a partial closing, we will take our territorial tour and try some of the potions we design tomorrow.
“In the preface to a new 1946 edition of Brave New World, Aldous Huxley writes these words, whose scope and limits should be grasped:

“If I were now to rewrite the book, I would offer the Savage a third alternative. Between the utopian and the primitive horns of this dilemma would lie the possibility of sanity, a possibility already realized, to some extent, in a community of exiles and refugees from the brave new world, living within the confines of a kind of Reservation. In this community, the economy would be decentralist and Henry Georgian, the politics Kropotkinesque and co-operative. Science and technology would be used as though, like the Sabbath, they had been made for man, not (as at present) that man must be adapted and enslaved to them.”

For now, I only use this fragment to invite you to create potions for humans, for our collectives—potions that empower them, that adapt to them, not that enslave them.

Like Hermione Granger, our corotos or knick-knacks (magazines, markers, flowers, cables…) can support us in world-building, in our potions. Just as an example, to move past so much poetry, the potions can be: activity designs, lists of questions, fanzines, scents that prepare people for something, drawings, poems… in short. Those potions depend on your skills, your interests, the communities you wish to care for, and the purpose you envision for a specific time-space.

Also, like Seamus Finnigan, we can have accidents. Ultimately, we are in a perpetual learning process where we will never have guarantees of what will happen, especially when we are dream-weaving alternative worlds. My only call is to care, harm-free action, and precaution as policies. My potions seek to follow these principles by seeing the potential in oneself and in others, in the “other,” positioning oneself not from fear, but from trust, respect, and co-responsibility. What will be the guiding values for your potions?

en/inspire/insp-tinkerer-inspiration.title: "Together, we solve better"
en/inspire/insp-tinkerer-inspiration.summary: Communities that come together to improve their connectivity.
en/inspire/insp-tinkerer-inspiration.content:
Is having internet access a problem for you? In a world where not everyone has internet and where we increasingly feel more alone, there are communities that have come together to answer life’s Big Questions while building connectivity networks. These networks have allowed them to improve their internet access and strengthen their community fabric through SOLE (Self-Organized Learning Environments). These communities use community antennas, low-cost technologies, and a scrappy, collaborative spirit to overcome barriers and solve connectivity problems that once seemed insurmountable.
What if it is right there, in this drive to solve connectivity problems, that the future of the internet is born? And what if every internet connection were a vital link between life stories coming together to change the world? We no longer want to be spectators; we want to be the protagonists of our own story.
SOLE Voltaje doesn’t just offer easy answers; instead, it poses questions that spark curiosity and empower people to find their own solutions.
These communities show us that, with ingenuity and determination, it is possible to turn connectivity challenges into opportunities. We use the internet in groups because it’s safer, and because every internet connection is a connection with other people—it’s a bond of solidarity and learning.
So, let’s celebrate these Colombian communities that are weaving a web of hope through the internet. Their work is a powerful reminder that together we can build a more connected future, where every voice counts and every story finds its place; it is a reminder that another internet is possible. This new way of connecting is just beginning. We call this the Library of the Future.
SOLE Voltaje
When someone faces a connectivity problem, SOLE Voltaje pops up with its sparky energy: “Have you tried restarting the router? It’s like giving your connection a cup of coffee!” But its approach goes beyond simple tricks; it invites everyone to think: “Is your network saturated because everyone is watching cat videos? What if you get together with others to use the internet as a group? Maybe it’s time to reach some agreements on how we want to use the internet.”
Library of the Future
In a corner of the future, there exists a Library that doesn’t depend on books, but on the relationships between people. This is a space where knowledge isn’t in one specific place, but in the vast network of the internet and the connections it enables between people and communities. Here, life’s Big Questions wait to be explored. This Library of the Future invites us to gather, share ideas, and learn together. In every corner, you can feel the energy of collaboration: groups of people diving into deep discussions, using technology not as a barrier, but as a bridge toward understanding. The Library of the Future teaches us that, through connection and dialogue, we can discover answers we hadn’t even considered.
In a world where curiosity and technology converge, the Library of the Future has found an unparalleled friend: SOLE Voltaje, a solution guide designed to light the path toward knowledge. Together, they create a vibrant space where the internet is not just a tool, but an ally in the search for life’s Big Questions.

title: “Guía rápida para arreglar tus vainas”
slug: guia-arreglar-vainas
¡Manos a la obra! Guía para arreglar tus vainas
¿Se te dañó algo en casa y no sabes ni por dónde empezar? ¡Tranquilo, que eso nos pasa a todos! Aquí te traigo unos consejos prácticos para que dejes de sufrir y te pongas en modo “yo mismo lo arreglo”.
Lo básico que debes tener a mano
No necesitas ser un experto, pero sí tener un “kit de supervivencia” básico. Si tienes esto, ya tienes medio camino ganado:

Destornilladores: De estrella y de pala (los infaltables).
Cinta aislante: La vieja confiable para cualquier cable rebelde.
Alicates: Para cuando toca hacer fuerza o doblar algo.
Un buen pegante: De esos que pegan hasta el alma.


“El que no tiene herramientas, no tiene excusas.” — Dicho popular de mi abuelo.

Pasos para no hacer un desastre

Observa bien: No te pongas a desarmar como loco. Mira primero cómo está ensamblado el asunto.
Toma fotos: Si vas a soltar cables o piezas pequeñas, ¡toma una foto! Así sabrás cómo iba todo cuando te toque armar de nuevo.
No fuerces nada: Si algo no entra, es porque no es ahí. No seas bruto, que a la fuerza solo vas a terminar rompiendo algo más.

¿Cuándo es mejor llamar a alguien que sepa?
Hay veces que es mejor no ponerse de creativo. Si ves que el problema es con:

Electricidad de alto voltaje: ¡Ni lo toques! Eso es peligroso.
Tuberías principales: No queremos que termines inundando la casa.
Equipos electrónicos muy finos: Si no sabes, mejor no le metas mano, que sale más caro el arreglo después.

Para más info, revisa nuestra sección de Consejos de Hogar o busca en el foro de Comunidad de Bricolaje.

¿Tienes algún truco bajo la manga? ¡Compártelo en los comentarios!

en/inspire/insp-voltaje-test01.title: "Test #01 SOLE Voltage"
en/inspire/insp-voltaje-test01.summary: We evaluate the functionality of three connectivity solutions.
en/inspire/insp-voltaje-test01.content:
Presentation
Hi, I’m Nicolás, the cacharreo (tinkering) guy at Voltaje. Today, we want to share the design of this User Test that we designed and executed at the beginning of 2024. We learned a ton during this process, and we’d love for you to be able to adopt these methods and use them to interact with your own communities.
Objective
To evaluate the functionality of three connectivity solutions currently documented on the Voltaje platform.
Solutions
The difficult technique
Installing a web server on a pocket computer.
SOLE – Voltaje · Connectivity solutions guide

The easy tinkering trick
How to improve my signal with a can?
Estimated duration: 10–15 minutes.
SOLE – Voltaje · Connectivity solutions guide

The easy technique
Restarting and sharing your phone’s internet with others.
Estimated duration: 10 minutes.
SOLE – Voltaje · Connectivity solutions guide

The difficult tinkering trick
Building a homemade 3G antenna.
Estimated duration: 40–60 minutes.
SOLE – Voltaje · Connectivity solutions guide
Audience
Profile 1 - Doña Marlén, interested (+), skill (-)
She is a person over 50, with a genuine interest in knowing how to use the internet to improve her way of life. She finds it difficult to use cell phones, computers, and browse the internet. She is a mother.
Profile 3 – Pepito, interested (-), knowledge (+)
He is a person between 14-21 years old, a student, likes to use social media, play video games, and is currently studying. He likes to have the latest tech gadgets and is well-informed about them.
Profile 2 - Paila Gorrea, interested (-), skill (+)
She is a person aged 30-40, works with NGOs coordinating projects, and lives between the city and the rural communities she works with. She interacts with large donors to secure funding for NGO projects.
Profile 4 – Juanita, need (+), knowledge (-)
Methodology
VOLTAJE is presented along with some categories of interest to us regarding its functionality. Then, guests are allowed to read and develop a solution individually, while simultaneously commenting on their observations in relation to the presented categories. This is repeated with another solution. Upon finishing the solution, specific questions are asked regarding the categories of interest, and finally, an open group feedback session is held.
Observer
Your task is to be present, taking careful notes on how the user develops a solution by reading the instructions. You must be attentive to note points of boredom and frustration.
Moderator
This is the person who presents and directs the final feedback. Other observers can participate by asking occasional questions, keeping the following recommendations in mind:

Avoid giving judgments and reflections.
Do not give opinions about the solutions.

This does not mean you cannot induce answers from the people.
Since the central categories are “readability and viability,” the conversation will focus on these. The “accessibility” category can be explored in detail at a time when VOLTAJE is more advanced.
Agenda









































TimeMomentDescriptionTools9:00–9:15Welcome• Thanks for coming, welcome to SOLE• Let’s get to know each other: Name, what you do• (Optional) Tell us about a time you had an internet problem and what you did• Where are you located? Profile lines (Knowledge, skill, motivation, and need)SnacksPositional mapsPost-its9:15–9:25Exploring Voltaje• What do you know about SOLE?• (Optional) Short SOLE video• Why are you here? (Sanjay)• Connectivity Solutions Guide• Reasons for not having internet: money, signal, knowledge• Self-management of connectivity (using internet in a group: learning, cheap, safe, fun)• You will test two prioritized solutions and give feedback• First solution: 20–30 min• Second solution: 40–60 min• We are not evaluating skills, but the solutions9:25–9:30Presentation of SOLE Voltaje and the exercise• How the Voltaje page is set up• Types of solutions• Meaning of icons• Structure of a solution9:30–11:00Testing the solutions• Device: cell phone or computer• Link sent via WhatsApp• Presentation of the 2 solutions and times• Build a homemade 3G antenna (40–60’)voltaje.solecolombia.org/#Construye%20una%20Antena%203G%20casera• How to improve my signal with a can (10–15’)voltaje.solecolombia.org/#%C2%BF%C3%B3mo%20mejorar%20mi%20se%C3%B1al%20con%20una%20lata%3F• Groups of 2 participants per solution• Observer per guest (takes notes)• The participant can express frustration or blockageEvaluation form11:00–13:00Group feedback• Guided conversation with questions• Listen to participant comments• Take notes in the feedback section
Observation during the test
Instructions:

Before the guest starts working on the solution, explain your role and why you are there in concrete terms.
You can hand the evaluation form to the participant once they have finished the solution or decided to stop.
Tell each participant to take their time and read each of the statements they are going to evaluate carefully.
10 minutes before finishing the test, ask the participant to stop their work and fill out the evaluation.

Observer’s role:

Foster a calm and trusting space for each participant. The observer must not judge what the participant is doing. This should be a supportive role.
Take note of the participants’ reactions and behaviors while they work on the solution; without making them uncomfortable, being invasive, or intimidating the participant.
Take note of the questions each participant has and suggest that they do/solve them however they think best; but without over-explaining, helping, or trying to answer their doubts.

Suggested questions: How would you solve that doubt or problem? What do you think is failing in the explanation or solution that is causing you to have that doubt or problem?

Invite participants to evaluate each of the solutions calmly and honestly. The more objective and critical the participants are, the more useful the session will be.

If you have any questions about your role as an observer during the test, make a note of them. You can only intervene if you see an imminent risk.
Final feedback questions
Reflection on the change in the profile of interest, knowledge, needs, and skill

Were there changes in how interested you are in tinkering with devices?
Was there a change in how much knowledge you think you have?
Was there a change in how much skill you think you have?
How did you find the experience, how did you feel?
How did you feel?
How was the timing?
What did you find most difficult?
What did you find easiest?
What did you learn?
If you were to do this exercise again, what would you change?

Analysis tools
Possible categories (draft)
Under the umbrella of functionality, we can include different categories of interest. I propose the following, which are recommended qualities when creating instructional texts.











































































ConceptDefinitionQuestionsLegibilityThis concept refers to graphic aspects, typography, color, contrast, text distribution, layout, etc.Is the font type and size easy to read?Do the colors make it easy to read?Is the page layout appropriate?Are the images accompanying the texts sufficient or excessive?ReadabilityThis concept refers to the ease with which the text can be read, its clarity, attractiveness, completeness, timing, and comprehensibility.Are there ambiguous instructions?Are there incomplete instructions?Do you consider the verb tenses and the wording of the solutions appropriate for this instruction?Is the solution complete, or is a detail missing?Is the reading difficult due to the writing style?StructuringThis concept refers to the order of the sections and, in general, the way the instruction is organized. Its internal logic and the relationship it facilitates for the reader so they don’t waste time.Do you think the structure is appropriate, or do you think it could be ordered better? Are all sections useful, or do you consider any to be unnecessary or missing?AccessibilityThis concept refers to whether the solutions contemplate multiple ways of receiving information: text, audio, video, image description, etc.Do you consider the solution accessible to different audiences?Do you consider there to be any population group that would find it difficult to access the solution?Do you consider the solution to be presented in a way that is accessible to beginners in the subject?

If the wording makes reading difficult. |
| Viability | This concept refers to whether the solution can be carried out, if it works; regarding the resources needed to do it and if the solution is safe. | Were you able to complete the task this solution proposed to solve?
Did you find the activity dangerous at any point? |
| Traction | This concept refers to whether the solution sparks the reader’s interest in doing the solution and encourages them to continue developing related solutions. | Did the way the solution is presented encourage you to develop it?
Did the way the solution is presented encourage you to continue developing similar solutions?
Did the way the solution is presented generate interest/motivation for you to continue developing? |
| Learning | This concept refers to whether the instruction allowed you to learn new concepts that help you understand how the solution works. | Did you understand how the solution works?
Did you learn new concepts? |
| User test | This is an open category for participants to provide feedback on the exercise design. |  |

Criteria evaluation matrix




















































































































































































































#CriterionStatement12341.1LegibilityI consider the font size and type to be appropriate for my reading.1.2The font color and contrast with the background make my reading easier.1.3The distribution and justification between texts and images facilitate reading and comprehension of the texts.2.1ReadabilityThe way the texts are written makes my reading easier.2.2The texts communicate complete instructions.2.3I know all the words used.3.1StructuringThe order of the instructions is appropriate.3.2The number of images accompanying the text is sufficient.3.3The way the instructions are organized allows me to save time.4.1AccessibilityThe instructions are appropriate for beginners in the subject.4.2The instructions are presented to be used from different devices.4.3The instructions allow access to different types of audiences.The instructions allow me to develop the solution individually and in a group.5.1ViabilityThe instruction allows for the development of a solution that works.5.2The materials needed to develop the solution are easily accessible.5.3The instructions have any dangerous steps.6.1TractionThe way the solution is presented encourages me to develop it.6.2The way the solution is presented encourages me to learn about other related solutions.6.3The way the solution is presented invites me to know more about this topic.7.1LearningI clearly understood how the solution works.7.2I learned new concepts related to the topic.7.3I can explain to someone how to develop the solution.
Materials





















































#MaterialQty.Link1Ethernet cable (m)1Available in the office.2Quick-drying epoxy glue.5The Sintesolda brand has worked ferreco.com/inicio/6276-adhesivo-epoxico-sintesolda-rapido-transparente.html—CLQ7n5qPA_NQjMA_PR7nAZRoC2WEQAvD_BwE3Plastic cable duct (2 cm)2504Cut-resistant gloves2articulo.mercadolibre.com.co/MCO-502525366-guantes-anti-corte-proteccion-trabajo-nitrilo-industriales-_JM#position=6&search_layout=stack&type=item&tracking_id=3c36b974-e272-4bf2-b8c2-692cbf774a855Rigid pole to mount the antenna (a guadua bamboo as long as possible, 6 3 meters).36Coaxial cable (m)127Pack of plastic zip ties (10-20 cm)1
Supporting concepts
Instruction
By the term “instructions,” I refer to all discourses that order behavior or establish conduct, with imperatives, periphrasis of obligation, enumerations of actions, lists of facts, graphic illustrations, etc. Instructions include cooking recipes, traffic codes, contest rules, appliance user manuals, medicine leaflets, employment contracts, or DIY guides. These types of texts govern our lives.
Criteria
Instructions should be:

For everyone. For beginners, who know nothing, and for experts, who verify details or solve problems.
Complete and precise: They must cover everything: all functions, all steps, all conditions, or all characteristics of the object or task.
Appropriate. It is convenient to order them to “serve” the reader. There are no universal structures or a canonical order. They should not waste time.
Manageable. Besides being understood, each instruction must be operational. The reader must grasp it with one reading and be able to execute it without difficulty.
Neutral. Without emotion, courtesy, irony, or humor.
Safe. Confusing instructions can cause accidents.
Comfortable: It is convenient to foresee how the instructions will be used and adapt them to the situation.






























Legibility criteriaExplanation1.1. SizeThe font size must be at least 14 pt.1.2. TextsTexts must be justified.1.3. ContrastThe contrast must be opposite and facilitate reading.1.4. LayoutThe distribution between texts and images facilitates reading and comprehension of the texts.1.5. TypographyThe course uses an accessible typeface. Example: Verdana or Trebuchet.

































Readability criteriaExplanation2.1. WordingThe wording of the solution facilitates the comprehension of the texts.2.2. ComprehensionThe instructions are easy to understand, regardless of the use of technical language.2.3. MotivationThe wording of the text stimulates and motivates progress in the development of the solution.2.4. Course duration and timingThe times for completing the solution are consistent with the instructions.2.5. StructureThe solution instructions are complete.2.6.The solutions need to explain details.
Recommendations
Below are other tips for writing instructions and recommendations:
Give each group of instructions a title. This can be the objective (install a program on the PC), the final product (project budget), or the topic (office etiquette rules). The title allows you to refer to the instructions in other parts of the text.
Choose the most appropriate terms. These must be precise and also simple so that the reader can understand them. In addition, ambiguous and confusing formulations should be avoided.
Select the appropriate verb form. It is better to use the imperative verb mode, which expresses a command or exhortation, using the “you” (e.g., avoid the terms) or formal “you” (e.g., avoid) forms. This way, we address the reader directly. The imperative is clearer than the impersonal (e.g., “it is answered”) or the infinitive (e.g., “to answer”). Regarding the form of address (informal or formal), the Writing Manual points out that this will depend on the degree of formality of the text.

Start with the verb. Starting each instruction with the verb makes the writing clearer. The first thing the reader sees, at the beginning of each line, is what they must do.
Avoid negations whenever possible. These are harder to understand than affirmations. It is better to formulate instructions affirmatively if feasible.
Eliminate repetitions. You should avoid reiterating indications. It is better to summarize them.
Homogeneity. It is convenient to maintain the chosen writing style in all instructions. For example, it is a mistake to start with a noun—as here, with “homogeneity”—if a conjugated verb is used in the rest of the instructions. It would be better to say “Write homogeneous instructions.”

Characteristics of an instructional text

The sequence of activities is presented in a correct and understandable chronological order, numbering them and using connectors that help in understanding the actions to achieve a result.
Graphic marks such as numbers, asterisks, or hyphens are used to differentiate or sequence the series of steps.
It can be accompanied by graphics, illustrations, and/or drawings, depending on the type of instructional text to be developed.
It presents clear, precise, and linear language. It must be understood by anyone.

Guidelines for writing an instructional text

Determine the intention of the text.
Describe the physical resources and functions that make up the action to be performed.
Organize the writing into two parts, headed by a subtitle that identifies its content.
Number each of the steps.
Respect the chronological sequence of the process steps in the writing.
Use verbs in the infinitive, imperative, or 3rd person.
Use chronological connectors: to start, in the first place, in the second place, finally,
then, after, so, from, before, next, immediately, etc.
Add some warnings and precautions that the user should keep in mind.
Use appropriate language according to the activity.
Write with clear and simple sentences.

Resources

Instructions for climbing a staircase
Julio Cortázar*

No one will have failed to observe that the ground frequently folds in such a way that one part rises at a right angle to the plane of the ground, and then the next part is placed parallel to this plane, to give way to a new perpendicular, a behavior that repeats in a spiral or broken line up to highly variable heights. By crouching down and placing the left hand on one of the vertical parts, and the right on the corresponding horizontal one, one is in momentary possession of a step or stair. Each of these steps, formed as seen by two elements, is situated somewhat higher and further forward than the previous one, a principle that gives meaning to the staircase, since any other combination would produce forms perhaps more beautiful or picturesque, but incapable of moving one from a ground floor to a first floor.
Staircases are climbed facing forward, as backward or sideways they are particularly uncomfortable. The natural attitude consists of standing, arms hanging without effort, head held high, though not so much that the eyes stop seeing the steps immediately above the one being stepped on, and breathing slowly and regularly. To climb a staircase, one begins by lifting that part of the body located on the right below, almost always wrapped in leather or suede, and which, with exceptions, fits exactly on the step. Once said part, which for brevity we will call the foot, is placed on the first step, the equivalent part on the left is picked up (also called a foot, but which must not be confused with the aforementioned foot), and bringing it to the height of the foot, it is made to follow until it is placed on the second step, with which the foot will rest on this one, and the foot will rest on the first. (The first steps are always the most difficult, until the necessary coordination is acquired. The coincidence of the name between the foot and the foot makes the explanation difficult. Take special care not to lift the foot and the foot at the same time).
Having arrived in this way at the second step, it is enough to repeat the movements alternately until finding the end of the staircase. One leaves it easily, with a slight tap of the heel that fixes it in its place, from which it will not move until the moment of the descent.

END*

en/inspire/insp-voltaje-test02.title: "SOLE Voltage Test #02"
en/inspire/insp-voltaje-test02.summary: Protocol for test 02 based on learnings from test 01.
en/inspire/insp-voltaje-test02.content:
This document aims to outline the protocol for conducting Test 02 of the Solutions Guide, based on the lessons and findings from Test 01, which took place on 03.02.2024.

What did we learn from Test 01?


Focus the drafting of the solutions on improving writing style, language clarity, and the logical order of instructions.
It is important that the solution’s tone makes participants feel supported through every step.
It is essential to understand that well-written steps depend on the strategic use of images, diagrams, or photographs to provide key and relevant information.
Efforts should be focused on improving: 1. the images accompanying each instruction; 2. the order, clarity, and organization of the instructions.
It is essential to have an initial section covering the safety conditions that must be ensured before starting the test.
Before starting the solutions (for the Guide), perhaps suggest that people find a comfortable, quiet, and safe space.
Participants mentioned that the soda can antenna solution was more motivating than challenging, while the homemade antenna solution felt more like a challenge/frustration than motivation. We need to figure out how to manage frustration.
The tone of the guide should be one of companionship and compassion; a tone that makes it clear that the solutions are not for experts and that anyone interested can do them. This tone is currently unclear. The guide’s ethical and political commitment should be evident in this tone. There is no clear communication strategy.
It is worth reviewing how typography, font size, and layout facilitate reading. It would be worth testing with people who have difficulty reading on a computer. Also, test the layout with a column-based distribution.


Progress: the solutions must make participants feel that they are moving forward. Participants must know where they are in the test and how much is left.
Companionship: the solutions must be written in such a way that participants feel accompanied through a colloquial and approachable tone.
Strategy:
Confirmation: the solutions must assure participants that they are on the right track and that their progress is indeed correct.

Types of images to be used for the tests

Result images: show the final result of the step or the solution being performed. These images allow participants to compare their progress with what the test requires.
Process images: show the steps necessary to reach a result or a specific step.
Context images: show the solutions with people in specific contexts.

Participant profiles
The following profiles can overlap. For example, there are people who may have very little knowledge about how the internet works, but may be very interested in learning for the test.













Interest: people interested in learning how to carry out a solution.Need: people who need the solutions to solve concrete problems.Knowledge: people who know a lot about how the internet works, or any of the guide’s pillars: electricity, space, community outreach, space management, or connectivity.Skills: people who have soft skills and/or motor skills to carry out the solutions.
2. Objectives of Test 02:

Evaluate the progress made on the solutions based on the lessons from Test 01.
Verify the changes produced in participants by the audio-reading format for the solutions.
Receive feedback on the solutions regarding “how to convene your community” and find the differences and similarities with the “the internet signal is bad” tests.

3. Questions to formulate Test 02:

Participant profiles: Based on the lessons and objectives, who and how many people should be part of the test? How do we divide the test for the profiles of interest, need, knowledge, and skills?
Test format: Should we carry out the solution virtually and remotely? What is the reason we should do it this way? Does remote mean doing the test with a synchronous observer or, conversely, giving a time frame of a week and a half (for example) to complete the test?
Care: What considerations and care should we have for the people who will perform these tests?
Expectations: What do we expect from the people who will perform the test?
Feedback/evaluation: How will we receive feedback/evaluation from the participants?
Roles: What roles within the SOLE team are necessary to carry out this test?

4. Proposal for Test 02 (answers to the questions in point 3):

Participant profiles: Test 02 will be carried out by participants remotely and virtually.


SOLUTION ITERATION TEST: evaluate if the rewriting of the Test 01 solutions improved the experience. Two of the participants from Test 01 could repeat the tests performed in Test 01.

READING TEST with Audio-reading (remote 1 week): With the initial 4 people, both homemade antenna and soda can.
EXECUTION TEST (remote 1 week): Invite 2 new people to execute the homemade antenna test. 2 new people for the soda can one.


SOLUTION START TEST: check the progress we have made for people who have not had contact with the Solutions Guide. Two new people could work on one or two solutions different from those prototyped in Test 01.

REMOTE 3G antenna installation: 2 Spinner Explorers.
IN-PERSON “Restart and share your phone’s internet with others.”


COMPARISON TEST BETWEEN CATEGORIES: check the necessary changes between the tests on “how to convene your community” and “the internet signal is bad.” The other two participants from Test 01 could work on the two new tests on “how to convene your community.”


Test format: Participants will have an estimated time of 1 week and a half to send the test results; this will allow us to evaluate, organically, how much interest they had in developing the test.
Care: Since it will be virtual, give people time to perform the test at their own pace. Make people feel calm, comfortable, and be honest with SOLE, both to say they don’t want to do the test and to provide feedback and evaluate the solutions.
Expectations:
Feedback/evaluation:




an entry form (before starting the test) and another upon finishing the test.


I suggest using the self-documentation method so that, during week 01, people can record their experience with the test.
