Common Ground Workshop
Title: Creating devices to reflect on our technological autonomy
Facilitators: Nicolás Gaitán; Manuela Cordoba and Mateo Acosta, SOLE Colombia Foundation
Duration: 90 minutes
Description: First, analog data visualization devices will be installed to spark reflection and dialogue among participants. Building on this, we will encourage participants to create their own devices with their own big questions to challenge the rest of the group.
Objective
To inspire the creation of reflective devices for managing data related to technological autonomy.
Time
1:30 h
Moments

Devices on autonomy, an inspiration (30 min)

Arrival at the space and interaction with the example devices. 5 different devices will be installed to allow participants to reflect on their differences… Additionally, there will be a space with inspirational and thought-provoking references.
Introduction to photo taking.

Device 1 - Colored stones: screen consumption


Question:
How much time do others spend looking at screens?
How much time do you spend looking at screens per day?
Materials: colored stones, spoon, canvas with a circular drawing, baskets to store the stones.


Device 2 - Decision tree: Sharing and privilege

Ideally, everyone should interact in a group with this device. At the end, each person who follows a path must place a dot.
jamboard.google.com/d/1Y34vGSI9O59fpOe5OWD6ck5qWBsgEy-hZfoSQ56dwbI/viewer


Device 3 - Technological privilege ladder

Take a step if your power doesn’t go out frequently.
Take a step forward if you don’t usually have trouble accessing the internet.
Take a step forward if you haven’t felt worried about the amount of gigabytes you consume on the internet.
Take a step forward if you have a postpaid internet plan.
Take a step forward if you have ever bought a cell phone for more than 300 USD.
Take a step forward if you have never had to solve an internet problem on your own.
Take a step forward if you have more computers than the number of people in your house.
Take a step forward if you pay for more than 2 internet services (e.g., Netflix, Spotify, Google Drive, iCloud, Mubi, meditation services, ChatGPT, etc.).
Take a step if you don’t usually spend time in public recreational and cultural spaces.

Materials: Masking tape, printout with the script of the questions.


Device 4 - Ribbons: call to autonomous action


How much of a “tinkerer” (cacharrero) do you consider yourself?
How curious are you about how the devices you use in your daily life work?
Materials: Colored ribbons, 3 sheets of poster board.


Device 5 - LEGO data; Awareness-information

If one LEGO brick represents 10 GB, place your assessments in relation to the following questions:

How many GB of internet do you think you consume per month?
How many GB of internet do you think you need?

One person consumes more than 500 GB per month.

www.populoos.es/blog/cuantos-GB-consume-persona-mes/
[www.highspeedinternet.com/es/recursos/cuantos-datos-de-internet-necesitas#:~:text=El%20usuario%20promedio%20de%20internet,un%20informe%20reciente%20de%20OpenVault](www.highspeedinternet.com/es/recursos/cuantos-datos-de-internet-necesitas#:~:text=El usuario promedio de internet,un informe reciente de OpenVault).

Most people need 600 GB per month.
20230606_SOLE+WLH_Prst_Taller de Inspiración SOLE

Library of references

We will leave a section where people can go to consult other ways of presenting data.

Presentation, workshop exhibition, and reflection on the data (15 minutes)

We present SOLE and Voltaje, and the tensions that emerge in our projects regarding data management, and finally, we move with the group of participants to reflect on their answers in the 4 devices.
Reflections
a. Device 1 - Colored stones: screen consumption.
The importance of tinkering (cacharrería) for the Latin American context, and how these forms allow for an approach to knowledge and local ways of learning.
b. Device 2 - Decision tree: Sharing and privilege
The paradoxes that distance our beliefs from our practices, and the mechanisms to mobilize them.
c. Device 3 - Privilege ladder: We are positioned from different places and histories, which enables or hinders our journey on Earth.
d. Device 4 - Ribbons: Estimating my internet usage
Real estimates of the cost of each type of consumption and a national comparison of the prices charged.
e. Device 5 - LEGO data; Awareness-information
Changing habits regarding access to online and offline information, new logics of cultural consumption.
General: Reflection, dialogue, and questioning VS extraction.

Designing your own devices (30 minutes)



Two truths and a lie regarding technology (10 minutes)
People will say two truths and a lie regarding technology, and the others will have to guess which one is the lie.


Device design (20 minutes)


Design a quick device to challenge, reflect, and dialogue about the use of technology in both your personal life and the organizations where you work. Think of questions that the rest of the participants can answer and that can generate great conversations and new questions on the subject.

Materials: Table with possible materials for designing the devices, adhesive tape, newspaper, post-its, markers, colored pencils, colored stones, ribbons, yarn, sheets of paper, adhesive dots, lentils.


Interaction with the devices (15 minutes)


Quick exhibition of the created devices and the defined questions.
Invitation for participants to interact with these devices throughout the day.
We close with a general reflection and a thank you.

Resource economy
The particularity of a reflective VS extractive question
The power of visualization in questioning our habits, beliefs, expectations, etc.

PURPOSE
Clarify user contributions to SOLE Voltaje.
Questions
Who wants to contribute?
Why do they want to contribute?
How is the contribution currently produced?
What obstacles (technical and non-technical) do users encounter when trying to contribute?
What non-technical changes can be introduced to incentivize contribution?
The day after, how does participant contribution become a daily habit?
What elements are relevant/important for group interaction with SOLE Voltaje?
Moments
The practical one: Tinkering station and SOLE as a practice
DESCRIPTION

What will be done?: Clarify user contribution through their active participation in tinkering workshops and alternative SOLE practices (as opposed to the usual practice under ideal conditions).
How will it be done?: Through tinkering activities and alternative SOLEs where participants can test this Station according to their motivation.
Why?: If people experience a creative tinkering workshop and alternative SOLEing, they can live and imagine use cases for their own challenges or personal/organizational projects and give us feedback regarding the event’s purpose questions.

Chatbox Station
DESCRIPTION
Could we propose a relationship with a Chatbot beyond inputs and outputs? Could a Chatbot, from now on Chatbox, invite us to discover the internet in a way that not even the Chatbox itself can anticipate?
With this station, we want to invite participants to discover the possibilities of SOLE Voltaje and the tinkering spirit by moving through the space. On the other hand, it is a provocation to reflect on those relationships between humans that machines cannot anticipate.
Phases
Moment 1: Chat Box Path: people will walk along a mat with EIGHT (8) possibilities that SOLE Voltaje has. Depending on where people stand, an infrared sensor with Arduino will produce sounds and effects that invite participants to explore the space in relation to where they are standing.

CONVENE/PEOPLE: Do you want to know tools to convene other people to use the internet in a group?
SPACE: Do you want to find a public space to use the internet?
EQUIPMENT: Do you want to get the technology necessary to connect to the internet?
ELECTRICITY: Do you want to find a solution when electricity fails or is intermittent?
SIGNAL: Do you want to find solutions when the internet signal fails or is intermittent?
EXPERIENCES: Do you want to know about the experiences of communities that are improving their internet connectivity?
OFFLINE TINKERING: Do you want to know how the internet and connectivity work in the place where you are?
QUESTIONS (DATA): Do you want to reflect on our relationship with the internet?

Moment 2: Discover the space: upon choosing an option, the ChatBox and the space indicate to the person that they can go explore the space to discover what interested them. Each moment should have a reflection or story that invites them to read, listen, and learn more.

PEOPLE: explore the space and find the tools to convene other people to use the internet in a group
SPACE: explore the space and find a public space to use the internet
EQUIPMENT: explore the space and get the technology necessary to connect to the internet
ELECTRICITY: explore the space and find a solution when electricity fails or is intermittent
SIGNAL: explore the space and find solutions when the internet signal fails or is intermittent
EXPERIENCES: explore the space and learn about the experiences of communities that are improving their internet connectivity
OFFLINE TINKERING: explore the space and learn how the internet and connectivity work in the place where you are
QUESTIONS (DATA): explore the space and reflect with some questions about our relationship with the internet

Moment 3: Return or continue:
Each moment will have 3 options that will be distributed randomly throughout the space and will enable multiple possibilities to discover and explore Voltaje. Upon finishing an option, the participant can return (or go for the first time) to the ChatBox or continue with other stories of the same option or other options.
Resources

Yarn of different colors
Post-its
Corrugated cardboard (half sheet)

How is feedback received? How does the tinkering spirit emerge according to the experience?
People will leave a little dot on the options they visited throughout the tour. At the end, we will ask why they visited those options and how they felt when visiting them.
ChatTinkering Station
DESCRIPTION
How do we realize that we are not alone in this tinkering business? How do we accompany and support each other in exploring solutions to improve our experience of using the Internet in a group?
The WhatsApp chat is a place for people who are having connectivity challenges or who are building Voltaje solutions to:

find a community that helps them get through specific difficulties they may have
be able to share/receive new solutions that are not in Voltaje
share/receive how in other places they are using solutions that may or may not be in Voltaje (for example, “5 tricks for…” or other content we can find on the internet and see how people react) - watch out at the end, the invitation is to use the internet in a group
share/receive interesting information about connectivity challenges and solutions in the world, discoveries, work in other places, initiatives…
provide support to those who venture to explore the Voltaje space, and the test, and find themselves lost - helper?

The purpose of the activity is to observe how people participating in the challenges interact with this channel, analyze if it is important and useful for them, and receive feedback on the interaction that develops that day to make the constructions and/or modifications required to fulfill its mission, and provide mutual support to the people who interact with Voltaje and the test.
PHASES
Purpose:
Experience using the WhatsApp chat to share and discuss connectivity solutions. Each challenge lasts 30 minutes and challenges can take place at the same time that participants interact with the rest of the installation activities. There is a group that starts at this station and is in charge of starting challenge 1; after 30 minutes, we notify them so that the next group starts challenge 2 (the same is repeated with 3).
Activities:
The presentation of each challenge is done by Bel through the WhatsApp group.

Challenge 1 (30 minutes): The group in charge of the challenge must decide among all the presentation entries which connectivity challenge they find the coolest. The discussion takes place live (between the people interacting in this group) and in the chat, with people who are not at the location. People who are in other stations can also participate in the discussion, but those who facilitate or lead this challenge are those in the starting group. In the chat, it must be clear which connectivity challenge they choose to solve.
Challenge 2 (30 minutes): The group in charge of Challenge 2 must find the solution for the challenge proposed in the first challenge, consulting the SOLE Voltaje guide and what they have experienced in the rest of the space. The discussion must be reflected in the chat and the decision of which solution is the most appropriate must be clear to all members of the chat. They can request opinions and experiences from all members. The tinkerers in the chat can stimulate the discussion and can also encourage the exploration of the space in the workshop, or experimentation in the other stations.
Challenge 3 (30 minutes): The group in charge picks up the baton from the previous group (they must understand it by reading the chat) and selects the interactions in the chat that they found especially useful or interesting. Then, they must analyze how the structure of the chat (such as message organization, type of responses, use of multimedia) contributed to the understanding and resolution of the problem.

en/inspire/insp-voltaje-tests.content:
The Voltaje tests have been our way of exploring, evaluating, and pushing the boundaries of the solutions and devices we’ve developed to spark that “tinkerer” spirit and foster an approach to technology and connectivity that leads us to create spaces for autonomous and community-led learning.
Thanks to everyone who has joined us for these tests, we’ve been able to keep finding ways to extend the “internet blanket” to many places and communities. Plus, we’ve gained a much better understanding of what we’re really doing here at Voltaje.

en/inspire/insp-what-is-internet.title: "What is the Internet?"
en/inspire/insp-what-is-internet.summary: The Internet is a blanket of solidarity that connects the world.
en/inspire/insp-what-is-internet.content:
Download this Inspiration to use it offline
When you think about the Internet, what’s the first thing that pops into your head?
If we think of libraries as a repository of human knowledge written in books, and that nowadays computers hold that information—plus a whole lot more stored as ones and zeros in their memory—then we could imagine the Internet as the sum of all the information created and saved on every computer on the planet, all connected through a network of cables and wireless signals, swapping that information back and forth.
The Internet is way more than that, but in a nutshell: it’s a massive, decentralized network of computers talking to each other.
There are other communication networks in the world, like the postal service, telephony, radio, or television. A big difference between those and the Internet is that on the Internet, people can communicate both ways and swap digital information super fast—at the speed of light!

en/inspire/insp-who-is-solecolombia.title: "SOLE Colombia: Who are we?"
en/inspire/insp-who-is-solecolombia.summary: We create an equitable future together, one Big Question at a time.
en/inspire/insp-who-is-solecolombia.content:
At SOLE Colombia, we’re building a fair and beautiful future together, one Big Question at a time.
We spark curiosity in groups of people, turning internet-enabled spaces into Self-Organized Learning Environments (SOLEs), so we can recognize our own power and help our lives and communities flourish.
We shake up the status quo by building communities that learn beyond borders and differences, bridging the gap between people and ideas to create a more vibrant, shared world.
Let’s change the world together!

en/new-here.title: ¿Nuevo aquí?
en/new-here.summary: ¿Primera vez en Voltaje? Empieza aquí para entender cómo funciona la plataforma y cómo puedes contribuir.
en/new-here.content:
New here?
Welcome to SOLE Voltaje! An initiative by SOLE Colombia dedicated to improving access to knowledge through community-based solutions for using the Internet as a group. There are three steps to get started with SOLE Voltaje:

Get Inspired: Explore our big questions, videos, and stories from the communities we’ve worked with.
Solve: Find a solution to help boost connectivity in your space, your community, or your region. Solutions are organized into categories of signal, electricity, devices, people, and space, because using the internet as a group requires more than just connectivity.
Got questions?: Share what you learn, write to us with your questions, join our “tinkerers” (cacharreros) WhatsApp group, and help build this movement for a more inclusive internet.

You also have an experience to learn what the Internet is and how it works, plus an invitation to help us spread the blanket of solidarity so others can connect too: SOLE Voltaje Disconnected.
Our “Tinkerer” (Cacharrero) Ethos

  
  


SOLE Colombia, 2024

Have you ever wondered how the Internet reaches your home? Why we pay so much to connect, or what it would be like to live disconnected? Connecting to the Internet might seem like magic, but it’s actually information traveling the world through servers—the physical places that make it possible for you to read this right now.
For many, the “connected” world remains a mystery, either because they lack access or because they don’t know how it works. But here, we like to question everything. We don’t just go along with the mystery; this is a safe space to explore. Together, we can understand, question, and reinvent the future of the Internet.
SOLE Voltaje is that constant tension between what we already know and what is yet to be discovered, between the need to be connected and the desire for freedom and technological autonomy. Here, we develop tools, provocative ideas, inspiration, and spaces for collective learning that drive the use of the Internet as a group to answer Big Questions, because we believe in another possible future for network connection: one that is open, secure, and where we can all decide how we want to be connected—humanly connected.
Everything you find here is the result of the collaboration and knowledge of “cacharreras/os”—as we call them in Colombia—people who don’t accept “it doesn’t work” as an answer, people willing to tinker, to take apart what no longer works until it functions again. We want more people in the world to be encouraged to build the Internet with their own hands. You, too, can be an active network tinkerer!
To change the world together
The goal of SOLE Voltaje is to enable individuals or organizations working with people who have no or limited Internet access to improve their situation in a self-managed way, as far as their own resources allow.
These resources include the amount of money they can dedicate to improving their situation, the time they have to self-learn, implement, and test solutions, the number of people who could join them on their journey, and the level of complexity of the solutions they can develop.
Over time, we hope that people in rural areas and digitally excluded communities can use and link various solutions together to finally have a permanent community space with connectivity and devices to learn, dialogue, and create flourishing communities using the Internet.
There is also a pedagogical purpose behind this guide to invite people to use technology, in a broad sense, to learn.
We would like to re-engage current users and invite new ones to be curious about the Internet and how it works, and how they can use it as a group to learn what they need or are interested in. That is why, within the solutions, there is also a glossary of terms that teaches users technical and non-technical concepts so they can become active Internet “tinkerers.”
What is SOLE Colombia?
SOLE Colombia is a non-profit organization whose purpose is to create an equitable and beautiful future together, one Big Question at a time.
We ignite the curiosity of groups of people, transforming spaces enabled for the Internet into Self-Organized Learning Environments (SOLE), to recognize our power and allow our lives and communities to flourish.
We shake up the status quo by creating networks of communities that learn beyond borders and differences, building bridges between people and ideas toward a more vibrant shared world.
Did you get hooked?
If you want to know more about our organization and how we are changing the world, visit our website here.

en/solve/solv-ally-with-places.title: How to ally with others who support your call?
en/solve/solv-ally-with-places.summary: Other actors can make your message reach further.
en/solve/solv-ally-with-places.content:
Hi, I’m Belén. I don’t know much about technology, but I love people, and I’m pretty good at building relationships with them. I arrived at SOLE some time ago and have learned a lot about the power of people and what we can achieve when we come together.
What does it mean to partner with places that bring people together?
There are many people and organizations that can help your message reach further and clearer, and who can turn your projects into a path for transformation in your community. Knowing how to reach them and grab their attention is a way to join forces to achieve great things.

What is it for?
Often, you want to count on your community to do things or learn together, but you find it hard to get people to join the movement, or you end up doing everything with the same old crowd.
With these recommendations, you can learn how to approach others so they support the call to action in your community.

What do you need?

Courage
Curiosity and the ability to listen
Something to take notes with


How to do it?

Step 1 → Define the purpose of your call. It will be easier to find allies

The first thing is always the “why” behind what you’re going to do. If you intend to partner with others, you must be clear about the purpose of what you’ll be doing with them; only then can you properly focus your search for those who can help you spread the word.
For example, if you’re looking for people to build an antenna, would it be better to look for them at a hardware store during the workday, or at the exit of a preschool? Perhaps a place where people go to find materials to build things or “tinker” (or cacharrear, as we say) is better. The hardware store owner might be a better ally than the school teachers for a call to build an antenna.
Although you shouldn’t underestimate the talent in your community, you can prioritize the people and places you want to reach by having a very clear “what for.”
If you can, define your proposal in detail: is it one event or a series of events? What do you need to have, buy, or equip your project with? Do you need more people, or are you doing it alone?


Step 2 → Locate the “connectors”—who they are and what they do

Look around you: in your neighborhood, your community, your town… you might even have allies in your own house!
Recognizing people and organizations with the power to bring others together, and partnering with them, is a strategic move to get what we want.
Think of people and places where there is a flow of people, people who talk to the community, or those who organize events. These types of actors are key for spreading the word… keep your purpose in mind so you can better see who has contact with the people you want to reach.
It’s worth asking ourselves how we can build networks to successfully call people to our activities. If you work on sharpening your skills to join forces with others, you’ll start to see how it gets easier and flows better every time.

Photo: SOLE Colombia


Step 3 → Read the interests of those who bring people together and how they align with yours

Just as you want to organize a specific event, like a SOLE, other people also have specific interests in the activities they want to promote.
Think about what catches the attention of each of these actors and how you can address both their interests and yours: including the other person in a negotiated agenda can win you a long-term ally, not just a one-time collaborator.
For example, if your interest is to create the habit of doing SOLEs in your community, you could partner with the Local Action Board (JAL). Understanding how to use the internet as a group to learn things together can meet the JAL’s goals related to planning and executing community development projects or guaranteeing digital rights for the community. It’s a nice way to open the conversation about the activity you want to organize and how the JAL can support your event.


Step 4 → Choose who you want to do what with

Now that you’ve identified the strategic actors and know how to align their goals with yours, choose the one you feel most comfortable working with for each of your objectives.

Photo: SOLE Colombia


Step 5 → Work on the invitation and the message you want to share

Lay out your ideas and prioritize them. Developing each of your ideas thoroughly and finding the best way to present them to your ally is a way to practice your pitch and how the information might best reach them.
You can create a script of possible questions and answers that might come up in the conversation. Put yourself in every possible scenario; keep in mind the objections and problems your ally might have regarding your proposal. Having most scenarios covered, with a possible answer or alternative solution, will make your proposal look strong and solid.
Proposing a meeting to show your ideas with order and calm is an excellent way to guarantee the attention of your potential ally. Agree on a time with the person or people who can say “yes” to your proposal, be punctual for that appointment, and prepare the meeting well.
Work on the order in which you’ll present the information: a careful and orderly speech will let your interlocutor know that you are clear about what you want to do and will give them confidence in working with you.
Don’t forget to make it very clear:

what you are inviting your ally to
what you will do and what you need from your ally
when you need it
for how long
who will be involved
how communication will work between you
how you will tell them what you achieved thanks to the relationship that unites you




Step 6 → Find out how you can present your proposal

Some allies might be available to you anytime, anywhere. Others have a more formal way of working or need to make decisions by consensus. Others might even need you to send a written proposal before you can talk to anyone.
Approach the person, organization, business, or any other ally and find out the best way to present your proposal. Follow the instructions and organize your time so you can respond punctually to their requirements.


Step 7 → Present your proposal and listen to your counterpart; the goal is to reach an agreement**

It’s time to show everything you’ve worked on! Trust yourself and the rigor with which you’ve prepared your proposal. We are sure that at this moment, with all the information you have, you’ll find the words to tell a good story that hooks your ally into doing things together.
Once you’ve made your point, listen carefully to your potential ally. There may be information you haven’t considered, so take note of the points that are weak or need to be expanded.
It’s also possible there will be a moment of negotiation: you and your ally should have a scenario where both can win. Open your eyes and ears to anything that might have value for their purpose and strive to build a solid relationship.


Step 8 → Formalize the commitments and get to work!

The moment your potential ally has everything clear, and you do too, it’s time to agree and clarify the next steps!
Put in writing what each person is committing to and what the next steps are; it’s always better so nothing is forgotten.
Thank the people who attended to you; starting to work together is just the beginning, and celebrating that you’ve reached an agreement is a way to honor this new relationship.

How do you know if this solution works?
You’ll know you’ve succeeded in contacting places that bring people together the moment you start speaking the same language and find common ground in the conversation.
For example, when someone who can bring others together pays attention to your proposal and wants you to meet their manager, or a colleague who can help you gather people. Or, when you find yourself adapting what you’re going to say to the interests of the person listening to you, creating a space where the ideas start to belong to both of you.
If you exercise your listening skills, you’ll soon be recognizing people with the power to bring others together and looking to get them interested.
If your purpose is to do a SOLE, you can start thinking of your Self-Organized Learning Environment as a place where various allies can start fulfilling their purposes thanks to your space, or, conversely, you can think of your ally’s space as a SOLE and benefit the people your ally brings together so they learn to use the internet as a group to live better together.
You can SOLE any activity or space!

Other possible Internets
These recommendations are simple and concise. When you go looking for allies, a lot will depend on your communication skills.
Remember that you won’t always manage to convince everyone to work with you; the important thing is to do it many times: “practice makes perfect.” And, at the same time, listen to your intuition to start creating a “radar” in yourself that alerts you to people who can be your allies… stay sharp!

en/solve/solv-bandwidth.title: How to make the most of my bandwidth?
en/solve/solv-bandwidth.summary: Practices that will allow you to optimize your connection.
en/solve/solv-bandwidth.content:
Make the most of your Internet service options
Hi, I’m Manu. I’m no tech expert, but I know how frustrating it is when a movie freezes or a video call drops. So, after doing a bit of digging, I found some tricks to improve your home connection that I want to share with you.

What does it mean to make the most of your bandwidth?
Making the most of your internet connection options is all about using all the settings and tools available to optimize your online experience in terms of performance, speed, security, and data efficiency.

What is it for?
Did you know that in the world of the Internet, there are two terms that often get mixed up? I’m talking about bandwidth and speed. Let’s break them down, and I’ll give you some tips so you can get the most out of the bandwidth and speed you’re paying for at home.
Bandwidth and speed: what’s the deal?
Imagine that bandwidth → is like a giant delivery truck; it can carry a whole bunch of packages (data) at once. The bigger the truck, the more packages it can haul. But here’s the kicker: speed is the time it takes for that truck to reach its destination. So, even if you have a massive truck (high bandwidth), if it doesn’t drive fast, the packages are just going to be sitting there waiting!
In short: High bandwidth lets you move a lot of data at the same time, but if the speed is low, that data will take a while to arrive. And that’s exactly what drives us crazy when we’re trying to watch a video or hop on a video call!

What do you need?

An Internet WiFi → service at home.
Patience and curiosity.


How to do it?

Step 1 → Use a network cable

If you can, connect your computer to the Router → using an Ethernet cable →. This is like switching from a delivery truck to a high-speed train. The difference is amazing! A wired connection will give you the best speed and stability.

Photo taken from Pexels, (2024).


Step 2 → Connect to 5GHz if you use Wi-Fi


Screenshot taken by Manuela Córdoba, (2024).
If you can’t use a cable, the next best option is to connect to your router’s 5GHz band. This is like having access to a fast lane on the highway: less traffic, more speed. Just keep in mind that it works best when you’re close to the router.


Step 3 → Don’t forget about 2.4GHz

If you’re a bit far from the router and notice the connection getting sluggish, switch to the 2.4GHz band. Even though it’s a bit slower than 5GHz, it can be more reliable. Think of it like a country road that’s always open, even if it isn’t as fast.

Photo taken from Google Photos, (2024).


Step 4 → Adjust your Wi-Fi Channel

Sometimes, the connection feels slow because there are too many people in your neighborhood using the same Wi-Fi channel. Changing the channel can make your connection faster and smoother. It’s like moving your party to a spot where there’s less noise.
Go to Improve your Router’s signal to follow the step-by-step guide


Step 5 → Keep your Router in shape

Finally, make sure your router is well-placed and up to date. Put it in a well-ventilated area away from other devices that might cause interference. A well-cared-for router is key to a good connection.

Photo taken by Manuela Córdoba, (2024).

How do you know if this solution is working?
If you’ve checked your speed, your network settings, and the data usage on your devices, and they match up with what you’re paying for in your contract, you can be sure you’re getting the most out of your Internet service.
By following these steps, you won’t just understand bandwidth and speed better—you’ll also be able to optimize your connection and enjoy your online activities without any hiccups.

Other possible Internets
To make sure you’re getting the most out of your service, besides checking your speed and bandwidth, you can run tests at different times of the day; sometimes speeds can vary depending on how busy the general network is.
You can also monitor your data usage, keep an eye on the data consumed by the apps and programs you use, and set some limits to keep your consumption in check.

en/solve/solv-bicigenerator.title: How to generate electricity using a bicycle?
en/solve/solv-bicigenerator.summary: Generate electricity by building a bike generator.
en/solve/solv-bicigenerator.content:
Hi, I’m Nicolás. I’m what you’d call a “tinkerer.” I’m an engineer, and I’m interested in how things work. I enjoy taking gadgets apart and putting them back together to see what makes them tick, and I also love figuring out how we can use available resources as a community.
What is a pedal generator?
A pedal generator is a system that converts the mechanical energy of a bicycle into electrical energy. Basically, it transforms the pedaling motion into electricity, allowing you to generate power for various purposes, such as charging electronic devices or even powering lighting systems. (Source: Ecologismos)

What is it for?
This solution is a step-by-step guide on how to buy and assemble a bicycle-powered electricity system. We’ve calculated it to keep a computer and a router running for 3 hours, which is the typical duration of a SOLE session.

What do you need?

Money to buy batteries, cables, a power inverter, and a controller.
Energy to pedal.
An old bicycle.
Care and plenty of enthusiasm to assemble the system.
A stand to keep the bicycle stationary.


How to do it?

Step 1 → Calculate energy consumption

Determine the energy consumption you need. In this case, we need to power a laptop and a router for 3 hours. This will define the capacity our system needs and how many hours we must pedal to generate the necessary electricity.

A laptop consumes 120W/h
A router consumes 15W/h

Now, we must calculate the energy expenditure required for the system. You can check this information on the back of your devices or on their chargers. For a SOLE session, for example, 3 hours are needed:

Laptop: 120W/h consumption for 3 hours is 360W
Router: 15W/h consumption for 3 hours is 45W

The sum of these two is 405W over 3 hours. If we divide 405/3h, we get 135 W/h.
The pedal machine can generate up to 200 watts/hour at a medium pedaling speed and up to 400 watts/hour at a high speed.



Step 2 → Estimate the specifications of the complementary equipment.

Remember that to assemble any power generation system, you need these components:
An electricity generator
This is any device capable of capturing and transforming some type of energy (mechanical, solar, thermal, hydraulic, chemical) into electrical energy. In this case, it’s the bicycle combined with an electric motor and a static stand, but we could also think of a gasoline generator, a solar panel, a Pelton turbine, a wind turbine, etc.



A charge controller
Its function is to regulate the flow of energy from the motor to the batteries, controlling both current and voltage. This ensures that the recharge happens under optimal conditions, doesn’t damage the batteries, and extends their lifespan.

A battery
It stores the generated energy in the form of chemical energy and releases it later as direct current in a controlled manner.

A power inverter
It converts the direct current coming out of the battery into alternating current so we can plug in our equipment.

Solar cable and accessories
This is an electrical cable robust enough to transmit the electrical energy we generate. Additionally, we can buy plastic connectors that help make the connections more secure so they don’t disconnect easily.

As you can see, you can use the same complementary system as you would for a solar panel setup. For this reason, we will calculate the equipment as if it were for a solar panel system, since they will have the same capacity.


Step 3 → How to estimate battery specifications?

We talked about an energy consumption of 405W over 3 hours, or 135 W/h. In addition to the total daily consumption, we need:

Days of autonomy (days): This refers to the days of use. If used every day, the autonomy is 5 or more days; if only used on weekends, we have 1 or 2 days. For our SOLE case, we will set it to a day and a half, 1.5.
Depth of discharge (DoD): For gel or AGM batteries, this value is 70%. For flooded lead-acid batteries, it is 50%.
Battery voltage (V): We choose this; since our devices are 12V, we will use that value.
Temperature and efficiency losses: We will assume 15%.

To calculate the battery capacity in Ampere-hours (Ah), we use the following formula: Ah = 1.15 * (Wh/day * days) / (DoD * V) = 1.15 * (135 * 1.5) / (70% * 12) = 27.72Ah. This is the minimum necessary capacity, so we decide to buy a 12V, 35Ah battery.



Step 4 → How to estimate controller specifications?

For this, we have to calculate the input and output current of the controller using these two equations:

To calculate the input current, we just have to multiply 3 values:

1.25: A safety factor of 1.25. This is done to calculate with 25% more than necessary to avoid errors from a calculation that is too tight. It is common engineering practice to over-dimension calculations for safety parameters in case of failure.
Imod,sc: Unit current of the photovoltaic panel under short-circuit conditions, which can be found on the back of the panel. For this case, it is 2.32 A.


Np: number of panels in series. For this case, there are 2.
Calculating, we get: Iinput = 1.25 * 2.32 A * 2 = 5.8 A. To calculate the output current, we have to add, multiply, and divide the following values:

1.25: A safety factor of 1.25.
Pdc: Direct current discharge power, which is the sum of the current of the devices we are going to connect that run on direct current. In this case, we have none, so it is 0.
Pac: Alternating current load power, which is the sum of the current of the devices we are going to connect that run on alternating current. In this case, a laptop consumes 120W/h and a router consumes 15W/h, for a total of 135 W/h.
Ninv: Inverter efficiency, around 90-95%.
Vbat: Battery voltage. We can read this on the selected battery. For this case, it is 12V.

Calculating, we get: Ioutput = 1.25 * (0 + (120 + 15) / 0.95) / 12 = 14.80 A. Finally, we just have to round our calculations. Iinput = 5.8 ≃ 6A. Ioutput = 14.80 ≃ 15A. So, our controller should support at least an input intensity of 6A and an output intensity of 15A. That’s why we bought a 20A one with a 12/24V voltage (it switches automatically).


Step 5 → How to estimate inverter specifications?

Since we are going to use low-consumption equipment, the inverter to use is a modified sine wave one. The calculation is done by over-dimensioning 25% above our total consumption. Remember that the total consumption is 405W. Thus, I = W * 1.25 = 405 * 1.25 = 506.25 W. This should be the minimum capacity of the inverter. In our case, we bought a 750W one.


Step 6 → How to know which cable to buy?

Usually, solar cables are sized using the AWG (American Wire Gauge) term to estimate the scale of the gauge. But for solar cables, the gauge is normally specified by its cross-section or area in mm². In Colombia, we can find gauges from 2.5mm² to 16mm² depending on the manufacturer.

It should be chosen in relation to the current to be transported. In this case, we will not transport more than 20A, so a 14 AWG cable, which is 2.5 mm², is fine. Regarding connectors, for our case, we bought two, but it will depend on the configuration each person builds.


Step 7 → Find a supplier

Look for an electrical supply provider and get a quote for this equipment. You can also ask them for advice to see if the calculations you made are correct or if there is any other way to optimize your power generation system. Compare costs between different suppliers and buy while keeping in mind the reliability of the place, the warranty, and the prices.

How to use it?
Precautions
Now that we have the motor, the bicycle, the battery, and the inverter, we must remember that the battery is the last thing to be connected.
A safety warning: We should only connect one pole at a time so we don’t get shocked. It’s good to work with rubber gloves, as they insulate us against possible electrocution. We recommend reading the section Basic precautions when working with electricity.
Connecting the circuit
The motor has a negative and a positive pole; it is important to identify which is which to build the new circuit. Generally, the positive is represented by red and the negative by black. In the case of connecting a motor, you must identify which way it spins when connected one way or the other; the motor must be connected so that it spins in the same direction the bicycle will spin, that is, “forward.” Remember that for this solution, what we are doing is running a motor in reverse; that is, by spinning the motor, an electromagnetic field will be created that will interact with the permanent magnets of the electric motor, generating an electric current.

Now, connect the negative and positive wires coming out of the motor to the controller; it is clearly marked on the controller where each wire connects. Then, cut two wires and strip their ends to make the connection to the battery.

Now connect these wires coming out of the controller to the battery, respecting the positive and negative connections.

When you have connected them, join the inverter wires to the battery, and that’s how you’ll have your system ready. Once the entire system is assembled, you will be able to plug the computer or the router into the inverter.

How to know if this solution works?
With this solution, you will manage to have electricity to power your SOLE; remember that this solution is calculated using the example of the electrical consumption of a router and a computer. If you want to have permanent electricity for more equipment, you must do your own calculations.

Other possible Internets
This solution only allows for energy independence for a router and a laptop for 3 hours at night, provided the panel has captured sunlight throughout the day. If you are using it during the day, this time can be extended, as the panel will be charging constantly while you use the electrical devices and discharge it.

en/solve/solv-build-3Gantenna.title: Build a homemade 3G antenna
en/solve/solv-build-3Gantenna.summary: Capture signal with a homemade antenna.
en/solve/solv-build-3Gantenna.content:
Hi, I’m Nicolás, and for a while now, I’ve been learning how to improve my connectivity. I’m no expert, but through internet searches, tutorials, and, above all, trial and error, I’ve learned a ton.
I’ve already tested and installed several solutions, and today, I’m sharing one of them with you: the DIY 3G antenna. Let’s get started!

What is building a DIY 3G antenna?
Building a 3G antenna means that by gathering and assembling easily accessible materials, you can boost the 3G and 4G signal strength of a cell phone or a MiFi-type modem →.

What is it for?
This DIY antenna will increase the capacity to receive the waves that carry the 4G signal → (mobile internet), thereby improving the connection quality on your cell phone or shared modem (MiFi →).

What do you need?


Aluminum rod, 3 mm thick (it must be exactly 3 mm).
50 cm of plastic wire channel (ideally 2 cm wide).
Quick-drying epoxy glue (usually comes in two tubes).
10 m of coaxial cable (or whatever length you need for the antenna to reach the connection point).
2 clamps or vises.
2 locking pliers.
20 cm of copper wire (recommended: 1 mm thick).
A ruler (even better if you have a “caliper,” as it allows for more precision).
Hacksaw (if you can get an electric grinder with a thin cutting disc, you’ll save a looot of time).
Fine-tip permanent marker (e.g., Sharpie).
Pencil.
Soldering iron, solder, soldering flux.
Pliers and wire cutters (the latter is optional).
Metal file.
Workbench with good lighting.
Plastic zip ties (also known as “zuchos”).
Pole to mount the antenna (a guadua bamboo pole as long as possible, or a rigid rod of any material).
Utility knife, cutter.
Wire stripper (optional).
Cell phone or shared modem (MiFi).
Also… good vibes.
Patience.
Lots of precision.


How to do it?

Step 0 → Before starting, some safety recommendations

This solution has an intermediate difficulty level and involves using tools that can cause accidents if you aren’t careful. That’s why it’s important to keep the following recommendations in mind:

When using any sharp object, position it so that the cutting force is directed away from your body, not toward it.
Keep pets and children away from the workspace, mainly because of the risk of contact with a hot soldering iron.
Before cutting, make sure the clamps or pliers holding the material don’t allow for the slightest movement when you apply force.
When using solder and epoxy glue, protect your work surface to avoid damaging it.
Do not hoist the antenna during a storm, as it could act as a lightning rod and attract a strike to your area.



Step 1 → Check the materials

Before starting, check and have all the necessary items on hand. If you aren’t familiar with any of the materials, you can find them in the photo where the materials are numbered.
You can buy these at your nearest hardware store since they are common items; it shouldn’t be too hard to find them. Perhaps the most difficult (and important) item on the list is the aluminum rod. Sometimes you can find elements made with this type of rod in the metal supports sold in stores that carry many imported products. At SOLE Voltaje, we have used different metals: copper, welding rods, and galvanized wire. We opted to buy a 3mm steel welding rod. If you can’t find aluminum at the hardware store, you can ask for other options; the important thing is that the diameter is as close as possible to 3mm or 1/8 of an inch.
Now, organize your workspace, keep these instructions handy, and divide the tasks among the participants: someone can be in charge of measuring, others of cutting, organizing, and gluing.


Step 2 → Understand the diagram

Below, we show you the final diagram and some of the assembly parts so you have a clearer idea of the final setup.


Step 3 → Measure, cut, and mark**

It’s time to start! Here we get to work; you must cut each of the 10 elements that make up the antenna. With the help of the caliper (or ruler), mark the length of each one and cut them with the hacksaw or grinder. It’s recommended to cut one or half a millimeter extra and finish adjusting the length by filing the edges with the metal file. Listed below are the lengths of the 10 metal rods you need to cut; in the world of antennas, these have specific names (director, reflector, and dipole) related to the function they perform.

This is the list of necessary cuts:

Reflector: 8.0 cm
Dipole: 18 cm (This should be the length of the element; the bent rod should be exactly 7.6 cm, for now, just cut the rod to this length).
Director #1: 7.6 cm
Director #2: 7.5 cm
Director #3: 7.4 cm
Director #4: 7.4 cm
Director #5: 7.3 cm
Director #6: 7.3 cm
Director #7: 7.2 cm
Director #8: 7.2 cm

📏 Remember that 10 mm = 1 cm

It’s important to mark each of the cuts with tape, as seen in the photo, to make the next step easier.



Step 4 → Bend the dipole

The dipole is an element bent into a “C” shape. Its total length should be 7.6 cm, but the rod needs to be a bit longer (approximately 18.0 cm). Making this piece is a trial-and-error task. In my case, it has worked well to slowly bend the rod against a circular tube 2 cm in diameter to give it the curve.



Step 5 → Assembling the antenna

We’re halfway through the process—don’t get discouraged, there’s very little left! Now it’s time to mount the elements onto the wire channel. This can be replaced by wood or any other material you have on hand, as long as it doesn’t conduct electricity.

On the surface of the channel, you need to mark the following distances, where each of the rod cuts made in the previous step will be placed later.

Reflector: 1.0 cm
Dipole: 5.0 cm
Director #1: 6.2 cm
Director #2: 9.2 cm
Director #3: 12.8 cm
Director #4: 17.0 cm
Director #5: 21.7 cm
Director #6: 26.7 cm
Director #7: 31.9 cm
Director #8: 37.4 cm

Once the lines are marked, you can glue each of the rods with epoxy glue onto the channel; however, we’ve seen that this configuration is very fragile and doesn’t make our antenna last very long. For this reason, we found a better way to attach the rods to the channel. We can use the hot soldering iron, which can easily pierce the plastic with its fine tip; so, with this tool, we will drill the sides until they have a sufficient diameter for the rod to pass through. Take advantage of the plastic while it’s still hot right after you drill it to pass the rod through and ensure it has the right diameter. This should be done on both sides of the channel so the rod can go all the way through.

Once you finish the 20 holes, you should disassemble the channel and use the metal file to remove the plastic burrs to allow the rods to enter easily.

Now, before positioning each of the rods, we must make a small cut to facilitate the entry of the dipole. To do this, we must disassemble the channel and use the hacksaw to make a vertical cut that crosses the sides of the second measurement (5.0 cm) until it reaches the hole we opened with the soldering iron.

Once the dipole is embedded, we can insert the other rods according to the order mentioned above.

You can add a bit of epoxy glue on the rod to ensure the elements remain well-adhered to the channel. Wait for the necessary time for the glue to dry before continuing with connecting the cable to your new antenna.



Step 6 → Prepare the cable

While the glue is drying, you can move on to preparing the coaxial cable. You can check the previous post to understand how a coaxial cable is made before taking it apart.

To do this part, you can use a wire stripper or a cutter to separate each layer of the cable; you must be careful when cutting so as not to break the first layer, which is a metal mesh. Thus, at one end, you need to leave the copper wire and the cable mesh free. You can carefully separate the mesh and then braid it back together.

At the other end, with the copper wire, make a wave shape, which will be the element that comes into contact with the phone or MiFi to improve the signal.



Step 7 → Solder the dipole

This is one of the most delicate steps; after this, we move on to assembly. Remember that the dipole is one of the fundamental components of the antenna; it must be soldered to the end of the coaxial cable that we separated into the mesh and the copper wire, and this, in turn, connects with a copper wire acting as a bridge between each end of the dipole. First, we make the bridge with the copper wire as seen in the image, where each end is braided and then soldered.

Once we have the copper wire soldered to the two ends of the coaxial, we can attach it to the dipole; for this, we can first tighten it a bit with pliers and then proceed to solder.

Remember that the dipole must be perpendicular to the channel, so to avoid sudden movements of the cable that would change this position, we must secure the cable with some plastic zip ties.



Step 8 → Final assembly

We’re finally done; you can now mount and install the antenna! To do this, make sure it is well-secured with plastic zip ties at the highest part of the pole; the antenna should be oriented so that the dipole is as close as possible to the pole.

Remember to also tie the cable to the pole so it doesn’t pull away from the solder points on the antenna. Now, hoist the pole and make sure the antenna is pointing in the direction of the nearest cell tower.
Now, at the other end of the cable, place your cell phone so that the copper coil is touching the back of the device.


The process of aiming the antenna must be done slowly and carefully; waves are very sensitive to movement. First, you can establish a “0” position, and from there, you can turn it to the right or left in small intervals. After each movement, you can check the connection quality with the cellular network from the phone’s “Settings” screen. This is a number expressed in decibels (dB); the higher it is, the lower the signal quality. You can also do it by looking at the signal icon intensity that appears at the top of the cell phone. The challenge is to find the spot where the decibel number is lowest or where the signal intensity icon is highest.

Now, you can proceed to secure the pole in this position and that’s it! Happy surfing!

Recommendations for potential trouble spots
If you are using solder and it keeps slipping, it might be that the tin solder you bought isn’t compatible with the metal of the rods you are using, so we recommend looking for different solder or trying to make contact between the cable and the rod by tightening them well with a wire. Normally, each metal is compatible with solder of the same metal (steel with steel solder, tin with tin solder).
__
How do I know if this solution works?
We can know if this solution works by doing speed tests →. You can compare by taking measurements with and without the antenna to recognize how much the signal improves with this device.
Through trial and error, you’ll feel more and more confident to tinker (or “cacharrear”), which means solving things by doing. Now, would you be up for trying another solution? Keep on surfing! See more solutions →

Other possible Internets
This solution can work to temporarily improve your connectivity conditions. The antenna will serve as an amplifier for the transmission and reception of waves for your devices.
Knowing this, how far would you like to go? Is this a solution you could build where you live? We hope it has been useful to you! And if it was, share it with others who you know could benefit from it.
See you soon! 👋🏽

en/solve/solv-buy-cellphone.title: How to buy a cell phone that is right for me?
en/solve/solv-buy-cellphone.summary: A cell phone that fits your capabilities and needs.
en/solve/solv-buy-cellphone.content:
Hi, I’m Nicolás, and just like you, I’ve been learning step-by-step how to improve my connectivity to do SOLE. I’m no expert, but through searches on Internet →, tutorials, and, above all, trial and error, I’ve learned a ton and set up some functional solutions.
What does it mean to buy the right cell phone for you?
In this specific solution, we’ll learn how to buy a Smartphone → based on your possibilities and needs. Below, you’ll find a series of information, criteria, and tips that aim to be as clear as possible so you can feel supported in making the decision of which phone to buy. The estimated reading time is 12 minutes and it consists of 10 items, but don’t be scared—you can read these items with the help of others. Remember that at SOLE Voltaje, we want to promote the collective use of the internet.

What is it for?
In this solution, you’ll find a few practical tips to help you make a much more informed decision about which cell phones are best for you.

Before we start, some ethical questions!
At SOLE Voltaje, we talk about supporting people in clarifying the ethical implications of a decision by problematizing the circumstances that lead you to make that decision. This solution starts from the assumption that you want to buy a cell phone—but do you really need it? This isn’t always the best option for you. Sometimes you have an old phone that a family member can give you, or for various reasons, you might prefer not to have a phone and it’s a better option for you to have a computer. If, after scanning your options, you definitely decide you need to buy a phone, this is the right place for you! Here, we advise you on what you should keep in mind when buying a cell phone.

What do you need?

Save money for the purchase.
Internet access.
A trusted store or dealer.
Curiosity.


How to do it?

Step 0 → How do I know if I need to buy a cell phone?

One of the characteristics of our current era is the great development of international and national markets; our phones are made in China and we can buy them in Colombia, we can go to the market and buy rice brought from Brazil. Furthermore, we find disproportionate consumption options: we can buy white rice, yellow rice, bulk rice, lemon-flavored rice, etc. There is an endless array of options to turn us into consumers of products we often don’t need, and we end up buying non-nutritious food, falling into yet another expense that doesn’t satisfy the main function of food: to nourish us! In the same way, we fill our homes with endless merchandise that ends up piled up or thrown away because, in the end, it was useless to us. That’s why we want to promote responsible consumption. For the case of a cell phone, we suggest you ask yourself the following questions to know if it’s a responsible purchase:

Do you need to buy a cell phone, or do you have other options to access the internet and make calls?
Can you buy another option that covers your internet connection and calls, and can be paid for by several people?
If you buy a cell phone, will your quality of life really improve, or will it get worse? For example, will you become addicted to watching content or being on social media, or will you be more stressed every month thinking about how to pay for this new expense?
Finally, is this new purchase really a priority for you?




Step 1 → What do I need a cell phone for?

Just like a car, the phone we choose must adapt to our main needs. It doesn’t make much sense to buy a 4x4 truck if you’re going to be driving through a city with paved avenues.
Now, think about what the most important activities will be and where you will spend the most time on your phone: Do you want to take lots of photos of your region? Then you should pay attention to the camera features; Are you going to be out in the middle of the countryside all day, or are you going to use your phone as a modem to share your internet with other people participating in a SOLE? A good battery would be fundamental; Do you want to use the internet to learn in a group? A large screen with good definition is important; Do you want to play a high-definition video game? You’ll need a good processor →; Do you need to work with several applications at once? Look at the RAM memory →; Do you need to have many applications and large files? Look at the internal storage.
Now that you’ve decided to buy a phone, I’ll give you an introduction using my own case as an example:

💡 At the beginning of 2024, I dropped my phone getting out of a taxi. Because of my work and contact with family and friends, it’s important for me to have a phone. A while ago, I decided I wouldn’t invest more than $1,000,000 COP in this tool. About 5 years ago, I discovered a new brand that was emerging; it had good prices and very good references from friends and users on the internet. This brand is Xiaomi. My last two phones had been from this brand, each costing around $700,000 COP.
However, I searched online for references and saw that there’s a new brand arriving that is affordable: Tecno. I looked at several references and saw that it’s currently the best-selling brand on Mercado Libre, so I looked for a phone with similar characteristics to the previous ones: 256 GB of internal memory, a decent processor, a battery of over 4000 mAh, a large screen, and at least 8 GB of RAM. These characteristics are compatible with my work and personal use; I don’t take professional photos, nor was I looking for it to play video games. Finally, I found a phone from this brand for $475,000 COP. This phone I bought was a Tecno Spark 20 Dual Sim with 256 GB. So far, I can say it has been an excellent purchase!


Now it’s your turn to identify what you need the phone for!


Step 2 → Set a budget

First of all, define what your budget will be. For this, you can calculate how many days of work you are willing to invest in this device. Don’t go into debt for a phone; many times they offer financing for 1 or 2 years, and the phone breaks or gets stolen before we finish paying for it.

Once you are clear on the above, you will know which features you should pay more attention to.


Camera
If you love taking photos, here are some aspects that are central when examining your device’s camera:


Resolution
This is what we commonly know as megapixels. Although it is very important, it is not everything we should look at when evaluating a camera. The more megapixels it has, the more detail you will see in the images. However, you should have a limit. The standard could be a 12 MP camera, because if it has good features and excellent image processing, you will get high-quality photos. If you start having higher resolution photos, the files will be very heavy and will fill up your phone’s internal storage quickly.




Sensor and lenses
A good cell phone camera must have a quality sensor, as well as several lenses. The latter, in fact, has already become a standard. When combined, they allow for better images. One of the most popular lenses is the wide-angle lens. Thanks to this, much more information is incorporated into the photographs and it provides a visual angle of up to 120 degrees, perfect for group photos or indoors where there isn’t much space.



Aperture
The lens aperture will be fundamental for a good photo; this feature defines how much light the camera can capture. It is identified by the letter f followed by a number, for example, f1.9 or f2.0. The lower this number, the greater the amount of light the camera will capture. For this reason, it is important that it be low, because with more light intake, the images will have more detail.



Screen
A screen will define whether our eyes get tired faster or slower, whether we will see a certain degree of detail or not, or how fast the battery will drain.

When you are clear that your phone should be a device used in a group, as happens when we do SOLE, this feature becomes important, since it is not so easy for several people to read on a small screen.

Screen size
The size of cell phone screens has increased over time, although for a few years now they have remained without growing much, since they lose their portability function in the pocket. We could say that most phones are between 3.5” and 6” (this measures the diagonal, that is, from one upper corner to the opposite lower corner). Really, this depends on your taste: do you want a large screen that allows you to watch a video from afar among several people, or do you prefer a small one so your phone doesn’t attract so much attention?




Screen technology
Full HD technology is more recent than HD, and the number of pixels is higher compared to HD, which works with 1,280 x 720 pixels. The Full HD system gives a much more realistic look to the image. This latest technology is only arriving in the latest phones with large panels, as high resolution doesn’t make much sense on small screens.


Screen type
There are different types of screens, but in the current market, two are the most popular: those with LCD technology, also known as inorganic, and those with OLED technologies, known as organic.


LCD: These are backlit liquid crystal screens that usually cover the entire panel. In the past, they were the most popular, but they are being produced in smaller quantities. Being backlit, they will consume more energy, but for this very reason, they look good under direct sunlight.


OLED: These screens differ from LCDs because their materials allow them to generate light by themselves when electricity is applied. This allows them to turn each pixel off or on independently, so they consume less energy. Furthermore, they end up being brighter and having better definition of the color black.



Internal storage
Internal storage defines the amount of files we can save on our phone; it’s like the hard drive → in a computer. This will determine how many programs you can have installed at once, and whether or not you can save all kinds of files. At the moment, we recommend buying a phone with at least 64 GB of internal memory. Also, check if it has the option to accept microSD cards to expand the capacity in the future.




RAM memory
This is the phone’s temporary memory; it helps with performance and gives a clue as to how fast applications open and how smoothly the phone runs. We recommend a minimum of 4GB of RAM.



Processor
The processor is the brain; it is the one that is always awake and receives instructions. The more cores the processor has, the better performance it will have, although it will also depend on the brand. Here, the best option is to look at the name of the processor used by the phone that catches your attention and do a little research on your own. Hopefully, it hasn’t been out for more than 4 years.




Battery



Compare it with another phone
Once you have some interesting options, it is important that you compare them. For this, you don’t have to do it manually; there are several pages that already do this automatically. Below, we leave you some:


Versus
Movilcelular
Here we compare my phone against a Motorola:

Besides the fact that the Tecno Spark 20 is better rated in its features, we can see that in the Colombian market they have the following prices:

Motorola Edge 30 Neo Dual SIM 128 GB very peri 8 GB RAM - $ 849,900 COP
Tecno Spark 20 Dual SIM 256 GB Black 8 GB RAM - $ 499,000 COP

💡 We can have a better phone saving $ 350,000 COP by taking the risk of trying an emerging brand.

Don’t be fooled
It is important that you constantly check emerging brands; usually, brands appear with little advertising, very good features, and a low price. However, many times out of habit and experience, we keep buying the same brand as our previous phone. For example, my best friend has been with the Motorola brand since college. I think that although it is a good brand, it has very high costs, and I prefer new, cheaper brands that have good references to save some money.
Another important element has to do with the warranty. When you live in a central city, it’s easy that if something happens to the phone, there is a branch of all available brands in case you have to use the warranty. But in less central cities, for example in Bucaramanga, the brand of my current phone, “Tecno,” doesn’t have an office, so if you live there, you would have to send the phone to Bogotá, pay more money, and wait longer for them to return it. But possibly in that city, there is a service center for more popular brands, as is the case with Motorola.

How much is enough?
This question is difficult to answer, but I think we can rephrase it as follows: Does the option you chose meet the need and intention you projected at the beginning? In the previous example, I showed you how I consider that the phone I currently have was a very good option for my lifestyle. This type of reasoning is what we want you to do when making a decision about the option you are going to buy.
