en/solve/solv-microwave.title: "How to connect two locations with a radio link?"
en/solve/solv-microwave.summary: "Install a wireless internet bridge between two distant points using directional antennas."
en/solve/solv-microwave.content:
Hi, I’m David, and this is one of those solutions I finally understood after a lot of exploring, asking around, tinkering, and obsessing over something that seemed impossible at first.
I didn’t arrive at this from a classroom. I got here by asking myself: is there a way to connect two distant places using the air as a path, without having to lay a cable? I still haven’t done it myself — this guide is part of the process of getting ready to try. When I started researching, there was no reliable cellular signal available, and the first answer I got was that it was impossible.
But I explored, asked questions, did my research, and discovered that what seemed impossible actually has a name and is done with two antennas, a bit of patience, and a desire to understand how information travels through the air.
They call it a radio link. And this guide is what I wish I had found from the very beginning.

What is a radio link?
A radio link → is a system that connects two places using radio waves as if they were an invisible bridge in the air.
Imagine you have a very powerful flashlight and you point it directly at another person who has a mirror. The light travels from one to the other without touching anything in between. That’s what a radio link does: instead of light, it uses an internet signal; instead of flashlights, it uses special antennas.
What makes this type of connection special is that the antennas don’t transmit in every direction (like your home WiFi, which is omnidirectional), but rather they focus all their energy toward a single point, like a megaphone that directs your voice exactly where you want it to go. This allows them to reach very far, from a few hundred meters to dozens of kilometers.
Technically, “radio link” is the general name. When high frequencies are used (above 1 GHz), they are also called microwave links. These are the same systems that telecommunications companies use to connect cell towers, but in smaller, more accessible versions for communities.

What is it for?
This solution is for bringing internet from a place that has a connection to one that doesn’t, when the distance between the two makes laying a cable impossible or too expensive.
Think of it this way: if there is fiber optic internet in the town center, and 8 kilometers away there is a rural village that has never had a connection, a radio link can be the bridge that joins those two spaces.
Some of the possibilities it opens up:

A single internet connection shared among several families or an entire community, reducing the cost for everyone.
Connecting a rural school to the internet without paying for cable infrastructure.
Bringing a signal from a high point (an antenna, a tower, a hill) down to homes in the valley.
Connecting a community organization’s headquarters with a neighboring antenna that already has a signal.

In Colombia, communities like those in Buenos Aires (Cauca) have built community networks using exactly this principle: one point with internet access that distributes the signal via radio links until it reaches the houses.
Buenos Aires - Cauca reference

Before you start…

Warning: this project requires working at heights and handling electrical equipment. If you are going to install antennas on roofs, poles, or towers, make sure to have someone watching from below, wear non-slip footwear, use harnesses and safety equipment (if you have them or can borrow them), and never work alone at heights.


Warning: this solution has an initial cost. The most basic equipment costs between USD 25 and USD 100 depending on the distance you need to cover (approximately 100,000 to 500,000 Colombian pesos). Although the equipment is durable (4–8 years if well cared for), the initial outlay requires planning.


Something to think about: before buying any equipment, do a line-of-sight study (we’ll explain how later). If there is no direct line of sight between the two points, the radio link won’t work and the money will be wasted. That step is free and it’s worth doing first.


What do you need?
Electronic Equipment
The equipment comes in two identical units: one for each end of the link.



































EquipmentFor what distanceApprox. PriceFrequencyTP-Link CPE210 (x2)Up to 5 kmUSD 25–35 each2.4 GHzTP-Link CPE510 (x2)Up to 15 kmUSD 35–50 each5 GHzTP-Link CPE610 (x2)Up to 23 kmUSD 55–80 each5 GHzUbiquiti NanoStation 5AC (x2)Up to 15 kmUSD 80–100 each5 GHz

Tip: for most community projects in Colombia, the CPE510 is the best starting point. It reaches up to 15 km, works in the 5 GHz band (which has less interference than 2.4 GHz), and its price is accessible. If the distance is less than 5 km or there is a lot of vegetation in the way, the CPE210 on 2.4 GHz might work better.

Each CPE includes in its box:

The antenna (the device itself)
A passive PoE adapter (the “little box” that powers the antenna with electricity through the network cable)
A short network cable

Installation Materials

UTP Cat5e or Cat6 network cable — needed from the antenna to the router at each end. The recommended maximum distance is 60 meters per run. Cat6 supports speeds of up to 1 Gbps, which is convenient if you ever have a high-speed connection.
2 poles or masts — one for each end. They can be 2-inch PVC pipes, galvanized iron pipes, or even straight, sturdy wooden posts. The height depends on what is between the two points (trees, buildings, hills).
Metal clamps to fix the antenna to the pole. These are usually included with the equipment.
Cable ties or plastic zip ties to secure the network cable to the pole.
Heat-shrink tubing or self-fusing tape to waterproof the cable connectors outdoors.
Drill bit and wall plugs if you need to pass the cable through walls.

Tools

Wrench or Allen key to tighten clamps
RJ-45 crimping tool and connectors (if you are going to make the cable ends yourself)
Multimeter (to check the cable)
Bubble level (to install the pole straight)
A computer or cell phone to access the configuration interface
Compass or a compass app on your phone

Prior Knowledge

Knowing how to use a computer and a web browser
Comfort with simple work at heights (installing on roofs or low poles)
Patience for alignment: it is the most delicate step
Someone who has a cell phone at both ends to communicate during installation (or two-way radios)


How to do it?


Step 1 → Study the terrain before buying anything

Before spending a single peso, you need to know if there is line of sight between the two points: that from one end you can see the other directly without anything in the middle.
Radio waves from a point-to-point link cannot pass through hills, buildings, or dense forests. If there is an obstacle in the way, the link won’t work or will work very poorly.
How to verify line of sight:
The fastest way is to physically go to both points and see if you can clearly see the other from one. If you can see them, it will likely work. If you can’t see them, you need to raise the antennas.
You can also do it from home using digital tools:

Open Google Earth Pro (it’s free).
Locate both points on the map.
Use the “Elevation Profile” tool (in the Tools → Ruler menu) to draw a line between the two points and see the terrain profile. If the terrain rises in the middle, there is a problem.
You can also use HeyWhatsThat — a free web tool that shows what you can see from a point at a certain height. It works very well in the United States; in Colombia, you have to do some testing because it isn’t always as accurate as it seems.

The Fresnel Zone: more than just line of sight
Here is something many people don’t know and that costs them dearly: it’s not enough for the two points to “see” each other. Radio waves don’t travel exactly in a straight line like light. They travel in a kind of ellipsoidal bubble called the Fresnel zone.
Imagine throwing a stone into water. The point where it lands creates circular waves that expand. Something similar happens with radio waves: although the “main beam” goes from antenna to antenna, around that beam there is a spherical zone of energy that also needs to be clear.
For the link to work well, at least 60% of the radius of the first Fresnel zone must be free of obstacles. The exact formula is complicated, but the rule of thumb is:

For a 5 km link at 5 GHz, the Fresnel zone has a maximum radius of about 5–6 meters at the midpoint of the path.
For a 15–20 km link at 5 GHz, that radius rises to about 15–17 meters.

That means if there is an 8-meter tree exactly in the middle of your 5 km link, you must raise your antennas so that the tree stays below the “cone” of the signal.

Tip: use the Fresnel zone calculator from RF Line of Sight Calculator to calculate exactly how much you need to raise your antennas.




Step 2 → Plan the height of the antennas

Once the line of sight is confirmed, decide at what height to install each antenna.
The general rule: the higher, the better, because you reduce the possibility of trees or new buildings blocking the signal in the future. But higher also means bigger, more expensive, and harder-to-install poles.
A practical height for community projects on relatively flat terrain:

For distances less than 5 km: 4–6 meters above the highest obstacle in the path.
For distances of 5–15 km: 6–10 meters or more, depending on the terrain.

If there are hills in the way, sometimes it’s better to put the antenna on the crest of the hill instead of raising it. This is called a “repeater node” and can be cheaper than a very tall tower.

Something to think about: if you have doubts about the height, erring on the side of higher is less costly than repeating the installation. A taller pole is easier to get than doing everything all over again.




Step 3 → Install the poles or masts

With the heights defined, install the physical supports where the antennas will be.
Support options:

1.5–2 inch galvanized iron pole: The most durable option. It resists wind, rain, and humidity. It can be buried in the ground with cement or bolted to a wall.
2-inch PVC pipe: Cheaper. Works well for heights under 4 meters. At greater heights, it can vibrate in the wind and misalign the antenna. Also, prolonged sun exposure degrades it over time and it can become brittle — if it’s going to be outdoors, consider painting or covering it.
Roof mast: A metal structure designed to be anchored to a roof without damaging it. Ideal if the installation is on a house or building.

How to fix the pole:
If it goes into the ground: dig a hole 40–60 cm deep, put the pole in, and fill with cement. Let it dry for 24 hours before mounting anything on top.
If it goes on a wall: use expansion plugs (like Fischer) with stainless steel screws. Stainless steel doesn’t rust in the rain.

Warning: if there are strong winds in your area, add guy wires (ropes or metal rods) to stabilize the pole at various angles. A fallen pole drags the antenna down and can damage it or hurt someone.




Step 4 → Mount the antenna on the pole

Each TP-Link CPE comes with a steel clamp. The process is:

Pass the clamp around the pole.
Hook the antenna onto the clamp (it slides into a slot).
Tighten the screws without tightening them all the way yet — you need to be able to rotate the antenna to align it in the next step.

The antenna has a correct orientation. The TP-Link CPE510 and CPE210 have the label facing forward (where the signal goes). The back (where the LAN port is) faces you when you are behind the pole.

Tip: before taking the antenna up the pole, connect the network cable and turn it on on the ground to verify that it powers up correctly. It is much easier to solve a technical problem down there than while climbing a pole.




Step 5 → Run the network cable from the antenna to the router

The network cable (UTP Cat5e or Cat6) is what carries both the electrical power (via PoE) and the data between the antenna and your network router.
Maximum length: 60 meters per run. If you need more distance between the antenna and the router, you must use a switch or repeater in the middle.
How to run the cable correctly:

Measure the necessary length before cutting — add an extra 20% for bends.
If the cable goes outdoors, secure it every 50 cm with plastic zip ties or cable clips so the wind doesn’t whip it around.
At points where the cable bends (when entering a wall, for example), leave a gentle curve. Sharp bends damage the internal fibers of the cable.
Where the cable enters a building, seal the hole with silicone so water doesn’t get in.

Waterproofing the outdoor connector:
The connection between the cable and the antenna is outdoors. It is one of the points that fails most often over time. Protect it like this:

Wrap the RJ-45 connector with self-fusing tape (available at any hardware store), starting from the bottom up so that water runs off.
If you want more protection, add a layer of rubber tape on top.


Warning: water entering through the connector is the number one cause of failures in radio links installed in the field. Take your time to waterproof it well. It’s worth it.




Step 6 → Connect the PoE adapter and access the configuration interface

The PoE adapter (the “little box” that comes with the CPE) has two ports:

POE: Connects to the antenna (the cable coming from above).
LAN: Connects to the computer or your network router.

It also has a power connector to plug into an electrical outlet. The antenna does NOT need direct power — it receives it through the network cable thanks to the PoE.
To access the configuration interface:

Connect the PoE adapter to the computer with a network cable in the LAN port.
Manually set your computer’s IP address to 192.168.0.100 (subnet mask 255.255.255.0).
Open a web browser and type http://192.168.0.254 in the address bar.
The configuration panel will appear. The default username and password are admin / admin (or whatever is on the device label).


Tip: if the CPE doesn’t respond at that address, try 192.168.1.1 or 192.168.0.1. If it still doesn’t work, reset the device to factory settings by holding the RESET button for 10 seconds.




Step 7 → Configure the first end as an “Access Point”

The end that has the internet connection (the one connected to the main router or the provider) is configured as an Access Point (AP).
In the TP-Link CPE interface (Pharos software):

Go to the Wireless section.
Under Mode, select Access Point.
Enter a network name (SSID) — it can be something like community-link-AP. Give it a name you’ll recognize.
Under Frequency, if you are using the CPE510, choose a channel in the 5 GHz band that isn’t being used by other nearby networks. If there are no other networks, any channel works.
Under Security, set a strong password. This link should not be accessible to just anyone.
Save the changes and reboot the device.


Something to think about: the network name (SSID) of the link can be made invisible so it isn’t visible from external devices. You configure this in the “Hide SSID” option. It makes the link more secure in areas with many networks.




Step 8 → Configure the second end as a “Client”

The second device (the one at the remote point, where you want to bring the internet) is configured as a Client.
Repeat the physical connection from Step 6 with the second CPE. Then:

Access the device’s interface in the same way.
Go to Wireless → Mode → Client.
Click Survey. The device will search for available networks.
In the list that appears, select the SSID you gave the first device.
Enter the network password.
Save and reboot.

When both devices are configured, one will automatically search for the other and establish the connection… as long as they are pointing toward each other.

You’re doing well: if you’ve made it this far, you have both devices configured. What’s left is the most exciting part — and also the most delicate: aligning them.




Step 9 → Align the antennas to find the strongest signal

This is the heart of the entire installation. A poorly aligned antenna can have a weak signal or none at all, even if the devices are perfectly configured.
Alignment is done in two stages: first coarse orientation (pointing toward the correct area) and then fine alignment (finding the exact point of maximum signal).
Key tool: The CPE client’s web interface has a section called Signal Strength or Signal Survey that shows the signal level in real-time. You can also use the tpPharOS app on your phone connected to the AP.
The value you are looking for: The RSSI (Received Signal Strength Indicator), measured in dBm. Reference ranges:

























RSSI ValueQuality-45 to -55 dBmExcellent. Very stable link.-55 to -65 dBmGood. Will work well for most uses.-65 to -75 dBmAcceptable. There may be drops in heavy rain.Worse than -75 dBmPoor. Likely instability. You need to check alignment or height.
Step-by-step alignment process:

Communicate with the person at the other end (by cell phone, radio, or hand signals if they are visible).
Orient the client antenna pointing approximately toward the direction where the AP is. A compass or compass app helps.
In the web interface (or app), observe the RSSI value. If you don’t see a signal from the AP, move the antenna slowly in a horizontal arc until you find it.
Once you find a signal, start the fine adjustment: move the antenna very slowly to the right and left, looking for the point where the RSSI is highest (the least negative number).
Fix the antenna at that point and repeat the movement vertically (up and down) to optimize that axis as well.
When you have the maximum on both axes, fully tighten the clamp screws.
The person at the other end does exactly the same with the AP.


Keep it up: alignment can take between 20 minutes and two hours, especially if the two points are very far away or if the terrain is uneven. It’s normal. Every tenth of a dB you gain in RSSI is worth it. Don’t rush this stage.


Tip: if you have two people at each end and they can talk by cell phone, alignment is much faster. One person moves, the other reports the value. You adjust together.




Step 10 → Verify that the link works correctly

With the antennas aligned and the devices running, it’s time to verify that the link has the quality needed for the use you will give it.
From the client’s web interface, go to the Status or Monitor section. Look for these indicators:
RSSI (signal level):
Make sure it’s in the green range: between -45 and -65 dBm. You already saw this in the previous step.
CCQ (Client Connection Quality):
This is a percentage that indicates the efficiency of the connection. A CCQ of 90% or more is excellent. Below 70%, the link is having trouble transmitting internet packets → correctly.
Real Throughput:
Open a browser on a computer connected to the client and test the speed with Fast.com or Speedtest.net. The result should be close (not equal, but proportional) to the speed at the source point.

Something to think about: if the RSSI is good but the speed is low, check if there is interference from other networks on the same channel. Channels are like traffic lanes or different colors: if many networks share the same channel, the space becomes saturated and the data gets trampled. Change the channel in the AP configuration and see if it improves.

Stability test:
Leave the link running for 30 minutes and observe if the RSSI remains stable or fluctuates. A stable link should vary by less than ±3 dBm. If the signal goes up and down a lot, it may indicate intermittent obstacles (like trees moving in the wind) or that the alignment isn’t completely fixed.

You’re doing well: if the RSSI is between -45 and -65 dBm, the CCQ is over 90%, and the speed test gives consistent results, you have a functional radio link. That “invisible bridge” you imagined at the beginning now exists.



Recommendations
Heavy rain and thick fog can temporarily degrade the signal, especially in the 5 GHz band. This is normal. If the link only fails during heavy downpours, consider improving the alignment or slightly increasing the transmit power in the device configuration. Keep in mind that increasing power consumes more electricity and can accelerate equipment wear over time.
Connectors and cables outdoors are the most vulnerable point of the installation. Check them every 6 months. Water entering through a small crack can damage the equipment in weeks. Good initial waterproofing is worth much more than repairing or replacing equipment.
If the link has to pass near trees, install the antennas with more margin than you think is necessary. Trees grow. A tree that is 4 meters tall today might be 6 meters in two years and start blocking the signal without you having moved.
Do not mix equipment from different brands in the same link if you can avoid it. TP-Link CPE with TP-Link CPE, Ubiquiti with Ubiquiti. Technically they can work in cross-combinations, but sometimes there are incompatibilities in proprietary protocols that reduce speed or stability.
Document everything: the direction of each antenna in degrees, the RSSI at the time of installation, the height of the mast, the length of the cable. You can do it on video, in a notebook, on a printed piece of paper kept in a plastic bag near the equipment, or on your phone. That record will save you hours if you ever have to check or repeat the installation.

How do you know if this solution works?
Technical signs of success:

RSSI between -45 and -65 dBm stably
CCQ above 90% constantly
Speed test at the remote point with reasonable results (minimum 5–10 Mbps for basic community use)
The link stays active for 24 hours without drops

Signs of community impact:

People at the remote point can make video calls or watch videos without drops.
Children at school can use online educational platforms.
The organization can upload photos, documents, or reports without having to travel to the town center.
Someone who previously paid for internet separately now shares it more economically with the community.


Other possible internets
A radio link is not just technology. It is a political decision by a community that says: we also have the right to connect, and we are going to build our own way of doing it.
In Mexico, indigenous communities in Oaxaca have been operating their own community telecommunications networks for years using exactly this principle. In the Colombian countryside, projects like those from Colnodo and ISOC have shown that it is possible. You don’t need to be a telecommunications company to build a data bridge between two villages.
You can also explore whether there are telecommunications companies, cooperatives, or entities that can donate equipment or establish a partnership with your community. In Colombia, there are calls from FONTIC and international organizations that support rural connectivity projects — that can reduce the initial cost.
Once you have the link installed, also consider configuring a secure DNS server (like Cloudflare’s 1.1.1.1 or Quad9’s 9.9.9.9) on your network so that browsing is safer and more private for the people who connect.
And if you found this guide useful, you can download or print it to have it available without needing to be connected when you need it most.
What would happen if the village up on the hill and the one down by the river decided to connect with each other, without depending on an operator that doesn’t reach them? What communities do you know that are at the right distance to make this a reality?

Related solutions
A radio link brings internet from one point to another, but at that remote point, you also need to distribute it. These solutions show you how to take that next step:

When the internet already reaches the remote point, this solution explains how to distribute it among several people without cables: How to share internet wirelessly? →
If you want to bring internet to areas that don’t have constant electricity, the bike generator can complement your project: How to generate electricity using a bicycle? →
Before installing the radio link, it is useful to know what type of signal and speed you have at the source point: How to perform an internet quality diagnosis? →
If the distance is too great for a radio link in free bands, a satellite antenna can be the alternative: How to get a satellite antenna? →
So that more people can connect once you have the internet at the remote point, this guide helps you organize the space: How to organize a community internet space? →


References

TP-Link. CPE510 — 5GHz 300Mbps 13dBi Outdoor CPE. Official technical specifications: tp-link.com/us/business-networking/pharos-cpe/cpe510/
TP-Link. CPE210 — 2.4GHz 300Mbps 9dBi Outdoor CPE. Official technical specifications: tp-link.com/us/business-networking/pharos-cpe/cpe210/
Sistelec. Radio links: Complete Guide. sistelec.es/blog/radioenlaces/
Data Alliance. Fresnel Zone: key for long-range WiFi links. data-alliance.net
Todotelco. Fresnel zones in radio links: Definition and Formulas. todotelco.com
Colnodo / APC. Community Networks: rural communication services in Latin America. colnodo.apc.org
Comunicaciones Inalámbricas Hoy. Free frequency bands. comunicacionesinalambricashoy.com
WifiSafe. Configuration manual for a Point-to-Point link between 2 Ubiquiti devices. wifisafe.com

en/solve/solv-need-3Gantenna.title: Do I need to buy a 3G/4G antenna?
en/solve/solv-need-3Gantenna.summary: Discover the antenna that suits you best.
en/solve/solv-need-3Gantenna.content:
Hi, I’m Sanjay. Along with Gabriel, another tech-savvy friend of mine, we made our first 3/4G antenna purchase after doing some digging into commercial solutions for connectivity issues.
In this guide, I’m going to offer you some tips on how to go about buying a 3/4G antenna.
What is a 3G or 4G antenna?
3G and 4G are abbreviations for the set of technologies needed to transmit voice and data over mobile networks.
This set includes everything from the types of cell phones and antennas to the communication protocols between them, all of which are necessary to send voice or data via cellular telephony.
I won’t get into the nitty-gritty, but just for curiosity’s sake, it’s worth knowing that the G stands for generation, and the numbers refer to the third and fourth generations of these technologies.
Previous generations didn’t allow for data transmission, only voice, like a radio. So, for example, old-school phones—which we call “flechas” (arrows) in Colombia—aren’t built to receive Internet data. To connect to the Internet, devices need to be 3G-enabled or higher, meaning they must be smartphones →.

What is a 3/4G antenna used for?
I recently learned that the Internet signal that reaches our phones travels through invisible electromagnetic waves. Phones have a small antenna inside that captures these waves, which is what gives us Internet access.
Gabriel and I have discovered that buying a commercial 3G or 4G antenna is one of the best ways to get a stable and reliable Internet connection. This is especially true for fixed locations like a house, a school, a library, or a shop, where you’re using mobile telephony in areas with poor coverage.
Basically, what the antenna does is capture and amplify the specific cellular data signal (3G or 4G) that’s traveling through the air as electromagnetic waves from a higher point than where you are—above trees, buildings, or hills—and brings it down to your level via a cable.
Once it’s there, the signal can be shared throughout the space by creating a WiFi network or via cable, using a modem or router. I know these terms might sound a bit confusing, but as you go through these recommendations, you’ll get a clearer picture of them.

If you want to know how to buy an antenna and what parameters you should keep in mind to search for and decide on the 3G/4G antenna that will improve your mobile Internet connection, follow our recommendations.

Before we start, a quick thought
Sometimes we decide to buy the cheapest option because we want to save money. But as they say, “cheap can turn out expensive,” and when it comes to technology like an antenna, this is usually true.
We’ve seen many antennas that end up as junk because they don’t do the job (like those from satellite TV providers). They get installed in cities and rural areas, creating electronic waste that, besides being an eyesore, never gets removed or reused.
It’s also important to be clear about the care and maintenance your purchase might require. Sometimes we buy something, and when it needs maintenance, we don’t have the time or resources to deal with it, and it ends up useless. When you team up with others, you can share the care and split the costs, making it much lighter and more manageable.
Make sure the antenna you buy works for your specific conditions and is the best option for you.

What do you need?

To recognize the geography of the place where you need the signal.
To identify which operator or operators work best in the region.
An antenna supplier.
Some money.
To meet with your community to identify the best option.


How to do it?
Below, we present the steps we consider when deciding what type of 3G/4G antenna to buy.

Step 1 → Determine if you need a 3/4G antenna

There are places where the cellular signal is very weak. You can confirm this on your phone by looking at the connection bars: you might see only one bar or something that says H+, E, or even no signal at all.
However, when you move a few meters or a few kilometers, the signal appears or improves, and you start seeing bars with the 3G or 4G symbol on your phone.
If this is your case, there might be cell towers around you that you don’t have a direct line of sight to, and therefore, you aren’t able to connect to the 3G/4G network from your initial spot.
Buying a 3G/4G antenna will allow you to have a stable Internet connection, but there must be cellular coverage in the area.
It’s not a cheap solution, but it is the most reliable way to establish an Internet access point for your community if you are in areas with low mobile coverage.
If there is no mobile coverage at all, you won’t be able to get connectivity with one of these antennas. To get it, you’ll have to resort to solutions like the ones we describe in the guide on How to buy a satellite internet service for non-interconnected places?, where there are various satellite solutions, though they tend to be more expensive.


Step 2 → Ask yourself these questions based on your needs

Where am I located geographically?
The first thing is to understand the geography of where you are. What you’re trying to identify are the cell towers that could provide you with a signal. For 3/4G antennas to work, they generally need to “see” a tower, or at least be pointed in the same direction.
If you live in a region with many mountains, it will be a bit harder to get a good signal compared to a flat area.
If possible, look for the nearest cell tower: look for tall towers with antennas. They are usually located on the highest mountain peaks to allow for greater coverage.
If you don’t know where the nearest cell tower is, you can also ask your neighbors; they might have already spotted it.


Taken from Wikimedia Commons

Which mobile phone providers have coverage in this area?

In rural areas or places far from urban centers, mobile operator coverage can be quite hit-or-miss.
Make sure to find the one that works best in the region. Ask your neighbors which one works best for them. Identify which ones have better coverage—meaning they provide a more stable and faster service.
💡 Keep in mind that the coverage of these providers changes over time as they install new relay antennas or as more people subscribe to their services, saturating their signal.

This information is important for the antenna supplier: make sure the modem they give you is “unlocked” (open bands), so you can use the operator you choose without restrictions.

Where are the nearest cell towers located?

Use a mobile app to identify which cell towers are closest.
To do this, search for “Cell towers” or “Cell signal” apps in the Google Play or Apple Store, download one, and use it to identify which antennas, and from which operators, are closest to where you are.
If there is no signal in the place where you want to test, you can download the antenna map in a place with a connection and carry it on your phone. It will allow you to interpret it by matching the geographic North with the map’s North.


What space do I want to provide with internet?

To decide where you are going to leave the modem connected, emitting a WiFi signal, it’s important to consider the geographic location and its access to electricity.
We recommend thinking about public spaces like schools, libraries, or community halls, since internet in those spaces can benefit more people.
If you want the connection for your home, it might be worth putting it in a space like the living room or dining room, rather than in the bedrooms. Spaces in the house meant for rest should be free of the device’s electromagnetic fields, which could affect you, and besides, physical obstacles can affect the signal in the rest of the house.

How much, and for what, will those who connect use the internet?

Defining how much you’re going to use the internet and what you want to use it for is important to know what to expect from the antenna you’re going to buy.
To refine your expectations, you can read How is Internet usage measured?

How much money do I, or do we, have to buy an antenna?

In Colombia, in 2024, one of the most powerful antennas on the market, with a robust 15-meter-long cable plus the modem, cost around COP 1,300,000 or USD 300.
But you don’t have to face this expense alone; think that the more people who contribute to the purchase of the antenna, the cheaper it will be per person. So, we encourage you to talk to family and neighbors to agree and share the signal.


Step 3 → Identify what you need to know to answer these questions

Recognize the topography of the place
After answering where you are, it’s important, if possible, to get the precise location of the place where you want to connect.
With the help of a ‣ app, locate the exact coordinates of the place where you want to install the antenna.
This data will be useful at the time of purchase. Suppliers usually have access to updated databases on the coverage of different phone providers, as well as their locations, which allows them to advise you more accurately on the type of antenna that best meets your specific needs.
Your phone may have an app to locate your coordinates. If you use Android, go to Google Maps. If you have an iPhone, go to Maps.
Find your location point, and you’ll be able to access the exact coordinates of where you are. Finally, write down this data to have it handy when you need it.


Where to buy the antenna?

You can do a SOLE to perform an Internet search where your Big Question contains terms like 4g signal booster antenna. The search should lead you to find nearby distributors.
When you talk to the company that distributes the technology, have all the data you can on hand. Together, you will find the best solution for the place where you are going to set up your Internet access point.

What should they give you when you have made the purchase of your antenna?

You have to keep in mind that for the antenna to work, it needs to be connected to a device. So, the minimum your antenna kit should contain is:

A 3/4G antenna
Basic mounting hardware
The connection cable
A 3/4G modem

Antenna
The necessary antenna is a Yagi type →. It can be similar to the one in the image above, or it can also be encapsulated in a plastic protector, which will protect the antenna and its connections from weather conditions, extending its useful life.
One thing to keep in mind with the antenna is its power. This data is expressed in dB: a 65dB antenna will have more power than a 15dB antenna. As a general rule, the further the antenna is from the provider, the more power you will need to establish a connection.

Cable
The cable to connect the antenna to the modem is similar to the coaxial cable → used in television connections. However, it is not the same. There is a wide variety of cable types, but at a minimum, for these types of applications, cables like RG-6 → should be used. That said, it is recommended to use shielded cables that minimize signal loss and reduce noise in the system.
You should not modify the cable the supplier gives you in any way: the splicing between the cable and the connectors at the ends is done in a way that minimizes noise in the system; any alteration can make all components completely useless.

Modem / Router
Normally, antenna kits come with a modem and a router, which will allow you to connect and share the mobile network signal captured by the antenna.
If you already have a modem, at the time of purchase, verify that it can connect to the antenna and, if necessary, that the supplier sends you the necessary adapters to make the connection.


Step 4 → Make the final decision

Depending on your geographic conditions, what you want to use it for, and your budget, ask the seller about all possible options.
Don’t forget to talk about the care and maintenance of the devices, especially the costs involved and how often you will have to assume them.
The most expensive one is not necessarily the one that will serve you best.

Don’t be fooled
Sometimes, sellers will want to propose more sophisticated and expensive solutions than what you actually need.
Ask a lot of questions. It’s the only way to learn and create criteria to find the best possible option.

How much is enough?
Buying an antenna with the necessary characteristics to access the mobile network will allow you to have a stable connection with which, for example, you can meet to learn how to learn, in a group, using the internet.
You can also watch movies, consult a doctor about a situation, communicate with family or friends… so let’s find new ways to use the internet!
Also, when you have a more stable connection, doing a SOLE will be easier.
A single antenna and a single connection, in a group, will be more than enough to enjoy all the options that the internet offers. Even more so, if you use the internet on shared computers, it will be safer, more private, and more fun.

Related solutions

4G antenna? →
How to use the game to learn how to take care of equipment as a community? →
How to buy a satellite antenna? →

Remember that at Voltaje ⚡⚡ you can find many more solutions to connect without fear to using the internet in a group. Go ahead and keep browsing! See more solutions →

en/solve/solv-organize-space.title: How to adapt a space for group Internet use?
en/solve/solv-organize-space.summary: How a space looks and feels is key to connecting with each other.
en/solve/solv-organize-space.content:
slug: solv-space-setup
path: es/solve/solv-space-setup
Hi! I’m Catalina, welcome 👋🏽
I wrote this solution because, over time, I’ve discovered how the objects around us shape the way we relate to one another. When I joined SOLE, I didn’t just learn a methodology; I discovered a whole way of promoting the use of the Internet in groups through small details (which aren’t actually that small), like how you arrange a meeting space.
Have you ever heard of this idea of using the Internet in a group? At SOLE, we’re still figuring it out. For now, we know it has to do with people getting together to use the Internet, but also with the devices or spaces we use (or invent) to connect, share, and learn with the Internet, especially in person.
Shall we set up your next meeting space together? I’ll walk you through it! 👇🏽

What does it mean to set up a space for group Internet use?

⚠️ Before you start, it’s important to know which space you’re going to use. If you don’t have one yet, this solution can help you find one: How to get a community hall or any community space to use the internet in a group?

Setting up a space refers to how we organize the elements inside it: chairs, tables, whiteboards, posters, projectors, whatever.
To host a SOLE, for example, we need to dis-organize the space to keep it from looking like a classroom. This is important because, to promote different ways of learning, it’s key that people don’t feel like they’re in a traditional learning environment.
This matters because the way a space is organized generates different interactions between people. Think, for example, of a church versus a restaurant.
In a church, all the chairs are arranged in rows facing the front. It’s a space where attention is directed toward one person (the priest), and where you aren’t really supposed to chat with others; that’s why you’re shoulder to shoulder. In a restaurant, however, people are organized in small groups. There are chairs around various tables where everyone can see each other. It’s a space made for interacting, for chatting, and of course, for eating.

What is it for?
Planning how a space is organized encourages certain interactions over others. When it comes to using the Internet in a group, we want people to be able to share a computer or the network, but also ideas and experiences—in other words, conversations.
So yes, this solution helps you organize a space to allow for group Internet use. But it goes further! Using the Internet in a group allows for self-managed learning, planning, and carrying out community projects. If you browse the Internet in a group, it’s harder to fall for traps or fake content because there are more humans there to analyze the information. But you can also do things that seem simple, like watching a movie, which can bring powerful results, like several people laughing at the same time.
In short, this solution promotes ways to (re)connect in a world where it’s becoming more and more common to feel lonely.

What do you need?

A space (your own or borrowed)
One table for every 4 people
More chairs than tables; enough for everyone (plastic ones are quite practical)
One computer for every 3-5 people (or at least tablets)
Webcam and microphone (one of the computers can serve this purpose)
A whiteboard or space where you can write (it could also be a piece of glass, a window, a blank poster, etc.)
Markers


How to do it?
Rather than a specific step-by-step guide, I prefer to share some recommendations for setting up your space, as well as different ways to configure it and the interactions each one might trigger.

Recommendation #1 → Plan your meeting, get what you need.

Do you know how many people you’re expecting? Have you planned your activity?
Having a plan for what you’ll do is key to knowing what you need.
Do you have tables, chairs, a whiteboard? If so, move on to the next step. If not, I can give you some tips on how to get them.
Community spaces usually have tables and chairs. Shops do too. You can ask to borrow them there, making it clear that you take responsibility for them (you can leave a written note that gives the owner peace of mind). If you choose to meet with people at a time when customers aren’t around as much, it’s more likely they’ll lend them to you.
Another option is to use things that look like them. At SOLE, for example, we use fruit and vegetable crates to simulate tables and chairs. They’re great! And they can often be recycled.
— Photo of SOLE stools


Recommendation #2 → Dis-organize the space!

Using the Internet in a group should feel like something pleasant. Something people choose to do, not something they have to do. The best way to do this is by making the space feel flexible.
Take a look at these three different ways to configure the space:
— Photo of spaces
What do they remind you of? How do they make you feel? Here 👇🏽 I’ll share how I remember/feel them:

This is the usual layout of a classroom or a conference space. There is one person (or several) at the front, who usually addresses the audience in a “one-way” manner, meaning the audience is there mainly to listen, not to intervene. The interaction is more hierarchical: the person at the front has the attention.
The circle or half-moon layout is, for example, how community meetings or dialogue circles are usually held. This way of positioning allows everyone to see each other and allows the sound of voices to circulate and reach everyone easily. This form invites everyone to interact in a “multi-directional” way, making the bond between those interacting less hierarchical.
This is the usual layout of a SOLE or a restaurant. It’s a way of positioning that promotes several “small conversations” at the same time. Unlike the first two, this layout allows more people to speak, so the number of people involved in the interaction is reduced. This is an excellent option when we want to cover more topics in the same amount of time or, as in a SOLE, when several people want to focus their attention on something particular.

There are a thousand ways to configure a space. Even these three I’m sharing can be mixed together. What I’m interested in showing you is that different ways of organizing a space promote different interactions, but also different hierarchies between the people participating in the interaction.
At SOLE, rather than organizing, we like to “dis-organize” the space, because the ideal is that it never looks like a classroom or a Community Action Board event. In group Internet use, it is key to promote horizontal (non-hierarchical) relationships, where you can chat within small groups, but also between groups.
— Photo of SOLE configuration.
I always recommend having a whiteboard or space to write that everyone can see. It works very well as a “memory aid” as conversations develop.

👆🏽 If you are going to host a SOLE, you can use the materials from the SOLE Kit to give the space more personality. If it’s not a SOLE, I still recommend decorating with posters or materials that get people in tune with the energy of the activity.



Recommendation #3 → Invent and discover the best way to set up your spaces

In our experience, this last configuration is the one that has worked best for us to use the Internet in a group. But this is just an idea. Remember that if there’s one thing that characterizes a “cacharrero” (tinkerer), it’s the exercise of trial and error, so go ahead and try more combinations or new ways to configure your spaces! Surely there will be other ways that work even better for you. Mind you, the only condition is that you share them on Voltaje! (Just kidding, it’s not a condition, but it would be very useful for other people 😋).
Good luck with your meeting!


How do you know if this solution works?
Think about what you had in mind when setting up your space. What was your goal? What did you expect to happen? Then (ideally at the end of the meeting), observe the space. What changed in it? What remained the same?
There is no magic formula to know if the space layout worked. But a good sign that it did is that the space has changed. Sometimes people (dis)organize the space even more. They move chairs, push tables together, find other places to write… Let them! That’s a great way to know that people are taking ownership of the place and that they felt the need to move through it as a result of the conversations they wanted to be part of.
Another way is during the meeting. It’s not always easy, but try to pay attention to the interactions between people: Where do they talk the most? Where do they laugh? Where do they reflect? Where do they rest? Pay attention to how the space is arranged every time you see different emotions unfolding.

Other possible Internets
Sometimes we dream not only of inventing new ways to configure the space, but also of new devices that allow us to interact better and better with the Internet, but in a group. Can you imagine if there were a computer with four keyboards? What would we have to do to write a letter with four hands? What kind of video games could we play? How much more could we learn together?
—four-keyboard computer imagination.
Thinking of new physical ways to foster collective interactions is very powerful in a world where individual interactions are increasingly promoted. How do you design for communities and not just for individuals? What can we do in a group that we can’t do alone? What worlds can we invent and build together?
At SOLE, we have been “inventing” a physical space where the Internet can be used in a group. We call it the SOLE Lab. In fact, there are already three in Colombia!

⚡⚡ Learn about the experience of the most recent one in this inspiration: We built a SOLE Lab in La Guajira to use the Internet in a group, and the others in the “Get Inspired” section.

But we want more communities in Colombia and the world to be able to have one! That’s why now in 2026 we are creating the “do it yourself” version of this space, which will be something like assembling furniture, but for a space.
—video SOLE Lab DIY
And what do you think? Hopefully, these questions encourage you to imagine other ways of relating to the Internet. Or as we say, other possible Internets!

Related solutions

Remember, if you don’t have a space yet, this solution might be useful: How to get a community hall or any community space to use the internet in a group? →
If you still don’t know how to invite people, check out this solution: How to write an invitation that gets people to show up? →


Remember that on Voltaje ⚡⚡ you can find many more solutions to connect without fear of using the internet in a group. Go ahead and keep browsing! See more solutions →

en/solve/solv-pocket-wikipedia.title: How to access an encyclopedia without internet?
en/solve/solv-pocket-wikipedia.summary: Install Kiwix, a pocket Wikipedia on your Raspberry Pi.
en/solve/solv-pocket-wikipedia.content:
Hi! I’m Gabriel and I’m an artist. I love technology and I’m one of the original tinkerers at SOLE Colombia. I’m no expert, but I’ve learned through trial and error, and that’s the best way to learn!

What is a pocket Wikipedia?
Imagine you could fit the world’s largest library into a little box that fits in your hand. That’s Kiwix: a program that stores all of Wikipedia (text and images included) so you can look things up even if you don’t have a single bit of internet.

What’s it for?
Having a pocket Wikipedia on your Raspberry Pi → lets you take knowledge anywhere: a rural school, a community center, or your own home. It’s like having your own water well instead of waiting for it to rain; the information is always there, ready for whenever someone has a Big Question.

What do you need?

Your Raspberry Pi up and running (think of it as the building for our library).
A computer to give it instructions.
Internet connection (just this once, to download the books).
Plenty of patience: downloading all of Wikipedia takes time—it’s better if you have someone to grab a coffee with while you wait!


How to do it?

Step 1 → Connect to your remote library

Before we start, make sure your Pi is turned on. We’re going to talk to it from our computer using a Terminal → and starting an SSH → connection. It’s like sending a radio message to someone inside the building.


Step 2 → Download the “librarian” (Kiwix)

Kiwix is in charge of searching for the information. First, we’re going to download its tools. Copy and paste this into your terminal:
wget download.kiwix.org/release/kiwix-tools/kiwix-tools_linux-armhf.tar.gz



Step 3 → Bring in the books (the compressed Wikipedia)

Now let’s go get the content. We’re going to download a version of Wikipedia in Spanish. It’s a heavy file (about 3.3GB), so this is where the coffee and conversation come in.
wget download.kiwix.org/zim/wikipedia/wikipedia_es_all_mini_2022-11.zim


Keep your chin up: if the internet is slow, don’t despair. Once it finishes, you’ll never need the internet to read this ever again!



Step 4 → Organize the library shelves

We have the files, now we need to put them in their place. We’re going to unzip the librarian’s tools and move them to the Pi’s “executable” folder.

Unzip:
tar -zxvf kiwix-tools_linux-armhf.tar.gz

Move to the right spot:
sudo mv kiwix-tools_linux-armhf-3.3.0-1/* /usr/local/bin





Step 5 → Locate the Wikipedia book

The .zim file (which is like a giant compressed book) needs to go into a special folder so the librarian can find it quickly:
sudo mv wikipedia_es_all_mini_2022-11.zim /var/local/


Step 6 → Hire a librarian who never sleeps

So you don’t have to turn the program on every time you restart the Pi, we’re going to create a “service.” This will make Kiwix start automatically as soon as you plug the Pi into power.
Create the configuration file:
sudo nano /etc/systemd/system/kiwix.service
Paste this content inside (use the arrow keys to navigate, Ctrl+O to save, and Ctrl+X to exit):
[Unit]
Description=Kiwix Service
After=network.target
 
[Service]
Type=simple
User=root
Group=root
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/kiwix-serve /var/local/wikipedia_es_all_mini_2022-11.zim -p 8080
Restart=always
RestartSec=3
 
[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target


You’re doing great: you’re almost finished! All that’s left is to give the command to turn it on.



Step 7 → Start your engines!

Now tell the Pi to recognize this new service and start it up right away:
sudo systemctl enable kiwix
sudo systemctl start kiwix


Step 8 → Open your library from any device

Done! Now, from any phone or computer connected to the same network as your Pi, open your browser and type: solevoltaje.local:8080.


How do I know if this solution works?
If you see the Wikipedia search bar when you go to that address and you can browse the articles, you did it! You have an entire encyclopedia living inside your little Raspberry Pi.

Other possible Internets
With your pocket Wikipedia, you can now host SOLE sessions in any park, mountain, or community hall, regardless of whether there’s cell service. You’re democratizing access to information and proving that knowledge doesn’t have to depend on a monthly subscription.

en/solve/solv-prueba-ia.title: How to download an encyclopedia to your cell phone?
en/solve/solv-prueba-ia.summary: Wikipedia in your pocket to use in places without a signal.
en/solve/solv-prueba-ia.content:
Using television as a learning tool to do SOLE
What is it for?
Imagine if you could turn the television into a space for communication and learning that doesn’t just go from the channel to the audience, but where the audience helps create the content and everyone ends up learning together. For places where the internet signal doesn’t reach, or if part of the audience can’t get online, using television can extend your reach, especially so that children and young people can explore and connect to the network.
So, if you have a mass-media or community TV channel, you can generate a Self-Organized Learning Environment, or SOLE by TV. This allows people in the community—whether they have internet or not—to learn and engage in dialogue through the television around Big Questions.
Doing a SOLE TV means creating a new type of television content built by asking the audience to answer a Big Question and then inviting people to send in their responses to be shared on a show. Having many responses allows us to generate a live conversation where we are all experts because we build the knowledge together… just like the internet!
What do you need?

A television channel (mass-media, community, or online).
A host.
An audience (at least 2 people).
A time slot for the TV show (you can call it SOLE TV).
Internet access and/or social media (optional).
A video recorder or cell phone (optional).
TV host energy.

How to do it?
Define the Big Question and the show date

Sole Colombia
BIG QUESTION: Define a Big Question that motivates self-organized learning using the available media. The Big Question is what will hook the audience into participating in this SOLE TV.
LIVE SHOW DATE: Set a date so the audience can participate and watch the show; you should start calling for responses to the Big Question about 15 days in advance.
Invite the audience to answer

Sole Colombia
CALL TO ACTION: Broadcast the Big Question through messages or short promos on the channel, inviting the audience to answer via an online form, social media comments, by calling the channel, or by recording clips on the street. In the invitation or online form, include the date of the live show and ask for contact information from those responding so you can reach out to them directly. Some people might have social media like WhatsApp or Facebook to participate through those channels. Others could participate by calling the channel directly or showing up in person at the station. You could also collect responses on the street by recording them with video equipment or a cell phone.
Plan the live show

Pexels
SHOW SCRIPT: While you receive responses to the Big Question, you can organize a simple rundown of the show and some audiovisual bumpers to accompany the live broadcast. For a 1-hour show, it’s worth thinking about the following:

How to present the Big Question?
Invite 2 to 5 people based on their submitted responses to participate in the live show and share their answers.
What other questions could deepen the learning during the live broadcast?
Select other responses to share during the broadcast.
What other methods could we use to interact with the audience?

Then, prepare a simple script for the show’s segments. Here is a reference:

Bumper, greeting, introduction of guests.
Presentation of the Big Question.
First round of responses between guests and audience submissions.
Invitation for the audience to participate via social media.
New questions to dig deeper.
Second round of responses between guests and audience submissions.
Conclusion of the conversation, thanks, and congratulations to the participants for their autonomous learning.

Broadcast the live show

Sole Colombia SOLE TV: Broadcast a live show using the script as a guide, but allow for an unstructured conversation combined with other pre-recorded audience responses and/or social media input to solve the Big Question together. Guests can do some research beforehand. You can also invite people to the show who have knowledge about the answer to share it, or people who are great conversationalists to stir up a lively discussion. The host or participants can dig deeper with new questions that arise.
What is achieved?
In many places, there is no internet signal, but there is television. Also, even if there is an internet signal, people might not be able to afford it. Therefore, television becomes a medium that can allow people to learn with or without the internet.
However, television is usually a one-way communication medium, from the broadcaster to the audience. The audience rarely gets to participate in building the learning at the station.
Successfully transforming television into a Self-Organized Learning Environment (SOLE) and a space for civic interaction allows communities without internet (or with limited access) to learn, dialogue, and create flourishing communities using television or a combination of television and the internet.
How far can it go?
Television is a very powerful medium because many people can access it for free. Especially for many children and young people, it may be the only communication device they have access to. It will never be the same as having internet access, as the internet is the largest library in the world, which also allows you to connect with millions of people across the planet. However, television also allows you to connect with many people; the challenge is for them to be able to dialogue with the television to learn together. This is what SOLE TV does.
Verification
2020, SOLE Colombia Team and Canal Capital. SOLE Capital: What are we doing to ensure the respect of children’s rights during this time of care?
Summary
2020, SOLE Colombia Team and Canal Capital. Encuentros Capital: The show of your dreams on public television

en/solve/solv-purchase-temp-satellite.title: How to buy a temporary satellite internet connection?
en/solve/solv-purchase-temp-satellite.summary: A code or PIN to access satellite internet.
en/solve/solv-purchase-temp-satellite.content:
A code or PIN to access satellite internet
Hi! I’m Belén. I didn’t write this entire solution, but while reviewing it, I remembered many SOLE sessions that work thanks to this workaround. Finding a place that sells a few data or minutes of satellite internet connection has allowed us to bring SOLE to places we never thought we’d reach.
What is getting an Internet PIN?
Accessing the internet via a satellite connection is a recommended method in places where cables or phone lines don’t reach, such as rural or remote areas. In a city, it serves as an alternative and somewhat affordable system compared to the usual ones.
In Colombia, a “satellite connection PIN” refers to a code or key that allows access to internet or communication services via satellites. These codes might be needed to activate a satellite internet service, like Starlink, or to configure satellite communication devices used in areas without terrestrial network coverage.
This solution explains how to access satellite internet as a pay-as-you-go service by the day or hour.
What is it for?
If you’re looking to use an internet connection for something specific, this is the ideal solution. For example, if you want to gather your community to learn things together using the internet as a group—that is, to hold a SOLE—having data to share across two or three computers so everyone can ask the web about the things they want to learn is the best way to guarantee a connection.
What do you need?

An internet provider in the area.
Money to pay for the PIN.
A device to access the internet.

How to do it?
Follow these steps to buy the PIN and get connected:

Step 1 → Check if this service exists in your area

First of all, you need to know if this service is regularly offered in your territory. This service exists in places where mobile data networks from conventional providers don’t reach; if they did, it would be more practical to just top up your phone with a data package or have a postpaid plan.
In some places, internet providers lease satellite connections where cable can’t reach or where they know locals can’t contract other types of mobile phone services. For example, here is a company that offers this type of service in Barranquilla: Zonawipi


Step 2 → Evaluate other options before deciding

If you found that the service is available in your area, it’s important to see if it’s economically convenient for you. If you have to keep buying PINs and traveling to another location every day to connect, this might not be the most viable option. Perhaps another solution would be better, like pooling money together to pay for community internet.
If it is definitely the most viable option, go ahead and buy it!


Step 3 → Buy the PIN and start browsing

Now that you’ve decided to buy a PIN, remember to make the most of it. Connection time will be restricted only to the areas where this network has coverage. In practice, it works like an Internet Café where you connect wirelessly with your own device.
Just follow the instructions on the paper where the purchased PIN comes. Usually, you need to connect to a WiFi → network, which will automatically redirect you to a link asking for the PIN number to grant you internet access. That’s it—now get connected and enjoy!
Remember, you’ll get great value out of your internet connection if you share it with others who can’t access this resource. A great way to learn and enjoy together is to hold a SOLE. SOLE is a methodology where real-life challenges can be solved through Big Questions using the internet. Does your community want to learn how to get better results from their crops? Do you want to know what games children in other countries play? Do you have questions about how a specific atmospheric phenomenon is produced or how to take advantage of climate changes? Hold a SOLE! You can find more information at Sole Colombia.

How do you know this solution works?
With this solution, you can achieve a temporary connection with internet access in a specific location.
Why might this solution work?
We have to carefully measure the bandwidth → offered by the service and, in general, the quality of the service used in relation to its cost. This solution is intended for non-recurring access, as it would become very expensive if it were to become a regular habit, and it would end up being cheaper to contract other types of services.

Related solutions

How to share internet from my cell phone? →
Which WiFi networks are free and available to connect to the internet? →

Remember that at Voltaje ⚡⚡ you can find many more solutions to connect without fear of using the internet as a group. Keep on browsing! See more solutions →
