en/solve/solv-raspberrypi-pocket-interne.title: How to install a web server on a pocket computer?
en/solve/solv-raspberrypi-pocket-interne.content:
Hi, I’m Gabriel. I’m an artist. I find digital devices, how they work, and the way we humans interact with them quite interesting. I consider myself a bit of a tinkerer—a cacharrero—and I invite you, if you’d like, to be one too.
What is a Raspberry Pi, or a pocket-sized Internet?
This solution will help you create a small internet on your local network with very few resources.
By installing and configuring a server → on the network, your community will be able to access the content hosted on it from their computers or phones. This way, you can have, for example, a copy of Wikipedia so everyone can check it whenever they need to, without needing to access the Internet → to do so.

What is it for?
If we’re talking about using the Internet to solve Big Questions and real-life challenges as a group, having content accessible without an Internet connection can be an excellent option: for example, if you are going to do a SOLE session in a very remote place where you know connectivity definitely won’t be viable.
Having downloadable content available offline will allow them to research and reach some conclusions, which they can expand upon later when they have an Internet connection or when they can connect an “Abuelita” (a cloud-based learning hub).
Do you want to know more about how to turn your space into a place for learning, or who the “Abuelitas de la Nube” are? Visit Solecolombia.org to learn how, and browse the site to find out more about the Nube de Abuelitas that can support the learning processes happening in your space.

How do you know if you need it?
Ask yourself how good your Internet connection is in the place where you’ll be connecting. At SOLE Colombia, we know the difficulties of many remote communities where the internet is scarce or hard to access, and a solution like this allows people to access downloaded content, which is almost like having access to their twins on the web.
This way, it becomes possible to browse a replica of parts of the Internet, learning to use technology in a different way.
Even though its benefits are many and obvious, this is a solution that requires a powerful spirit of tinkering and high doses of commitment and patience… we are sure you can manage to set up your own little pocket internet!

What do you need?

Raspberry Pi
32 GB Class 10 MicroSD card
Power supply for the Raspberry Pi - check the specifications on Raspberry Pi
Ethernet cable →
MicroSD to USB memory adapter.
Case for RPI (optional)
Internet connection
A computer
Patience


How to do it?
Below are the steps to get your server up and running:

Step 1 → Prepare your Raspberry Pi

For this solution, we are using a Raspberry Pi v4, but previous versions should work without any issues.
If you are starting with a new Raspberry Pi and have a plastic case, assemble the heat sink on the RPI processor and place it inside its protective case before continuing.
The Raspberry Pi developers have created a tool to facilitate the downloading, installation, and configuration of the MicroSD cards that will hold the operating system the RPI runs on.

Install the specific software for your operating system, Raspberry Pi Imager

To install it on your computer, visit www.raspberrypi.com/software/. There, you can download the version of Raspberry Pi Imager that works on your operating system (Windows, Linux, or Mac). Once you install it, you can continue with the next step.


Connect the MicroSD to your computer

Before running the Raspberry Pi Imager, you must connect the MicroSD → memory card to your computer.
To do this, you need to use a USB adapter if your device doesn’t have a slot for it.
Once you verify that the memory is detected by the computer, run the Raspberry Pi Imager and continue with the solution.

Open the Raspberry Pi Imager and choose your operating system




Step 2 → Connect and configure your Pi


Locate it in the Pi Imager

Now that our Pi is connected to power and our local network, we need to locate it so we can connect to it.
Before this, a small note: we will perform the following steps using a Terminal. If you use a Unix-type operating system (Linux, MacOS), simply search for the terminal and you can follow the steps there (see below for how to do it). If you use Windows, you can use CMD for this step, and to connect to the Pi, you can use Putty.
To locate the Pi in a Terminal, we use the ping program. This will try to send a small data packet to the address we indicate and will tell us, among other things, the IP → address of the computer.
Here we will use the name we gave our Pi, in our case solevoltaje. In the terminal, we type ping solevoltaje.local. The program responds, among other things, with the IP → 192.168.0.25, which indicates that our Pi is available for us to connect and start working.


Connect to the Pi

For the connection between your Pi and other devices to be secure, we connect to our Pi via the SSH → protocol. To do this, we type ssh solevoltaje@solevoltaje.local or use the IP address ssh solevoltaje@192.168.0.25 in our terminal.
Remember that we must place our username and domain name or IP → in the parameters we provide to SSH: ssh <username>@<domain name>.
As soon as the connection is established, the system will ask for the password. Type the same one you entered during the configuration in the previous steps and finish by pressing the enter key.

Update the software


Once we are connected to the Pi, we must perform a couple of administrative tasks. The first is to update our operating system’s software. We do this by typing the following in the terminal:
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade

Once the task of downloading and configuring the new software is finished, we can continue with the solution.

The commands we enter in this line start with sudo to have superuser permissions and be able to apply changes to the system.


Expand the SWAP


Now, it is necessary to expand the SWAP memory space so our Pi can easily handle operations that require more memory than what we have available in the RAM Memory →. Perform the following steps one after another:
First, deactivate the SWAP memory:
sudo dphys-swapfile swapoff

Then, edit the configuration file and change the size to our needs:
sudo nano /etc/dphys-swapfile

In the file, look for the line that says CONF_SWAPSIZE=100 by default and change it to CONF_SWAPSIZE=2048. Then, save and exit the text editor.
Now we need to activate the new configuration:
sudo dphys-swapfile setup

Reactivate the SWAP memory:
sudo dphys-swapfile swapon

Finally, restart the Pi so all programs have access to the new SWAP:
sudo reboot

This last command restarts the Pi, closing our remote connection. You must wait a couple of minutes for the process to complete and then reconnect via the SSH protocol to continue.

Now, install the server


After all this preparatory process, which is simpler than it seems, we proceed to install nginx, a program that will allow our Pi to function as a web server →, so we can access resources hosted there from other devices using a web browser.
Once we are connected to the Pi, we type in the terminal:
sudo apt install nginx

This line downloads, installs, and starts our server.


Step 3 → Test that the server is working correctly


Now, we test that everything is working.
To do this, on our computer, we open a web browser window and in the address bar, we type solevoltaje.local
If everything is working correctly, we should see a page like the one in the image that says Welcome to nginx.

How do you know if this solution works?
With this solution, you will manage to have a local server that allows you to host content that will be visible on the local network.
This way, you can download useful material for SOLE sessions and not need Internet access to answer the Big Questions. You can also think about loading content you would like to take to a remote place or share with other people, for example, movies, educational material, instructions, online games… or anything you can download to use with others!
Thanks to the fact that the Pi is so small, you can take it to different places and have a pocket-sized Internet.

Other possible internets
With this solution, you will have a portable server; however, it doesn’t have any information to share yet. We recommend you check out the other solutions we have in the guide so you can make the most of your new server.

Related solutions

Do you want to share your internet wirelessly? →
How to have access to an encyclopedia without having internet? →
How to use games to learn how to take care of equipment as a community? →

Remember that at Voltaje ⚡⚡ you can find many more solutions to connect without fear of using the internet as a group. Go ahead and keep browsing! See more solutions →

en/solve/solv-save-data-phone.title: How to make the most of my cell phone plan?
en/solve/solv-save-data-phone.summary: Practical tips and reflections to manage your plan so your data lasts for what matters.
en/solve/solv-save-data-phone.content:
Hi! I’m Catalina, welcome 👋🏽
Has it ever happened to you that you get a message saying your data has run out and you have no idea where it went? Well, this is the solution for you!
I’m not a tech expert, but by building on this solution that Nicolás wrote a few months ago, I started “tinkering” with my phone’s settings and discovered there are several “leaky faucets” where “our internet is draining away.” I’ve learned that with a couple of tweaks and, above all, by being more mindful of how we use our phones, we can make the same plan last much longer.
Here I’ll show you how I did it!

What does it mean to make the most of my mobile plan?
In simple terms, it’s learning to configure your phone so it only spends data on what you decide. But it goes further than that. Learning to make the most of your plan is taking control of how you use the data you pay for. Sometimes, what we need isn’t more internet, but better-used internet.
That’s why it’s important to ask ourselves a key question before we start: what do I want to spend my data on? Often, we waste it watching content we don’t even care about, just out of habit.

What is this for and what can you achieve?
This solution allows you to have real control over your spending and ensures you don’t end up disconnected halfway through the month. Ultimately, this can save you money and gives you the freedom to use your internet for what truly brings value to you and your community.

What do you need?

Your phone with an active data plan.
Patience to check and configure your phone’s settings (every phone can be quite different).
A “tinkerer’s” spirit: don’t be afraid to explore your phone’s menus!


How to do it?

⚠️ For these tricks to work, it’s best to do them while connected to a WiFi network (at a park or a neighbor’s house), so you don’t waste your own data while configuring the savings.


Step 1 → Identify who is “eating” your data

Go to your phone’s settings and look for the “Data usage” or “Mobile network” option, or something similar. There, you’ll see a list of the apps that have used the most internet over the last month.



Step 2 → Set a limit so you don’t get any surprises

In that same data menu, look for “Data limit” or “Data warning.” Set it up so your phone alerts you when you reach a daily amount (for example, 600 MB). It’s a way of telling yourself: “Watch out! You’ve already spent today’s allowance.”



Step 3 → Activate “app-by-app” savings

Go into the apps you use the most (like Instagram, Facebook, or YouTube). Look in their own settings for the “Data saver” or “Content quality” option. Turn it on so that videos DO NOT play automatically. This way, you only spend internet on the video you actually want to watch.



Recommendations

Do I really need this right now? Before opening a heavy app, ask yourself if it can wait until you’re in a free WiFi zone.
Clean up your phone: Turn off “Auto-update” for apps in the Play Store; that can eat up entire gigabytes without you even noticing.
The airplane mode trick: If you aren’t going to use your phone for a long while, turn off mobile data. You prevent the phone from wasting internet “searching” for a signal or background updates.


How do I know if this solution is working?
Other possible internets
Managing our individual data well is the first step toward thinking about a collective internet. When we stop being passive consumers of what social media pushes on us, we start using technology for what truly serves us.
Imagine if what we save individually could be pooled to pay for a community connection that belongs to everyone. Other internets are possible when we remember that the internet is a tool, not an end in itself. By taking care of your data, you are taking care of a resource that allows you to stay connected to what you love.

Recommended solutions

If you’re thinking about switching carriers, check this first: How to choose the right mobile plan? →
To see if your savings are affecting your experience: How to measure your internet speed? →
Once you’re a savings expert, teach others: Sharing internet from your phone →


References

How to make the most of your data plan - La Nación

en/solve/solv-second-life-computer.title: How to give a second life to an old computer by installing Linux?
en/solve/solv-second-life-computer.summary: Download and install Ubuntu to make your old computer fast and useful again.
en/solve/solv-second-life-computer.content:
Hi! I’m David. One of the things that frustrates me the most is seeing how a perfectly good computer becomes slow and unusable just because the operating system → (almost always Windows →) gets too heavy over the years. It’s like trying to make someone run with a backpack full of rocks. I did some digging and discovered that you don’t have to toss your gear: you can take off that heavy backpack by installing a free, lightweight system called Linux →. Here, I’ll show you how to do it step by step.

What is installing Linux → Ubuntu?
It’s changing the main program that makes your computer run. Ubuntu is one of the friendliest and easiest-to-use versions (or “flavors”) of Linux →. It completely replaces your old system with a new, free, and much lighter one.
What is it for?
It’s for reviving that old computer you have tucked away because it “doesn’t work anymore” or “is too slow.” By installing a system that requires fewer resources, the machine will turn on quickly again, you’ll be able to browse the internet → without it freezing up, and you’ll be able to use free office programs. It’s an excellent way to avoid creating electronic waste and save some cash.
Before you start…

Heads up: This process will wipe absolutely everything on your computer and the USB drive → you use. Make sure to save your photos, documents, and important files on another drive or in the cloud before you begin.

What do you need?

An old computer (that still turns on).
An empty USB drive → of at least 16GB.
An internet → connection (to download the initial files).
A bit of patience (the download and installation take some time).

How to do it?

Step 1 → Download the necessary files

To get started, you need to download two things from the internet.
First, the Linux Ubuntu installer. Go to their official website ubuntu.com and look for the “Download” section. Save the file to your computer.

Second, you need a free program called RUFUS. This program will help us put the installer onto the USB in a special way. Download it at rufus.ie/en/.


Step 2 → Prepare the USB drive

Plug your USB drive into the computer. Remember that everything on it will be erased. Open the RUFUS program you just downloaded (it doesn’t need to be installed, it just opens).

In RUFUS, make sure your USB is selected at the top. Then, click “Select” and find the Ubuntu file you downloaded in Step 1. Finally, click “Start.”


You’re doing great: Wait a few minutes for the program to finish. You’ll know it’s ready when the green bar fills up and says “READY.” Your USB is now ready to install!



Step 3 → Boot the computer from the USB


Now comes the step that scares a lot of people, but it’s simple. Turn off the old computer. Plug in the USB. When you turn it on, you need to repeatedly press a specific key (usually F12, F2, or Esc) before the old system loads, so that a Boot Menu appears.

Tip: If you don’t know which key it is, search on your phone: “How to access the boot menu on [your computer brand]“.


In this menu, use the keyboard arrows to select your USB drive (it usually has the brand name of the drive or says “USB Device”) and press Enter.

Step 4 → Start the installation

If you did it right, a black menu with white letters will appear. Select the “Try or install Ubuntu” option and press Enter.

After a few seconds, a graphical screen will appear. On the left, find and select your preferred language. Then click the big button that says “Install Ubuntu.”

The system will ask you to test your keyboard layout. Type a few letters (like the “ñ” or punctuation marks) to make sure they work correctly.


Step 5 → Erase the old disk and install Ubuntu

You will arrive at a screen that asks for the “Installation type.” To leave your computer like new and erase any trace of Windows and its issues, select “Something else” or “Erase disk and install Ubuntu” (if this direct option appears, take it).

If you used “Something else,” you will see a list of divisions (partitions) of your old hard drive →. Select them one by one and press the minus sign button (”-”) until none are left, to clean house completely.

Then, you can go back and select the recommended option: “Erase disk and install Ubuntu.” Click “Install Now.”

My suggestion is that if you haven’t backed up your disk, this is the time. My recommendation is to create a partition using the new partition button on the largest disk, leave at least 40GB for Linux, and with that, you can move files from one system to the other.



Hang in there: A warning window will pop up saying that the disks will be overwritten. It’s normal to be scared, but it’s just the system confirming that you are sure about erasing everything old. Click “Continue.”



Step 6 → Set up your user and location

The system will ask where you are to set the correct time. Click on the map and press continue.

A button will appear; look for Bogotá (Colombia) or your country’s capital to get the local time.


Now, choose a name for your computer, your username, and a password. Don’t forget it! This password is your key to the machine. You can choose whether you want it to ask for it every time you turn on the computer or to log in automatically.


Step 7 → Finish and restart

Now all that’s left is to wait. The system will copy all the necessary files. You can make yourself a coffee while you look at the images showing you what new things the system brings.


You’re doing great: When everything finishes, a message will appear saying “Installation complete.” Click “Restart now.”


The screen will go black and will ask you, in English, to remove the installation medium (“Please remove the installation medium, then press ENTER”).

Take out your USB drive and press Enter.


And that’s it! Your computer will turn on with its new system, fresh, clean, and fast.

Recommendations if you get stuck

If your computer doesn’t recognize the USB and always starts in Windows, check if you have an option called “Secure Boot” enabled on your computer (on the same screen where you entered the Boot Menu). Sometimes you have to disable it to install new systems.
If you see that Ubuntu is still a bit slow for your computer (because it’s suuuper old), there are even lighter versions like Lubuntu or Xubuntu. The installation process is exactly the same.

How to know if this solution works?
When you turn on the computer without the USB drive connected, you will no longer see the Windows logo. Instead, you will see the Ubuntu logo and will quickly arrive at a clean and functional desktop where you can connect to the internet and browse without issues.
Other possible internets
You will be able to make equipment that people thought was broken or obsolete available to the community. By not depending on expensive licenses or needing the latest Processor (CPU) → on the market, any group can set up a small computer lab by recycling technology that others discard. It’s an act of technological independence.
Recommended solutions

How to choose a good computer for the community? →
How to share internet from your computer to others? →

References

Installation guide video (YouTube): Ubuntu Installation Tutorial

You’ve already given that computer a new chance to be useful. Sometimes, things just need us to look at them from another perspective to shine again.

en/solve/solv-share-computers.title: How to share available computers?
en/solve/solv-share-computers.summary: Discover how powerful it is to use the Internet in a group.
en/solve/solv-share-computers.content:
Sole Colombia
Hi, I’m Sanjay. For the last ten years, I’ve been doing SOLE, and I’ve brought SOLE Colombia to where it is today. For years, I’ve seen how many devices end up gathering dust in school closets, or are barely used because the person in charge thinks there are too many strict rules to follow.
What is sharing available computers and managing their loan?
With this solution, I want to focus on the importance of using the Internet → as a group. It’s a completely different experience: it’s about sharing devices, which opens the door for us to walk the paths of the Internet together. You’ll have the chance to get hands-on with the devices we all use and look after—they are the gateway to living better together while using the Internet.
What is it for?
Sharing computers is a win-win for everyone. We don’t need as much money to buy or maintain them because we can split the cost among more people, and more people get to benefit from using them, too.
When we share computers and use them together, they become a safe space to learn and do things as a team: that’s how we look after the spaces we enter, avoid dangerous or inappropriate websites by watching out for each other, better understand the information we’re reviewing by discussing it, find common interests, and interact with each other instead of just with the machines… we turn technology into a playground where we can all hang out. SOLE is the perfect tool to share your computers with an interesting, common purpose: solving Big Questions. Want to know how? Come on in and find out at SoleColombia
What do you need?

Computers to share.
A place with electricity.
Generosity.

How to do it?


Step 1: Manage the computers
The first thing we need is the computers to share; we can find these in a public library or a school. There are usually government programs that provide these computers, and often they just sit there unused because people don’t know how to access them.
Once you identify the place, look for the person in charge—they’ll be the key to your success. Tell them about your goal for using the computers, like doing a SOLE session or anything else. Also, mention how hard or impossible it is for your community to have access to their own computers. Then, set a date and time for when you’ll come with your community so that both sides are committed.

Photo: Sole Colombia


Step 2: Agree on some ground rules for sharing
Now that the place and the computers are secured, gather your community and talk about the arrangements you made so they can see the legwork involved and share the responsibility with you. Then, talk about the basic care needed and ask them if they can think of other ways to look after the equipment. Remember, this first time will be decisive in whether they keep lending you computers in the future or not.

Photo: Sole Colombia


Step 3: Let’s share!
Contact the person in charge of the library or public space and head over with your crew to enjoy using the internet as a group. Always remember to enjoy the devices in a shared way—for example, you can have 4 people sitting at the same computer.


How do you know if this solution works?
This solution is a series of recommendations that give you a roadmap to more easily manage computers in a public space to share with your community.
Other possible Internets
This solution won’t get you computers permanently, and in places with little government presence, you might not find places that will lend you these computers.

en/solve/solv-share-internet-cellphone.title: How to share the Internet from my cell phone?
en/solve/solv-share-internet-cellphone.summary: Configure and share your phone's internet with others.
en/solve/solv-share-internet-cellphone.content:
Hi! This solution was written by Nicolás, one of the tech-savvy folks—or cacharreros—at SOLE Colombia.
I’m Belén, and I’m reviewing it. Even though I love tinkering with tech, sometimes I find it hard to understand how things work. I guess I’ve got a few years on me and everything changes so fast… when I started using computers, they were basically just typewriters. But not anymore! I encourage you to lose the fear and just dive in!
What is setting up a personal WiFi → hotspot?
Did you know your smartphone has a nearly permanent connection to the Internet? Usually, your cell phone plan comes with a data package that lets you get online.
That connection can sometimes get slow or glitchy, and it needs a refresh. But you might also want to share it with others—want to know how? Keep reading.
What is it for?
You might want to share your data plan’s Internet signal with other people. But it can also happen that, even with an Internet connection, the pages you want to open load with difficulty, or your data call connection isn’t working well.
Almost always, the best way to get everything back up and running is to restart everything from scratch.
Once you’ve restarted, you’ll be able to share your phone’s Internet signal to do a SOLE with your community!
What do you need?

A cell phone.
Enough data on your phone to share with others.
A generous spirit.

How to do it?

Step 1 → Restart your data connection**

Swipe down from the top of your phone to access the control panel. Once there, select the “Mobile data” option, turn it off for a few seconds, and turn it back on. Wait a moment for the phone to reconnect to the cellular network, and that’s it! Your connection will be fresh and working properly.

Want another trick? Turn on airplane mode; that will force all your phone’s settings related to the Internet signal to reset.



Step 2: Set up your mobile hotspot**

Go to settings and look for **"Mobile hotspot"** or just **"Hotspot"**.

In this menu, look for the option to **"Configure mobile hotspot"**. You'll see several details; for now, we only care about setting the name of the [[en/glossary/conc-wifi|WiFi signal →]] you're creating and the access password.

Once you've changed them, tap the checkmark (or the save button) to save the new settings.




Step 3: Share the internet
Swipe down from the top of your phone to access the control panel, where you can find the “Mobile Hotspot” option or something similar.
Just turn it on to share the Internet signal with whoever you want.
If you want to do a SOLE, this is an excellent solution to make sure all the computers can perform their searches. You know that at SOLE Colombia, we are always thinking about how to make the most of the resources we have individually to help our communities improve their Internet experience… there’s nothing like using it as a group!



How do I know if this solution works?
With this recipe, you can reset your phone’s cellular network settings. This will improve browsing speed and connection stability. You’ll be able to share it with other phones and/or computers and search the Internet for the answers to the Big Questions that drive your SOLE.
Other possible Internets
Restarting the cellular network connection will improve your connection and you’ll be able to browse a bit faster, but the geographic area where you are must have coverage from your provider.
This recipe won’t work if the phone signal in your area is poor. Learning to share the internet will be a very important step for when you manage to get computers, as it’s easier to use the internet in a group with larger screens.

en/solve/solv-share-internet-computer.title: How to share internet from your computer?
en/solve/solv-share-internet-computer.summary: Turn your computer into an Internet router.
en/solve/solv-share-internet-computer.content:
Hi! I’m Catalina, welcome to this solution 👋🏽
The first version of this solution was written by a colleague, Nicolás, and I’ve added a few finishing touches so we can walk through it together.
This, like other solutions, is designed so that anyone can do it. I’m no tech expert, and I managed to pull it off! So, shall we dive in and give it a go? Remember, if you have any questions, you can join the Cacharreras Community →, where we help each other out with our connectivity (and connection) together.
What is sharing Internet from your computer?
In short, it means setting up your computer to turn it into an internet router →, which is basically a device capable of distributing an Internet signal to other gadgets. It’s similar to when you use your phone to share your internet →.

What is it for?
Sometimes we’re in places where we only have an Internet connection on one computer and we don’t know the Wi-Fi → password. How do we make the most of that single connection point? With this solution, we can turn THAT computer into an access point or “hotspot” for everyone.

What do you need?

A computer (ideally connected to the Internet via an Ethernet → cable).
Cell phones or other devices without Internet access.
Patience.


How to do it?

Step 0 → How do I know if my computer works for this solution?

Any computer will work if its Internet connection is via cable, meaning not through a Wi-Fi network. Even older computers can become high-powered routers by tweaking a few settings in their operating system →, but they do require a wired connection.
If your computer isn’t connected by cable and it’s a newer model, it might still work: for a computer to function as a router by receiving and distributing a signal via Wi-Fi, its wireless network card needs a capability called Monitor Mode. The easiest way to find out if your computer has this card is the good old-fashioned “tinkerer’s” way: just try it out!
So, let’s get started! 👇🏽


Step 1 → Go to your computer’s Internet settings

⚠️⚠️ Keep in mind that Nicolás wrote this solution using a very popular operating system in Colombia: Windows 10. If you have a different operating system, your screen might look a bit different, but the idea is the same.
To start, select the Start button (the Windows symbol button). In the settings window, look for the following options: Settings > Network & Internet > Mobile hotspot (click through each option to find the next one).




Step 2 → Activate and configure the Internet zone.

When you’re in the hotspot window, turn on the option to share your internet with other devices. In the image below 👇🏽, you can see that you can share Internet via Wi-Fi or Bluetooth. Handy, right?



Step 3 → Connect other people!

You’re all set to share your Internet with others! In the “Mobile hotspot” window, you’ll find the network name and the password. If you want to change them, you can do so using the “Edit” button.

How do I know if this solution is working?
On another device (computer, phone, tablet, etc.), turn on the Wi-Fi search (or Bluetooth if you chose to share that way). If you find the network you set up on your computer, you’re halfway there.
Now, connect that other device to the network. If you can browse the web, it means you did it!

Other possible Internets
With this solution, you can provide Internet access to more devices in one place without needing the password for the original network. If you share with other devices, more people will be able to get online. This alternative allows you to share Internet with up to 8 devices and is geographically limited to the range of the network generated by the computer.
After that, you can encourage group Internet use to learn how to solve challenges as a community 💪🏽🛠️ .

Related solutions

You can test how good the connection is while using your computer as a modem by measuring the Internet speed: How to check your Internet connection speed? →
To use the Internet in a group, you need… people. Who’s up for working with you on a topic? This solution can help you invite people: How to write an invitation that gets people together? →
How you organize the space is key to encouraging group Internet use; here we tell you how you can do it: How to set up a space for group Internet use? →

en/solve/solv-share-internet-wirelessly.title: Do you want to share your internet wirelessly?
en/solve/solv-share-internet-wirelessly.content:
Set up your Raspberry Pi
Share your pocket internet
Hi, I’m Gabriel. I’m an artist. I find digital devices, how they work, and the way we humans interact with them fascinating. I consider myself a tinkerer, and I invite you, if you’d like, to be one too.
I wrote the solution Raspberry Pi: A little pocket internet so you could set it up, and now, I’m here to help you share your device’s signal with other people or other devices.
What does it mean to share your Raspberry Pi’s internet?
Having a computer the size of a credit card, being able to connect it to the Internet, and on top of that, being able to share that connection with the other computers you have for doing SOLE, is like opening the doors to the world’s largest library!
It’s turning any space into a Self-Organized Learning Environment where you can open the doors to the creativity needed to solve challenges—complex or simple—in your community. INCREDIBLE, right?
To do SOLE, there are only three fundamental things: people, a few computers with an internet connection, and Big Questions.
What is it for?
With this recipe, you will be able to turn your Raspberry Pi → into a portable Router, so your community can connect wirelessly and access the information hosted there, and if you have a wired Internet connection, you can share that too.
What do you need?

A Raspberry Pi
A computer
Internet connection - you can check the solution How to know what type of Internet signal you have? to make sure what kind of connection you have and if it’s active
Lots of patience

How to do it?

Moment 1: Connect to your Pi
First things first, make sure you have a working Raspberry Pi. If you need help with this, check out the recipe Raspberry Pi: A little pocket internet where we tell you how to get started with this device.
Once you have your system up and running, connect to your Raspberry Pi via a Terminal → by starting an SSH → connection.
Make sure you have an Internet connection to continue with the following steps.
Moment 2: Update your Raspberry Pi system


The first step is to perform a system-wide update to ensure we have the latest versions of the programs running on our Pi.
To do this, just type the following into the terminal:
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade

The system will let us know which packages need to be updated. To continue with the process, we must accept by typing y and pressing the enter key.

Moment 3: Install the necessary software


Next, we need to install two programs on our Pi:
sudo apt install -y hostapd dnsmasq

This command will install hostapd, which is a utility that allows us to use our Pi’s wireless as a wireless access point, and dnsmasq, which will allow us to set up a server → DNS → and DHCP → to allow users to connect to the server → and get the necessary network settings to access it.

Moment 4: Configure a static IP
Disable the wireless interface


In this step, we will configure a static IP address on our Pi’s wireless interface. It is important that you are not connected wirelessly to the Pi, because during the following steps, wireless communication will be suspended. So, make sure you are connected via a cable, or have a screen and keyboard connected directly to the Pi to continue.
Network settings on the Pi are handled by the dhcpcd program; it is responsible for requesting and assigning the necessary IP addresses for the available network interfaces. Right now, we have to tell this program to ignore the wireless interface. To do this, we must edit the configuration file:
sudo nano /etc/dhcpcd.conf

… and at the end of it, add this line:
denyinterfaces wlan0

To exit and save the changes, press ctrl + x followed by y when prompted.

Assign a static IP


Now we must assign a static IP address to the wlan0 interface in a different range than our wired network. Let’s edit the file:
sudo nano /etc/network/interfaces

Don’t be afraid. It looks complex, but if you’ve made it this far, you’re almost there. Add the following to the end:
allow-hotplug wlan0
iface wlan0 inet static
    address 192.168.10.1
    netmask 255.255.255.0
    network 192.168.10.0
    broadcast 192.168.10.255

What we are doing is configuring this interface to have the IP 192.168.10.1.
To exit and save the changes, press ctrl + x followed by y when prompted.

Moment 5: Configure our wireless access point


It’s time to tell hostapd how to operate. We are going to tell it to broadcast the network name (SSID) and operate on a specific channel. We will put these settings in the file:
sudo nano /etc/hostapd/hostapd.conf

… where we add the following data:
interface=wlan0
driver=nl80211
ssid=SOLEVOLTAJE
hw_mode=g
channel=11
ieee80211n=1
wmm_enabled=1
ht_capab=[HT40][SHORT-GI-20][DSSS_CCK-40]
macaddr_acl=0
auth_algs=1
ignore_broadcast_ssid=0
wpa=2
wpa_key_mgmt=WPA-PSK
wpa_passphrase=LACONTRASENADEACCESO
rsn_pairwise=CCMP

You can change a few things here:

The network name: we configure this on the ssid= line; in our example, the network will be called SOLEVOLTAJE.
The channel: channel=11 is saying we are going to operate on channel 11, but we can change it to whichever works best in our location.
The access password: for security, it is necessary to assign a key to connect to the network. We do this by assigning it on the wpa_passphrase=LACONTRASENADEACCESO line.

Now we must inform hostapd where the configuration is located. We do this by editing the file:
sudo nano /etc/default/hostapd

… and adding the following line to it:
DAEMON_CONF=


Moment 6: Start the services

Before restarting our Pi, we must enable the services so they run every time we turn it on.
To do this, type the following into the terminal:
sudo systemctl unmask hostapd
sudo systemctl enable hostapd
sudo systemctl start hostapd

sudo systemctl unmask dnsmasq
sudo systemctl enable dnsmasq
sudo systemctl start dnsmasq

… and finally, we restart the Pi to do our first test:
sudo reboot now


Moment 7: Do a first test


From another computer or phone, search the wireless networks for the one we just created, in our case SOLEVOLTAJE, and connect to it.
If you check the network settings, you should see that the assigned IP address is in the range we selected in the dnsmasq configuration. In our case, the device has been assigned the IP 192.168.10.143.


Moment 8: You can now share the wired connection


At this point, those who connect to our access point will be able to see the files and services we have configured on our Raspberry Pi. If you want to share the wired Internet connection via the wireless network, continue with the following steps.

Moment 9: Forward traffic to the wired connection


It is necessary for our system to forward traffic from the wireless interface to the wired one in order to share the connection. At this point, we have to edit the file:
sudo nano /etc/sysctl.conf

In its content, we look for the line that says #net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 and remove the # at the beginning to indicate that we want to activate this directive. Once we make this change, we save the file and continue to the next step.

Moment 10: Finally, secure the Firewall


We are now at the last step of the configuration. Here we have to tell the Firewall → to allow network traffic to pass between the wireless and wired interfaces. To do this, enter these commands into our terminal:
sudo iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -o eth0 -j MASQUERADE
sudo iptables -A FORWARD -i eth0 -o wlan0 -m state --state RELATED,ESTABLISHED -j ACCEPT
sudo iptables -A FORWARD -i wlan0 -o eth0 -j ACCEPT

At this point, we should already have internet on our wireless clients! However, we need to make sure these changes aren’t lost when we restart our Pi. To do this, we are going to save the configuration in a text file:
sudo sh -c "iptables-save > /etc/iptables.ipv4.nat"


Moment 11: Now, with Internet!


After this long process, the clients connected to our Pi will be able to access the Internet connection shared from our Raspberry Pi… SUCCESS!
Did you get tangled up in any of the steps? Tell us how to complete this solution to make it clearer.
Other possible internets
With this recipe, you can set up a portable Router, which is useful for carrying content on your Raspberry Pi and sharing it with the community without needing a constant Internet connection.
Additionally, if you have a wired connection, you can share it to make your SOLE sessions more powerful.
Why might this solution work?
Having a portable, low-power router allows us to easily take our content to multiple places where the Internet connection is not constant.
However, the number of clients our Pi can support is low. If you are going to connect more than 10 people at the same time, the connection speed might get a bit slow, and to solve that, you should look for a more powerful router.
If you made it this far, you’ve learned a ton of things that you can share with your community and, in doing so, improve connectivity conditions. Using the Internet as a group is a challenging experience, both in terms of technology and in terms of community. Doing SOLE is a way to use the Internet as a group to live better together.

en/solve/solv-sole-tv.title: "How to use television for group learning?"
en/solve/solv-sole-tv.summary: Turn your community television into a space for dialogue and learning with SOLE TV.
en/solve/solv-sole-tv.content:
Hey there! It’s such a joy to greet you all here. I’ve always believed that television doesn’t have to be just a box that talks at us; it can be a window for us to listen to one another. It happened to me that while watching shows, I’d ask myself: “What if we could answer back, too?“. I’ve learned that when we get together to tinker with the media we already have—like the neighborhood or town channel—magical things happen. I’m no expert in big-budget productions, but I am an expert at sparking good conversations, and today I want to share how you can turn the TV into a giant, fun classroom. Go for it, curiosity is the best engine!

What is SOLE TV?
It’s a proposal to transform television into a Self-Organized Learning Environment (SOLE). It consists of creating television content built by asking the audience to answer a Big Question and then inviting people to send in their responses to share them on a live show. It’s a way for everyone to end up learning together, turning a traditional medium into a network of shared knowledge.

What is it for?
Imagine if you could transform television into a space for communication and learning that doesn’t just go from the channel to the audience, but where the audience participates in creating the TV content and everyone ends up learning together. For places where the internet signal doesn’t reach, or if part of the audience cannot access the internet, using television can extend the reach, especially so that children and young people can navigate and connect to the web.
So, if you have a mass-market or community television channel, you can generate a Self-Organized Learning Environment or SOLE via TV. This allows people in the community, whether they have internet or not, to learn and dialogue through television around Big Questions.
Doing a SOLE TV means creating a new type of television content that is built by asking the audience to answer a Big Question and then inviting people to send in responses to share them on a show. Having many responses allows us to generate a conversation, live, where we are all experts because we build the knowledge together… just like the Internet!

Before you start…
To make your television show a safe and exciting space, remember that coordination is key. You don’t need to be an expert producer, but you do need a lot of willingness to organize the voices of your community.

Attention: Make sure you have the broadcasting permits from the community channel and, if you are going to film minors on the street, always ask for their parents’ consent.


What do you need?
To set up your SOLE TV, gather these tools and get ready with the best energy:

A television channel (mass-market, community, or internet-based).
A host with lots of energy, spark, and listening skills.
An audience willing to participate (at least 2 people to start the chat).
A fixed time slot for the show (you can call it SOLE TV).
Internet access and/or social media to receive responses (optional).
A video recorder or cell phone to capture voices on the street (optional).
TV host energy.
Lots of curiosity and a desire to learn from what others say.
Patience to organize the responses that come in.


How to do it?

Step 1 → Define the Big Question and the show date


Sole Colombia
BIG QUESTION: Define a Big Question that motivates self-organized learning using the available media. The Big Question will be what hooks the audience into participating in this SOLE TV. It should be something that invites investigation and cannot be answered with a simple yes or no.
LIVE SHOW DATE: Define a date so the audience can participate and watch the show; you should call for responses to the Big Question about 15 days in advance to give everyone time to research.


Step 2 → Invite the audience to answer it


Sole Colombia
CALL TO ACTION: Broadcast the Big Question through messages or short commercials on the channel, inviting the audience to answer it via an online form, social media comments, calling the channel, or recording on the street. In the invitation or online form, include the date of the live show and request contact information from those responding so you can reach them directly. Some people might have social media like WhatsApp or Facebook to participate through those means. Others could participate by calling the channel directly or participating in person at the station. You could also collect responses on the street, recording them with video equipment or a cell phone.


Step 3 → Plan the live show


Pexels
SHOW SCRIPT: While you receive the responses to the Big Question, you can organize a simple show rundown and audiovisual bumpers to accompany the live broadcast. For a 1-hour show, it’s worth thinking about how to present the question, invite between 2 and 5 people to give their answers live, and select other audience responses to share.
Prepare a simple script with these moments:

Bumper, greeting, and introduction of guests.
Presentation of the Big Question.
First round of responses (guests and audience).
Invitation to participate via social media or phone.
New questions to dig deeper.
Second round of responses.
Conclusion, thanks, and congratulations on the autonomous learning.



Step 4 → Broadcast the live show


Sole Colombia
SOLE TV: Broadcast a live show using the script as a reference, but allowing for an unstructured conversation combined with other pre-recorded audience responses and/or social media input to solve the Big Question together. Guests can research beforehand. You can also invite people to the show who have knowledge about the answer to share it in the space, or people who are good conversationalists to stir up a great discussion. The host or participants can dig deeper with new questions that arise.

Recommendations

Value every response: It doesn’t matter if the answer is short or simple; what’s valuable is the act of participating and building together.
Keep it flowing: If the host notices a topic is stalling, they can throw out a “provocative question” to revive the chat.
Use what you have: If there is no internet for a form, use a physical ballot box in the town square to collect written responses.


How to know if this solution works?
To verify the success of your SOLE TV, you can observe these technical and social points:

Increased participation: Did you receive responses from people who don’t usually participate in the channel? Did messages arrive from distant rural areas?
Citizen interaction: Managing to transform television into a Self-Organized Learning Environment (SOLE) and a space for citizen interaction allows communities to learn and dialogue. If you see people still discussing the question at the store or the market, it’s working!
Sense of belonging: Does the audience suggest new questions for the next show? That means they already feel like owners of the space.


Other possible internets
Television is a very powerful medium because many people can access it for free. Especially for many children and young people, it may be the only communication device they have access to. It will never be the same as having access to the Internet, as the internet is the largest library in the world. However, television also allows you to connect with many people; the rest lies in them being able to dialogue with the television to learn together. This is what SOLE TV does: turn a mass medium into a bridge of solidarity and shared knowledge.

Related solutions

To learn how to organize the internet that will be used to receive the show’s responses. [How to organize a neighborhood internet →] acordar-con-un-vecino-voltaje-desconectado.md →
A fundamental tool for the community to learn how to take care of their equipment while waiting for the next episode. [How to use games to learn how to take care of equipment →] como-usar-el-juego-para-aprender-a-cuidar-equipos-en-comunidad-solutions-db.md →

en/solve/solv-spread-message.title: How to spread a message?
en/solve/solv-spread-message.summary: Reach the hearts of the people moved by your message.
en/solve/solv-spread-message.content:
Hey there! Manu here. Today I want to share some powerful techniques you can use to get your message out to more people and create a positive impact in your community.
What does it mean to spread your message?
When it comes to spreading a message that really matters to us, we want to make sure it reaches as many people as possible, and that those people actually respond to our call.
In this solution, I’ll share some strategies so you can test which medium is the best fit for getting your message across.

What is it for?
Knowing how to best spread your message will allow you to reach your audience more efficiently. You’ll be able to reach a wider audience, one more specialized in what you want to tell them, and you’ll be able to inform, spread, and inspire… in the best way possible!
Having others appreciate the value and importance of what you’re saying is tied to how you spread it, so if you want to “reach people better” and make more strategic decisions, you need to…

What do you need?

Colored paper and/or poster board.
Colored pencils, markers, and felt-tip pens.
A computer or smartphone → with internet access to send messages via WhatsApp.
Comfortable shoes to connect with the community in person.
A good dose of enthusiasm and authenticity.


How to do it?


Moment 0: Define what you want to say and what you want your audience to do
To define your message in detail, you can review the Create a powerful message solution, where you can define exactly what you want to spread and the purpose of your communication.
Now, to know if your outreach is powerful, you need to include a key aspect in your message: the call to action. This refers to the specific action you are asking the person to take once they have received your message, which will confirm to you that it has indeed reached them.
For example, a call to action could be “sign up on the list below.” As soon as you see a series of names written down, you’ll know your message has been spread effectively. In digital media, you can use reactions (emojis, comments) to see if people are viewing your content, or design some other way to get people to interact with you and confirm that your message reached them.


Moment 1: First things first, who is your target audience? Who do you want to reach?
You need to think about your audience before deciding which channel to use to transmit your message. You can adapt to different media; the important thing is that the message reaches the person you want to reach.
Keep in mind that if you have partnered with a place that draws a crowd (you can check out the solution How to partner with places that draw a crowd?), your partner might already know the people they are good at bringing together very well. If so, let your partner advise you and learn from how they do things!
If you are already clear about who you want to invite or call upon with your message, a good tactic is to use the communication channels most used by those people.


💡 For example, if your target audience is young people between 18 and 25 interested in technology, platforms like WhatsApp and other social networks could be effective channels to reach them.
Activity:

Describe your target audience on a sheet of paper and ask yourself: what do the people you want to reach do? How old are they? What do they like to do?
Draw the communication media those people would normally use: do they use social media? Do they read newspapers? Do they listen to community radio?
Underline the winning media on your list.


Done! When you finish this exercise, you’ll know that the media listed on your sheet are the ones you should focus on to transmit your message.

Moment 2: Second, define the channel — how are you going to reach them?
Digital dissemination channels

WhatsApp, Instagram, email, Facebook, phone—it doesn’t matter which one. What matters is that they are accessible media for your audience, that is, the people you want to call or reach.
In Colombia, WhatsApp is used a lot to send messages. I invite you to exploit all the resources it has: send voice notes, messages, photos, make a group, you can even create polls to decide what time works best for all your guests to participate.
Here is an example of what an invitation sent via WhatsApp could look like:


Analog dissemination channels

Create posters and flyers
Put up posters and flyers that convey your message in strategic places. Go to the places where your community gathers, like local shops or community centers.
You can also knock on your neighbors’ doors and hand them the invitation in person.
Here I share some posters we put up in shops to invite the Boca de Camarones community to build The Library of the Future:

Hit the streets
Time to put on your most comfortable shoes and go out to win over the community!
Go to the places where the people in your community, or their leaders, gather… Give yourself the chance to jump in and talk to strangers; it’s your time to shine!
When you approach people, tell them why your activity is so important.
Listen carefully and show genuine interest in what they say. Build authentic connections and make new friends while sharing your passion.
Every conversation is an opportunity to learn and make the impact of your activity even greater!


Moment 3: Seek help from others, there is strength in numbers

By joining forces with others, we multiply our impact. Team up with your peers, community leaders, friends, and family who share your values and goals. Invite them to join in and infect them with your message so they can replicate it; that way, you ensure your activity is on everyone’s lips.
Seek support from organizations, community radio stations, local media, schools, or community action boards committed to your cause or activity. Approach their spaces, share the importance of your activity, and provide the details of your call, such as dates and times, clearly. They will surely be able to help you replicate the call.
Remember, word-of-mouth is key to expanding your impact. Work as a team and make your message reach more people!

Moment 4: Receive responses and evaluate the success of your campaign

Remember we talked about the call to action earlier? Are the people you directed the message to doing what you asked them to do? Bravo! Then you did succeed in spreading your message.
Evaluate the reception and impact of your message—everything counts! For example, the hearts people give your message on WhatsApp, the comments, or the messages you’ve received hearing the direct response from someone in your community.
How to know if this solution is working?
It is important that you monitor how your message reaches your audience. To know this, sometimes it is enough to ask what they thought, if it reached them with enough clarity, and if they felt the way you carried out the dissemination was relevant and sufficient.
There are some indicators you can use to evaluate the proper dissemination of a message:

If you have been able to deliver it and someone has received it.
If any of the calls to action have had an effect.
If other people received the message, even if they weren’t the ones you initially targeted.
If you receive good feedback.

Other possible Internets
If you aren’t getting the responses you expect, or something in the dissemination doesn’t seem to be working well, it’s time to review.
Make sure your message:

Has relevant content; focus on your audience (there are some important considerations below).
Is focused on a target audience.
Is a well-written message; check the grammar, spelling, and syntax, and make sure it’s easy to understand.
That the way you send it is aligned with your audience (time, day of the week, the medium you use to spread it…).
It is important to be respectful, both with people’s data and with the way and time we communicate things; keep that in mind.

Communication is a living process; you can review it as many times as you want, and each time you will do it better. The more you practice, the better and more easily you will be able to create powerful messages and spread them more efficiently and effectively.
Remember that together we can achieve great things!
Write to us at @sole_colombia and, if you need it, we can help you get more reach on social media.
Dare to share your initiatives! Make your message reach everyone in the community!

en/solve/solv-tricks-mobile-signal.title: Three tricks to improve your mobile signal
en/solve/solv-tricks-mobile-signal.summary: With a few adjustments, you can increase your mobile signal strength.
en/solve/solv-tricks-mobile-signal.content:
Hi! I’m Sanjay, and I’d like to welcome you to SOLE Voltaje. I’m no connectivity expert, but knowing a few tricks to boost my signal has made my life a whole lot easier, and I’m going to help you discover them too. I’d love it if, by the end, you could tell me if this solution worked for you, if it helped, and how it made you feel. Let’s get to it!
What does it mean to boost your mobile signal in a space?
Boosting your phone’s mobile signal means that, with a few tweaks, you can increase the strength of the signal your phone receives and transmits, which improves the quality and reliability of your connection.

What is it for?
Can’t hear the other person, or do your calls keep dropping? Are you about to start a SOLE and the pages won’t load or your search is crawling? You can hunt for a stronger signal for your phone to get better service and speed up your SOLE sessions. Here, you’ll find some simple tricks to improve your mobile connection at home and make collaborative learning in your community a breeze.

What do you need?

Smartphone →
Mobile data connection


How to do it?

Step 1 → Change rooms
If you’re at home, try different rooms to find the best signal. Think about where the cell tower might be and what kind of building materials could be blocking your connection. Find that sweet spot to boost your signal.



Step 2 → Take off your phone case
Get rid of any barriers that might be messing with your signal. Some poorly designed cases can block the antenna, so take it off and see if your reception improves. Sometimes, the best solution is the simplest one.



Step 3 → Toggle Airplane Mode on and off
Give your phone a quick breather. Forcing it to search for networks by turning Airplane Mode on and off can be super helpful, especially after you’ve moved to a new spot. This step helps your phone automatically pick the best signal available.


How do you know if this solution is working?
By following these steps, you’re essentially resetting and fine-tuning your mobile connection settings. This won’t just boost your browsing experience; it’ll also make it easier to share that signal with other devices during your SOLE sessions.

Other possible Internets
Resetting your connection is a great way to improve your signal’s speed and stability. However, keep in mind that signal quality also depends on the coverage in your area. These tricks will help you explore the Internet faster, but you do need to be in a zone with decent carrier coverage!
Remember, for communities that are pros at SOLE, having a solid connection is key. Learning how to share your Internet is a big step toward future sessions with computers, making group learning on bigger screens much easier. Sharing your connection is the first step toward an even more enriching SOLE! 📶✨

en/solve/solv-type-internet-signal.title: How to know what type of WiFi signal your router emits?
en/solve/solv-type-internet-signal.summary: Learn how the internet reaches your device.
en/solve/solv-type-internet-signal.content:
Hi, I’m Belén. I’m no internet expert; in fact, I’m starting to feel a bit old and there’s a lot about connectivity that goes over my head. If you feel the same way, this information will shed some light on things. If you don’t feel like me, but want to better understand the differences between signals and how they relate to how your devices work, this info will clear up your doubts.
What does it mean to know the type of signal your device has?
Internet signals can be classified in several ways. At SOLE Colombia, we’ve chosen this classification based on the medium through which the signals are transmitted.
For now, the existing signals are:

Cable signal, the fastest and most stable

Fiber optic: uses pulsed light to transmit data through special cables. It is the fastest and most stable type of signal known.
Coaxial cable →: transmits data through copper cables (the same ones used for cable TV).
DSL (Digital Subscriber Line): uses telephone lines to transmit data. It’s less fast, but it uses a network that has been around for a long time, so it already reaches many places and doesn’t need a new installation.


Wireless signal, which connects through the air and needs signal repeaters

Wi-Fi (Wireless Fidelity): uses radio waves, in different standards, to broadcast the signal to the devices that make up its network.
Mobile network (3G/4G/5G): uses the infrastructure of mobile phone signals to provide internet access and operates on a specific wave spectrum. The difference between them has to do with speed; 3G is the slowest and oldest, 5G the fastest and most recent. Some devices on the market weren’t built to support 5G, and it’s not available in many places around the world because the necessary developments to detect the wave spectrum haven’t been rolled out yet. Just between us, 5G technology still raises some concerns regarding data security, and the lack of spectrum regulation limits the developments needed to incorporate it worldwide 🫢


Satellite, which travels through space and needs a satellite dish

GEO, or based on geostationary orbit satellites: they are very far from Earth and provide greater stability, making them ideal for remote areas. You might recognize names like Viasat and HughesNet, which are providers of this technology.
LEO, or based on low Earth orbit satellites: they are closer to Earth, between 500 and 2000 km. They are faster compared to GEO, but require more devices to provide coverage to the same area. You might recognize names of providers for this service: Starlink, OneWeb, Amazon Kuiper, and Telesat Lightspeed.
MEO, or based on medium Earth orbit satellites: they are located between LEO and GEO and are the least common. The commercialization of this type of connection has been aimed at sectors like navigation (GPS) and high-end business services, so they aren’t as visible to the average end-user.



Depending on the type of device you have, you will have access to different possible sources of internet signal. Below you can see what type of signal each device allows:
Devices and signals:















































DeviceWiredWifiMobileSatelliteComputerSomeAllNoneNoneTabletNoneAllSomeNoneCell phoneNoneAllAllNoneSmart TVSomeAllNoneNoneIOT (Internet of Things)SomeAllNoneNone
What is this for?
Sometimes I get overwhelmed by error messages on electronic gadgets, and I get so frustrated when the device doesn’t respond! However, I’ve learned a lot. Among other things, that some internet signals work better than others, and also that some devices work better than others with different signals. I hope this information helps you better understand this connectivity stuff and helps you use your electronic devices better.
What do you need?

Your device, where you want to check the type of signal you have
Curiosity

How to do it?
How to know if you have a cable signal?
Having a cable internet service guarantees that you are getting 100% of the signal your provider gives you. If you have an ethernet cable → connected to your computer, you should have a cable signal.

What to do if the connection doesn’t work?

Check the lights on the Router →: look for the ones that indicate the Ethernet connection (they are usually green/orange and blink when there is activity). If they are red or not lit, check the power connection. You can restart the router and start over; it almost always works.
Verify the connection on the device: check the connection status in your equipment’s settings; it should confirm if you are connected.
Check the Ethernet cable: check if it is well connected, both at the router and your device, and that it is in good condition.
If nothing works, contact your service provider.



How to know if you have a Wi-Fi signal?
Looking at the WiFi icon 🛜 is the fastest way to check your connection: the more bars that are colored, the better your signal. If the icon has an alert sign, it means there is a problem or it is unavailable. If the icon is disabled or has a line through it, it means it is turned off and you need to turn it on.

What to do if the connection doesn’t work?

Access Wi-Fi settings: from your device’s settings, you can access the available networks. If one of them appears as “connected,” you are connected to that network. If you don’t see “connected” on any of them, you might need to choose one and enter a password, or the signal might be weak. You can try turning the router off and on again, and the computer too; often this works to reset all the information and start from scratch. Putting the device in ‘airplane mode’ also helps.
Check signal strength: in the device settings, you can check how strong the signal is for each available network. Moving closer to the router or removing obstacles between you can improve the signal.
If nothing works, contact your service provider; there might be an error in the configuration.



How to know if you have a mobile signal?
Look at the top corner of your cell phone. You will find some mobile signal bars 📶: if you see one or more bars, the phone is receiving a signal and reading your SIM card →. You can also confirm this in your phone’s settings and check the signal strength.

What to do if the connection doesn’t work?

Check that your SIM card is installed correctly: it is through the card that your mobile connection provider authorizes you to use their network. It has happened to me that I put the SIM card → in upside down and there was no way to connect or make calls.
Activate mobile data: make sure ‘mobile data’ is active, as well as ‘mobile networks’.
Check signal strength: usually this information is in the ‘mobile networks’ and ‘data usage’ section, or in ‘about phone’ and ‘signal strength’, and you can find them in the device’s settings icon.
Verify network settings: you can check if there is any error in the network configuration; if you don’t understand much, you can call your service provider.
Consult your operator’s coverage maps: you might be in an area where there is no coverage and you will have to configure one of the other internet connection options.
If nothing works, contact your service provider; there might be an error in the configuration.



How to know if you have a satellite signal?
Installing a satellite signal implies that you had to install a software package to be able to operate the connection with your satellite dish → 📡. If your antenna is well installed and pointing toward the satellite, the weather is good and there are no clouds or storms on the way, the router is on, and you have good visibility, you should be able to enjoy a good connection.

What to do if the connection doesn’t work?

Verify the physical condition of the satellite dish: it must be installed correctly, in a place with a clear view of the sky, without obstacles like buildings or trees around.
Verify weather conditions: the presence of clouds or an approaching storm can affect the satellite signal.
Verify the antenna’s orientation toward the satellite: for this, you will need to check the elevation (vertical) and azimuth (horizontal) angles. You will need a compass and an antenna alignment app, as well as a signal meter. You can make progressive adjustments to fine-tune the signal reception.
Verify the router connection: check that it is on, the Ethernet cable is connected correctly to the satellite modem and the router, and that the cable is in good condition.
Verify the signal on your device: some satellite internet systems have signal monitoring software that can provide valuable data to know if it is connected correctly.
Test the speed: you can do a check by consulting “Be an Internet Scientist.”
If nothing works, contact your service provider; there might be an error in the configuration.



How to know if this solution works?
I’ve learned a lot by completing this solution, and I’d love to know if, after reading it and interacting with it, you feel the same way.
I encourage you to keep tinkering (“cacharreando”), and to do it with someone else; it’s always more pleasant, fun, and full of new questions that can lead you to delve deeper into all these topics.
Other possible Internets
Remember that the Internet is for everyone and by everyone; the more we know it, the better we will know how to use it… sending you a hug!

en/solve/solv-usb-internet-router.title: "Is a USB modem the best option for me?"
en/solve/solv-usb-internet-router.summary: "Evaluate if a USB modem is the right solution to get internet on your device."
en/solve/solv-usb-internet-router.content:
Hi there! I’m Catalina, welcome 👋🏽. The first version of this guide was written by my colleague, Nicolás, and I’ve polished it up so we can walk through it together.
Are you wondering if a USB modem is the right way to get your computer online? Let’s figure it out together!
What is a USB modem?
It’s a compact device, shaped like a thumb drive, that lets you insert a SIM card → (just like the one in your phone) to give your computer an Internet connection.
What is it for?
It allows you to get online on devices that don’t have WiFi or a wired (Ethernet) connection by tapping into mobile network signals. Plus, once it’s plugged in, your computer can become a Wi-Fi hotspot →! This means you can share the signal with others, making it a great community or collective alternative to help cut down on costs.
Do I really need one?
Before you go buying anything, take a breather. Is this actually the best move for your situation?

Do you have a stable mobile signal where you are? If the answer is no, this won’t work well.
Does someone in your community already have a device they could lend you or share?
Have you looked at other options? Sometimes, just sharing data from your phone (tethering) is enough without needing to buy extra hardware.
Is the monthly cost of a data plan sustainable for you or your community?

Options to consider





























DeviceWhat it does wellWhat it lacksCan it be shared?USB ModemPortable, direct PC connectionNeeds a stable mobile signalYes, by sharing via PCTetheringFree (uses your own phone)Drains phone batteryYes4G Router with SIMStronger WiFi coverageNeeds a constant power sourceYes, that’s its job
How to do it
If you’ve weighed your options and decided this is what you need, follow these steps:

Step 1 → Choose the carrier with the best signal

Not all carriers have the same strength in every area. Ask your neighbors which network works best for them or run an internet speed test → with different SIM cards if you can get your hands on them.

Step 2 → Get the device

You can look for one directly through your preferred carrier or on online marketplaces like Mercado Libre. Search for “USB WiFi modem.” Make sure the device is “unlocked” so you can switch carriers if the signal is spotty.

Step 3 → Initial setup


Insert the SIM card into the modem.
Plug it into your computer’s USB port.
If the device doesn’t install itself, look for the software that usually pops up in an internal folder when you open the USB drive in your file manager.
Follow the on-screen instructions.

Don’t get fooled
The market often sells these USBs as “unlimited internet.” There is no such thing as truly unlimited plans. Almost always, after you hit a certain amount of gigabytes, your speed will drop drastically. Read the “fine print” of the plan contract before you pay.
How much is enough?
You don’t need top-tier speeds just to browse, look up info, or read the news. If you’re sharing the connection, a moderate plan can go a long way if everyone uses it responsibly.
